Given the important role of network topology and component interactions in cascading failure propagation in power systems, graph-based DRL approaches, including Graph-DQN, Graph-A2C, and Graph-PPO frameworks, are developed to capture and utilize the topological information of power systems. The proposed frameworks are evaluated on the IEEE 39, 57, and 118 bus systems and benchmarked against the unmitigated case, random and heuristic-based switching strategies as baselines, as well as their corresponding graph-agnostic DRL counterparts. The results demonstrate the importance of incorporating graph information into these mitigation frameworks, leading to reduced cascade size, load loss, and network clustering.

title: A Study of Fixed versus Adaptive Step Sizes for Phasor Dynamics Simulations
abstract: Transient phasor dynamics simulations model the response of power systems to disturbances using differential-algebraic equations (DAEs). Fixed-step integration is widely used to solve these DAEs numerically, but a step size suitable for resolving a fault transient may be unnecessarily small during the rest of a simulation. In this work, we provide a quantitative comparison of fixed and adaptive backward differentiation formulas on a suite of seven grid test cases ranging from 200 to 70,000 buses. Adaptive step sizes automatically shrink near faults, perturbations, and controller limits, and grow during less active portions of the simulation. At the global error achieved by a fixed quarter-cycle step size, adaptive results give 1.8 to 2.6 times speedups. Local error distributions, step size profiles, and work-precision plots show how accuracy, nonlinear solver, and step selection contribute to these differences. The results establish adaptive integration as the preferred approach for these simulations.

title: Thermodynamic Degeneracy and Distinct Horizon Geometries of Rotating Kaluza-Klein Black Holes in Independent External Electric and Magnetic Fields
abstract: We construct an exact finite-rotation solution of four-dimensional Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton theory at the Kaluza-Klein coupling, immersed in independent external electric and magnetic fields. Exact algebraic balance identities reveal two distinct regular nonextremal branches with identical horizon area, quasi-local angular momentum, and electromagnetic fluxes. Under a common, explicitly specified reference prescription for the axial clock, rotational frame, and electromagnetic potentials, the two branches also have identical thermodynamic readouts, including energy, temperature, angular velocity, and electric and magnetic potentials. Nevertheless, the two branches possess nonisometric intrinsic horizon geometries, with every positive axisymmetric scalar-Laplacian eigenvalue strictly ordered between them. Thus, identical thermodynamic readouts do not uniquely determine the intrinsic geometry of a black hole horizon. We further establish that the exterior admits consistent asymptotic matching to two distinct exact rotating cylindrical backgrounds associated with its northern and southern polar regions. Their metric, dilaton, and electromagnetic fields become compatible in the angular overlap region, with uniform matching extending to both symmetry axes. Every regular noncritical exterior, including the supercritical branches, is globally hyperbolic.

title: Dynamics of a spinning body with scalar multipoles
abstract: We construct an effective worldline action for a spinning compact object in theories of gravity with massless, non-minimally coupled scalar fields. To this end, we generalize the standard skeletonized approach used in General Relativity to model the stress-energy tensor of a small body in a background spacetime, dressing its multipolar structure with the scalar field. Within a pole-dipole approximation, we derive a modified set of Mathisson-Papapetrou-Dixon equations of motion for the spinning body, together with the field equations for the scalar field and the metric. We consider both parity-even and parity-odd scalars. We tailor this formalism to model the evolution of asymmetric binaries, such as Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals (EMRIs), by systematically expanding the relevant equations in powers of the binary mass ratio and deriving the dynamics up to first post-adiabatic (1PA) order, along with the self-force equations needed to determine the particle's acceleration. For a parity-even scalar, the 1PA dynamics depends only on the mass, spin, and scalar charge of the secondary, plus a single self-coupling constant. For a pseudoscalar, we find that the binary dynamics coincides with General Relativity through 1PA.

title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.

title: When Does Subspace Direction Matter for LoRA? Regime Analysis of the Magnitude Principle in Few-Shot Adaptation
abstract: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $ρ$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.

title: The balance of evidence indicates a slowing AMOC
abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future. The question of whether the AMOC is already weakening is still somewhat controversial. Continuous monitoring is only available for the past two decades, a period too short to tease apart contributions of natural variability and climate change. Reconstructions of AMOC strength going back further in time have different limitations which are debated in the literature. Here we compile and discuss this heterogeneous body of evidence, focusing on latitudes south of 45°N where northward and southward flow are separated vertically. We conclude that the balance of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports a past and ongoing AMOC slowing in response to global warming, although some uncertainty remains regarding its magnitude and timing.

title: Evergreen leaves and universal lifetime laws in preferential-attachment trees
abstract: We study leaf lifetimes in general preferential-attachment trees. First we characterize the existence of evergreen leaves, that is, vertices that remain leaves forever. When no evergreen leaves exist, we establish, for a broad class of attachment functions, a remarkable one-parameter universality: the normalizations and limiting laws for various characteristics of leaf lifetimes depend on the attachment function only through a single numerical parameter. In particular, we obtain a shifted Pareto limit law for individual lifetimes and a joint functional limit theorem for the lifetime and label of the longest-lasting leaf. The limiting two-dimensional process, which we call the beta-decorated Fréchet extremal process, admits an elegant representation in terms of the Stoev--Taqqu extremal integral and the sets of optimal choices considered by Molchanov and Strokorb. We also establish a Poisson point-process limit for rescaled leaf lifetimes and corresponding labels, a finiteness criterion for long-lasting leaves, and a functional central limit theorem for their number at the critical threshold.

title: The Spectral Distribution of Matrix Least Squares Solutions, and the Ellipsoid Fitting Problem
abstract: We study the spectral distribution of the least squares solution to a random linear system whose unknown is a symmetric matrix. In the normalized and isotropic setting, we derive a closed-form description of the support of the spectral distribution. As an application, we consider the ellipsoid fitting problem: given $n$ standard Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, does there exist a centered ellipsoid passing through all of them? It was recently shown that this problem has a sharp phase transition at $n \approx d^2/4$. On the satisfiability side, unlike earlier results, these sharp results do not rely on least squares candidates. We show that the least squares candidates considered in earlier works have a threshold of positive semi-definiteness at $n \approx d^2/10$, which was previously observed numerically and predicted non-rigorously using statistical physics methods. Moreover, we show that the corresponding least squares dual certificates have a threshold of positive definiteness at $n \approx 2d^2/5$. Our approach combines several matrix concentration tools. A key technical ingredient, which may be of independent interest, is showing that a certain kernel matrix is well-conditioned with high probability until $n \approx d^2/2$.

title: Bits, Not Boxes: Label-Free Layer Selection for Visual Localization in VLMs
abstract: Attention maps cheaply show where a vision-language model (VLM) looks, but attention sinks make them unreliable for localization. Contrasting the question with a generic prompt suppresses sinks, yet only some layers localize the queried object. Existing methods find these layers with box annotations or fixed rules. We show that attention itself can identify them. A question changes how much a head attends to the image and where this attention goes. The two effects separate exactly, and the second, measured in bits on unlabeled questions, indicates which layers localize. WhereBits turns these where-to-look bits into a layer prior and combines it with per-head contrastive scores. Its three design constants were fixed once on labeled COCO data, and a new model or resolution needs only unlabeled questions. Across eight VLMs, WhereBits matches the pointing accuracy of box-tuned layers on COCO and RefCOCO and ranks target tokens better. This advantage holds on a held-out model family and at higher resolutions. Its COCO pointing accuracy is 0.72, against 0.22 for mean attention. In training-free zoom-in, its crops raise V* accuracy by 6.0 points under forced-choice evaluation.

title: The Chaotic Dynamics of Coupled Maps with Convection and Diffusion
abstract: We explore the fundamental role of convective and diffusive coupling on the spatiotemporal chaos of a large one-dimensional lattice of coupled maps on a ring. Extensively chaotic dynamics persist over nearly the entire range of spatial coupling strengths that yield numerically stable dynamics. The spatial coupling affects the shape of the spectrum of Lyapunov exponents, for increasing convective coupling the leading Lyapunov exponents increase while the large negative Lyapunov exponents decrease resulting in a significant increase in the fractal dimension of the dynamics. Convective coupling increases the localization of the leading Lyapunov vector and adds significant power to the high-wavenumber components of the spectrum of covariant Lyapunov vectors while increasing their entanglement. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the diffusive coupling matrix remain insightful quantities in the presence of nonlinear convective coupling. We discuss the implications of these findings for high-dimensional chaotic dynamics of large transport systems.

title: Replicating chaotic dynamics from sparse sensors with recurrent latent states
abstract: Forecasting a high-dimensional nonlinear system from a few point sensors requires an estimate of the current state and a model of its evolution. Reduced-order models usually take the full state as input, so with only sparse sensors they require an auxiliary full-state estimate whose error is inherited by the latent representation. We instead build the latent state from sensor measurements alone, using a shallow recurrent decoder (SHRED) network that encodes a history of point measurements, and train an echo state network to advance that latent state autonomously. We show that the resulting latent dynamics replicate the long-term dynamical invariants of the underlying system rather than merely tracking its short-term trajectory. For the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, the autonomous latent model reproduces the leading Lyapunov exponents of the full system from 25 of 128 state components, using a latent state with 6-14% as many components as the full state. Because Lyapunov exponents are invariant under smooth coordinate changes, this is consistent with the recurrent encoder recovering an embedding of the attractor, in the spirit of Takens' delay embedding theorem. The recurrent encoding also decouples forecast skill from reconstruction accuracy. SHRED reconstructs less accurately than a convolutional autoencoder given the full state, yet it forecasts comparably on the simpler chaotic case and better on the more complex one. For Kolmogorov flow, with sensors at 6% of grid points and a latent state 0.3% the size of the vorticity field, the autonomous model remains on the learned latent manifold over long horizons.

title: Efficient interlayer interactions in non-planar molecule/transition-metal dichalcogenide two-dimensional heterostructure
abstract: Integration of molecules and two-dimensional (2D) atomic materials offer new opportunities for hybrid electronic devices. Most progress has focused on interfacing planar molecule. In contrast, incorporating non-planar molecules into 2D heterostructures remains challenging due to the three-dimensional orientations of ligands. Here we investigate interlayer interactions between discrete non-planar spin-crossover (SCO) molecules, [Fe(tBu2qsal)2] (FTBQS), monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) spacers through optical spectroscopies. FTBQS features bulk molecular crystal layers and can be mechanically exfoliated, enabling deterministic assembly of clean hybrid heterostructures. Robust photoluminescence (PL) quenching, even with an hBN spacer, indicates efficient Förster resonance energy transfer with a long decay distance. Gate-dependent optical spectroscopy further identifies charge transfer from the doping shifts in the TMD layers due to the TMD/FTBQS electronic band alignment. Our results establish efficient interlayer interactions between non-plana, discrete molecules and 2D crystals for hybrid electrical, optical, and spintronic devices.

title: How to Receive Focused Beams in Near-Field MIMO? Analytical Combiners and Array Size Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates receive combining for near-field beamfocusing in line-of-sight channels with antenna array misalignment. We propose and evaluate two analytical combiners: analog ANF-AC and digital ANF-DC. Beyond focusing the beam toward the transmitter, ANF-AC benefits from the proposed phase-flip corrections (PFCs), while ANF-DC additionally exploits Dirichlet-kernel-based amplitude tapering. ANF-AC closely matches theoretically optimal analog equal-gain combining (EGC), with an SNR gap below 0.006 dB. Similarly, ANF-DC matches optimal digital maximum-ratio combining (MRC). We then leverage the analytical properties of these combiners for link-level evaluation and optimization, deriving a closed-form expression for the optimal transmitter-receiver array-size trade-off that maximizes received SNR with analog combining. We also show that the optimized analog receiver performs within 0.84 dB of its fully digital MRC-equivalent counterpart. These results demonstrate that optimized analog combining (with potentially lower implementation complexity and cost, particularly at higher frequencies) can get close to the fully digital performance. Beyond the theoretical insights presented, the analytical tractability and EGC-like / MRC-like performance of our combiners enable accurate network-level mathematical studies of beamfocusing, such as coverage, capacity, and interference analysis and optimization toward efficient 6G+ near-field MIMO communication systems.

title: Symmetries of symplectic Khovanov-Rozansky homology
abstract: We study the behavior of Manolescu's construction of symplectic Khovanov-Rozansky homology under symmetries. Specifically, for k<n we construct a localization spectral sequence from the symplectic sl(n) homology of a knot to the direct sum of the symplectic sl(k) and sl(n-k) homologies of the same knot, giving a geometric analog of rank-reducing spectral sequences arising from deformations on the non-symplectic theory. We also prove the existence of a localization spectral sequence relating the symplectic Khovanov--Rozansky homology of a two-periodic link to the symplectic Khovanov-Rozansky homology of the quotient link, in analogy to a theorem of Seidel and Smith for symplectic Khovanov homology. The proofs rely on a generalization of the localization theorem of Seidel-Smith and Large for equivariant Lagrangian Floer cohomology with respect to order two actions; in particular, we extend the theory to the case that the fixed set of the action carries a stable normal real polarization.

title: Plausibly Exogenous Instruments in Probit Models: Sensitivity Bounds for Average Partial and Interaction Effects
abstract: Sensitivity analysis for imperfect instruments usually targets a linear two-stage least squares coefficient, yet many applications have binary outcomes and probability-scale targets. We extend the plausibly exogenous framework to the control-function probit, targeting average partial and interaction effects. We derive the generated-regressor variance, union and local-to-zero intervals, and their asymptotic coverage under stated model and calibration conditions. A violation stated on the wrong latent scale can miscalibrate the interval by a factor set by the endogeneity correlation. Applications to Catholic schooling, sibling sex composition and Confucian clans compare probit and linear analyses. Stata and R implementations accompany the analysis.

title: Minimax estimation for simultaneous deconvolution model in random design using wavelets
abstract: Simultaneous deconvolution model is investigated when the design points are random and follow bounded densities and errors are either $i.i.d.$ or long-memory dependent. We propose wavelet hard-thresholding estimators, and show that they achieve asymptotically near-optimal convergence rates for the $L^2$-risk when the response function belongs to Besov space under both $i.i.d.$ errors and homoskedastic, long-memory errors. However, under heteroskedastic, long-memory errors the estimator is not optimal. For the $i.i.d.$ errors, the convergence rates are {identical} to those found in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design {and $i.i.d.$ errors}. However, for long-memory dependent errors, the convergence rates are new {and completely different from those in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design and long-memory errors}.

title: Conformally Calibrated Adaptive Computation in Neural Operators
abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.

title: Hebbian self-organization of monosynaptic reflexes in a biologically realistic multiarticular limb
abstract: Spinal monosynaptic reflexes depend on patterns of connectivity between muscle spindle afferents and motoneurons that should reflect musculoskeletal dynamics. One possibility is that the details of these circuits are specified genetically, but this requires an unlikely coevolution of musculoskeletal and neural elements. Here we show how biomechanical structure can determine the connectivity of self-organized spinal circuits. Using a neuromechanical model combining a multi-joint limb, proprioceptive feedback, and Hebbian plasticity driven by motor babbling, we find that biologically realistic connectivity emerges spontaneously when babbling is neither too sparse nor too frequent. This results in strong homonymous projections, weaker heteronymous projections among functional synergists, and very weak connections among antagonists. This outcome also depends on musculoskeletal morphometry. Heteronymous synergies form when proximal muscles are strongest---the characteristic gradient of mammalian limbs--whereas excessively strong biarticular muscles lead to unphysiological antagonist coupling. The mechanisms differ: homonymous connections arise from direct sensorimotor correlation during fusimotor coactivation by beta motoneurons, while heteronymous connections depend on multi-joint dynamics that emerge only after homonymous reflexes stabilize and increasing muscle strength generates multisegmental motion. Overall, this study provides a mechanistic basis for fetal sensorimotor development and generates testable predictions about the consequences of naturally occurring and experimentally induced variations.

title: TransFIRA+: Transfer Learning for Biometric Recognizability Assessment
abstract: Biometric recognition in surveillance, video, and web imagery must contend with extreme variation in pose, blur, illumination, occlusion, and distance, where visual quality metrics fail to predict whether inputs are recognizable to the deployed encoder. Existing face image quality assessment methods rely on visual heuristics, curated annotations, or costly generative pipelines, leaving their predictions detached from the encoder's decision geometry. We introduce TransFIRA, a lightweight framework that grounds recognizability directly in embedding space. TransFIRA derives class-center similarity (CCS) and class-center angular separation (CCAS) from a pretrained encoder's embeddings and learns to predict them from images without quality annotations. Using predicted CCS for template weighting and CCAS>0 as a natural filtering threshold yields state-of-the-art face verification performance on BRIAR, raising TAR at $10^{-6}$ FMR from 0.085 with uniform averaging to 0.598. The predicted scores also reveal how image degradations affect encoder-specific recognizability. TransFIRA+ extends this framework to cross-camera multimodal person identification in untrimmed surveillance video. In this setting, body recognizability scores saturate within a narrow range, making direct weighting effectively uniform. We introduce a post-hoc sigmoid calibration that transforms these saturated scores into informative weights without retraining. After calibration, the BRIAR-trained TransFIRA predictor improves fused face and body identification on two unseen multi-camera datasets, outperforming detector-confidence weighting and uncalibrated CCS-rank weighting. Together, TransFIRA and TransFIRA+ demonstrate that encoder-grounded recognizability generalizes across biometric modalities and recognition settings.

title: RummiAlgebra: A Polynomial Representation Framework for Game-Based Algebra Learning with Jokers
abstract: Connecting symbolic expressions to manipulable objects is a recurring challenge in introductory algebra. This paper presents RummiAlgebra, a design-oriented framework and browser-based prototype that maps a Rummikub-style tile-rearrangement task to polynomial addition, common-factor extraction, finite geometric sums, and context-dependent substitution. A numbered colored tile is encoded as a monomial c x^v, while a physical joker is represented by a distinct symbol J_i whose algebraic role is fixed only for a particular candidate arrangement. We define admissible polynomial forms for runs and groups and establish an inventory-conservation invariant. A soundness-and-completeness proof shows that physical-tile accounting together with the algebraic run/group templates characterizes valid final arrangements under the stated classroom rules; polynomial equality alone is insufficient. Four detailed examples illustrate decomposition, competing factorizations, one- and two-joker substitutions, and optimization as an optional extension. A targeted review distinguishes the approach from established Rummikub solvers, Rummikub-inspired arithmetic-sequence activities, algebra-tile manipulatives, and polynomial games. The prototype implements six small challenges and a separate rule-and-expression checker; their optimal scores were checked against an independent exhaustive reference enumerator. These checks establish agreement for the examples but do not establish learning effectiveness or novelty of the underlying algebraic operations. We close with a classroom sequence, assessment constructs, and a controlled evaluation protocol. The claimed contribution is a formally specified pedagogical correspondence and an interactive proof-oriented activity, not a new asymptotically faster Rummikub solver.

title: Gaussian Splatoms: Direct Atomic Structure Identification in Electron Tomography
abstract: Atomic electron tomography (AET) computationally reconstructs the 3D atomic structure of materials from a series of 2D projection measurements acquired at different tilt angles. Inspired by Gaussian splatting techniques from computer vision, we introduce an atom-centric parameterization for modeling AET samples. Instead of a conventional volumetric representation with a grid of voxels, we model the sample as a list of atoms, where each atom is a 3D Gaussian characterized by learned location, scale, and amplitude. The Gaussian model is a natural fit for atoms that allows us to easily incorporate prior information grounded in physics; we impose isotropy of atoms, a minimum interatomic distance, and realistic atomic radii. We show in simulation that our method is more robust than volumetric baselines to real-world imaging challenges, including a limited number of measurements and low electron dose. We further show that our method yields a more physically plausible reconstruction of an experimental 23,000 atom iron-platinum nanoparticle than a previously published volumetric reconstruction. Beyond tomography, our representation is a promising tool for any atomic resolution imaging modality (e.g. multislice electron ptychography).

title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

title: Mining the time axis with TRON. IV. MeerKAT detects a radio burst from a nearby M~dwarf
abstract: We report the detection of a minute-timescale, highly circularly polarised ($\sim100\%$) radio burst from an active M dwarf (spectral type M1Ve), PM J14111$-$6155, located 19.6 pc from the Sun. Identified in the 1.28 GHz SMGPS using 8-second integrations from the TRON-pipeline, the burst peaked at 7.7 mJy. Visibility-based dynamic spectra reveal a drifting, band-limited emission feature ($\sim$300 MHz FWHM) with a maximum cut-off near 1.65 GHz, associated with electron cyclotron maser instability (ECMI), implying the existence of large-scale magnetic topologies ($B_* \approx 0.59$ kG). A non-detection ($3σ$ upper limit) four hours later points to intermittent or rotationally modulated beamed emission. An analysis of both TESS and ground-based survey data failed to recover an unambiguous rotational period for the optical counterpart. Follow-up SALT spectroscopy confirms its active chromospheric state, exhibiting prominent emission in the Ca {\sc ii} infrared triplet, Balmer lines, and persistent double-peaked H$α$ emission ($44.6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ peak separation) attributable to optically thick self-absorption. This discovery demonstrates that the coordinated use of time-series optical photometry, high-resolution spectroscopy, and high-cadence spectropolarimetric radio imaging enables direct probing of coherent radio emission from the magnetically active atmospheres of nearby M dwarfs.

title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
abstract: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.

title: Dynamic Vacuum Energy in Weyl Integrable Spacetime Part I: Implications for Inflationary Cosmology
abstract: We explore a dynamic vacuum energy scenario within the Weyl Integrable Spacetime (WIS) framework and provide the Friedmann--Lemaître (FL) cosmology equations under a metric endowed with a lapse function. We pay particular attention to the implications of inflationary dynamics. We show that the explicit vacuum decay source cancels in the FL acceleration equation, where the Hubble slow-roll parameter is controlled by the non-vacuum sector alone, while the dynamic vacuum defined in proper time $Λ(τ)$ itself continues to enter the observables through the expansion rate. We identify the warm inflation (WI) dissipation coefficient with one half of the logarithmic decay rate of the vacuum energy, $Υ=-\tfrac{1}{2} d\lnΛ/dτ$, hence the phenomenological friction coefficient is tied to the vacuum sector rather than computed from explicit inflaton--bath microphysics. Notably, we show that the dissipation ratio $(Q)$ is not a free parameter: the cosmological constant hierarchy constrains it through $Q N_{e,\mathrm I}\simeq46$, where $N_{e,\mathrm I}$ is the total number of e-folds of expansion during vacuum decay. For a moderate pre-observable transient, this robustly gives $Q=\mathcal O(1)$. The graceful exit and the observable parameters are obtained and are in line with cosmological observations. These results indicate that our model is viable and provide a well-posed starting point for a subsequent numerical analysis.

title: NIRJALA: Draining the Sea out of Gaussian Splatting with Three-Path Optics and Reversible Physics
abstract: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, backscattered light, and scene light scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present NIRJALA (Sanskrit for "without water"), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model, adds a range-saturating forward-scattering term to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and bound how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor, ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both directions, so scene content cannot hide inside the water. SAMARASA collects the physics-informed objectives, including a range-binned colour prior. To score water removal against ground truth, we built SAJALA ("with water"), a 30-scene suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44 FPS. We also discuss where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and the limits of our evaluation.

title: Finite regularity moduli stacks through diffeology
abstract: Diffeological non-Abelian Hodge theory motivates the study of $C^r$ families of Higgs bundles and flat bundles for finite $r$. In this article, we provide a uniform language for treating moduli stacks parametrizing such objects in terms of diffeology. More specifically, we develop a theory of stacks presentable by diffeological groupoids over the site of $C^r$ manifolds for arbitrary $r$. As an application, we construct moduli stacks over the sites of $C^r$ manifolds parametrizing $C^r$ vector bundles over a smooth manifold, and $C^r$ families of Higgs bundles and of flat bundles over a complex manifold. We also construct $C^r$ versions of the non-Abelian Hodge filtration stack, interpolating between Higgs bundles and flat bundles through $λ$--connections. We show that all these stacks are presentable by diffeological groupoids. Finally, we construct moduli stacks parametrizing $C^r$ families of $Δ^n$--shaped diagrams of these objects, and show that they assemble into simplicial stacks whose levels are all presentable by diffeological groupoids.

title: Probing horizonless compact objects through observable signatures and images of accretion disk
abstract: The observed images of M87$^*$ and Sgr A$^*$ by Event Horizon Telescope motivate us to study the spacetime geometry and accretion flow dynamics around compact objects beyond the Kerr/Schwarzschild scenario. In this work, we investigate the properties of a steady, inviscid, axisymmetric, advective accretion flow around the Zipoy-Voorhees ($γ$-metric) spacetime by solving the relativistic hydrodynamic equations. The $γ$-metric is a static, axisymmetric generalization of the Schwarzschild geometry and is characterized by a mass ($M_\bullet$) and a deformation parameter ($γ$). We examine how the deformation parameter $γ$ influences the effective potential, the location and nature of the critical points, and the resulting accretion flow topologies. Then, using relativistic thermal bremsstrahlung emissivity, we compute the spectral energy distribution and bolometric luminosity of the flow. We find that $γ$ affects the luminosity in opposite ways for the flow having outer critical point (O-type) and that having inner critical point (I-type). Finally, combining the flow properties with general relativistic ray tracing, we construct synthetic images of the accretion disk for different values of $γ$ and observer inclination angles. The resulting observed flux distribution independently confirms the trends obtained from the luminosity and spectral analyses. Although the shadow of the $γ$-metric has been shown to be consistent with the observed shadow radii of M87$^*$ and Sgr A$^*$, its accretion flow topology, the resulting radiative properties and image differ from the Schwarzschild case, thereby giving a complementary way to probe the deviations from the Schwarzschild paradigm.

title: Folded out-of-time-order correlators in double-scaled SYK
abstract: Harlow and Zhao arXiv:2607.14215 have identified ``anti-scrambling'' as a characteristic signature of cosmological horizons in de Sitter space, and proposed that it can be realized in a quantum system with bounded energy by Euclidean time ``folding" of out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs). We implement this prescription in the DSSYK model. We use arXiv:2303.03474 to define an infinite-temperature ($β=0$) DSSYK OTOC that in the semiclassical limit of small values of the double-scaling parameter $λ$ reproduces the usual AdS eikonal shockwave behavior with its characteristic time delay, and then apply the Harlow-Zhao fold with the ``fake'' DSSYK inverse temperature $β_f$ playing the role of $β$. We demonstrate both numerically and analytically that the resulting folded OTOC displays anti-scrambling. The exact DSSYK evaluation tracks the semiclassical de Sitter eikonal formula in the scrambling regime, including a time advance instead of a time delay.The direction of the fold selects the side from which the continued eikonal amplitude approaches its branch cut. We show how our results are consistent with recent ``no-go" constraints. We compare the folded correlator with the two-shell analysis of arXiv:2607.14215: the growing term of the two-shell dilaton invariant appears in DSSYK with the same exponent, but as an imaginary part, while its real part, which would signal the backreaction that ends in a crunch, only moves by $O(λ)$ for thermal-scale probes. We also generalize to finite $β$; we find reasonable agreement with the de Sitter eikonal form for sufficiently high temperatures, but at lower temperatures the folded correlator is dominated by a pair of complex conjugate saddles, an anti-Stokes crossover that prevents retrieval of the eikonal behavior from the folded OTOC.

title: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
abstract: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.

title: Maximising the Open Magnetic Flux of a Star
abstract: We consider how to distribute the magnetic flux on a star's surface in order to maximise the proportion of open magnetic flux predicted by the potential field source surface model. The proportion of open flux is shown to be maximised by concentrating all of the positive and negative flux at antipodal points. For a typical source surface height, this enhances the open flux by 35% compared to a dipolar distribution. Even if the flux is spread over finite polar caps -- as on the Sun around Solar Minimum -- the open flux is still substantially enhanced compared to the dipole. Nevertheless, we show that the dipole approximation over-estimates the open flux for this kind of flux distribution.

title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

title: The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter of the ePIC detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
authors: for the ePIC Barrel Imaging Calorimeter
abstract: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is a next-generation facility expected to address fundamental open questions in nuclear physics, including the structure and dynamics of gluons in nucleons and nuclei. The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter (BIC) is the electromagnetic calorimeter of the ePIC detector, designed to meet the stringent performance requirements of the EIC, providing precise measurements and particle identification of scattered electrons, photons, and neutral mesons. The BIC is a high-granularity sampling calorimeter based on lead absorbers interleaved with scintillating fibers, complemented by pixelated imaging layers based on the AstroPix monolithic active pixel sensor. This hybrid design enables both accurate energy and position measurements, as well as three-dimensional shower reconstruction, making it a key component for realizing the full physics potential of the EIC. The BIC has successfully completed its Preliminary Design Review last year and is currently progressing toward the Final Design Review. In this talk, I will present an overview of the BIC concept and focus on its current status and performance results from bench tests, system integration studies, and recent beam tests.

title: On the local boundedness of weak solutions to doubly nonlinear equations with variable exponents
abstract: We establish local boundedness, together with quantitative estimates, for non-negative weak sub-solutions to a class of doubly nonlinear parabolic equations whose prototype is \[ (u^q)_t-\operatorname{div} \Big(|Du|^{p(x,t)-2}Du\Big)=0, \qquad p(x,t)>1,\quad q>0. \] The results are obtained under a logarithmic continuity condition on the variable exponent $p(x,t)$ and suitable relations between $q$ and the local bounds of $p(x,t)$. In certain ranges of the exponents, an additional local integrability assumption is required.

title: Wasserstein Target Diagram for Model Evaluation
abstract: The target diagram is often used in geosciences, which provides a visualization tool for model evaluation and shows the temporal or spatial matching of data. However, its construction requires paired data of equal sample sizes, limiting its application to model comparisons involving unpaired samples or probability distributions. In this study, we propose the Wasserstein target diagram based on the 2-Wasserstein distance from optimal transport. Unlike the original target diagram, the Wasserstein target diagram does not require paired data of equal sizes and evaluates models from the probability distribution perspective. We further establish that the two target diagrams coincide when the given paired data are comonotone, which is common in climate science, such as cumulative precipitation and solar radiation. Through two simulation studies and an application to wind speed distribution fitting, we demonstrate that the proposed diagram can detect the probability distribution discrepancies that the original target diagram may not distinguish. The Wasserstein target diagram therefore lifts the model evaluation to the probability level and provides a complementary approach to estimating the agreement in probability distributions.

title: Antidirected paths on five vertices in 5-chromatic digraphs
abstract: We prove that every 5-chromatic digraph containing no copy of the regular tournament on five vertices contains both antidirected paths on five vertices. This answers a question posed by El Sahili in 2004. The proof uses an edge bound for 5-critical graphs to constrain the out-degrees in a counterexample and obtain a contradiction by constructing a proper 4-colouring.

title: Beyond Area: Perimeter Optimization in the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Problem
abstract: The planar Skorokhod embedding problem asks for a simply connected planar domain whose Brownian exit distribution has a prescribed real marginal $μ$. We investigate the minimization of conformal perimeter over the class of all such embeddings. We first establish the main existence theorem showing that whenever a finite-perimeter embedding exists, the infimum is attained (and vice versa). We derive necessary conditions for finiteness and sufficient conditions based on logarithmic integrability of the density. In particular, we demonstrate that finite area does not guarantee the existence of an embedding with finite perimeter. Although Gross's canonical embedding minimizes area, we construct an explicit family of domains for which Brownian symmetrization strictly increases perimeter, disproving its universal perimeter minimality. On the positive side, using Pruss's containment theorem and inequalities from convex geometry, we establish a general lower bound in terms of the convex hull of the Gross domain. Consequently, whenever the Gross embedding is bounded and convex, it is the unique perimeter minimizer. Finally, we formulate an open problem concerning the relationship between the existence of finite-perimeter embeddings and the regularity of Gross's canonical embedding.

title: Quantum Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport in spacetime through spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac distributions and spatiotemporal states
abstract: Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport is a mathematical framework that determines the most efficient way to transform one probability distribution into another while minimizing a given cost function. Its central constructions include the Wasserstein distances, which quantify the space of probability distributions, and dual formulations that link to convex analysis. Its standard quantum generalization replaces probability distributions with density operators and cost function with positive semidefinite cost operator, which should be regarded as spatial quantum optimal transport. In this work, we propose the quantum optimal transport problem in spacetime through the spatiotemporal phase-space Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution and spatiotemporal states and through spatiotemporal state. We show that the two formalisms are equivalent and related via spatiotemporal operator frames. In the Kirkwood-Dirac phase-space formalism, the spatiotemporal distribution and the cost function are complex-valued, and the spatiotemporal couplings are Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions that yield the correct marginals for the local states. In the spatiotemporal state formalism, the cost operators are generally non-Hermitian, and the spatiotemporal couplings are generally non-Hermitian and yield the correct reduced local states. The Margenau-Hill phase-space distribution gives rise to a real-valued optimal transport in spatiotemporal phase space; in the spatiotemporal state formalism, this corresponds to a Hermitian spatiotemporal coupling state. We give a rigorous definitions and a careful discussion of its duality. We also introduce a spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein metric based on a metric in spatiotemporal phase spaces and show that it satisfies the metric axioms.

title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.

title: Minimal super dominating sets of maximum cardinality
abstract: Let $G = (V,E)$ be a graph. A subset $S \subseteq V$ of vertices is a super dominating set if every vertex $v \in V - S$ has a neighbour $u \in S$, whose only neighbour in $V - S$ is $v$. A set $S \subseteq V$ is called open irredundant if every vertex $u \in S$ has at least one neighbour $v \in V - S$ whose only neighbour in $S$ is $u$. In this paper we establish connections between super dominating sets and open irredundant sets, similar to the connections that exist between dominating sets and irredundant sets. In particular, we define the new parameter $Γ_{sp}(G)$ as the maximum cardinality of a minimal super dominating set of $G$ and calculate $Γ_{sp}(G)$ for some families of graphs $G$. Finally we present some properties of open irredundant sets and we will develop Gallai theorems involving domination, super domination and open irredundance parameters of graphs.

title: On counting integer symmetric matrices of fixed determinant in families of slant boxes
abstract: In this article, we develop an upper bound for the number of integral symmetric matrices of fixed determinant in a slant box with coefficients bounded by some given power of the volume of the slant box. We develop a counting method that expands on Shankar-Siad-Swaminathan's work on rank-3 integer symmetric matrices of fixed determinant to higher-rank matrices using geometry-of-numbers methods and invariant theory on the splitting of quadratic forms associated with the determinant formula into corresponding linear forms. We expect this generalization will allow us to apply the counting results to arithmetic statistics frameworks. In forthcoming work, we will apply the counting results to study the distribution of 2-torsion subgroups of class groups of unit-monogenised number fields.

title: Sub-Doppler Cooling of Potassium-41 in a Hybrid Quadrupole-Octupole Symmetry Magneto-Optical Trap
abstract: Sub-Doppler cooling processes rely on the near-degeneracy of the Zeeman sub-levels of the atom. Effective sub-Doppler cooling is only achieved when the ac-Stark shift of the molasses light is significantly larger than the Zeeman shift. This condition is typically achieved by switching off all magnetic gradients, and using Helmholtz coils to cancel Earth's magnetic field. Another way to achieve a nearly zero magnetic field gradient is to superimpose a second pair of oppositely oriented quadrupole coils with a different spatial geometry. At the ideal current ratio, this creates an octupole-symmetry magnetic field for the atoms. The resulting octupole magnetic field has a gradient increasing quadratically from zero at the center. In this work, the effectiveness of sub-Doppler cooling and trapping using D2 and D1 light is evaluated in such a hybrid trap for $^{41}$K. The temperature, lifetime, and phase-space density of the atoms are measured. For both D2 and D1 light, the octupole MOT is found to have a longer lifetime, while maintaining a similar temperature to the zero-field case. D1 gray-molasses temperatures down to $3.8(1)~μ$K and phase-space density up to $5.3(4)\times10^{-5}$ are measured for $14.3(1)\times10^6$ $^{41}$ atoms. The effectiveness of the hybrid quadrupole-octupole trap suggests the possibility of increasing the loading time for atoms into an optical dipole trap with active sub-Doppler cooling.

title: Laplace Bayesian transport maps for generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields
abstract: Transport maps provide a powerful framework for the generative modeling of complex, non-Gaussian spatial fields, such as those encountered in climate science. By mapping a complicated target distribution to a standard Gaussian reference distribution, they can serve as efficient stochastic surrogates. However, current Bayesian transport maps, which are modeled using autoregressive Gaussian processes, typically rely on empirical Bayes estimates that ignore hyperparameter uncertainty. Here, we contrast this point-estimate approach with a fully Bayesian model that provides posterior uncertainty quantification in transport map hyperparameters. To avoid the high cost of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), we also propose a Laplace approximation to the hyperparameter posteriors, which can be computed at negligible additional computational cost relative to empirical Bayes. We provide numerical evidence and a real-data climate application demonstrating that these Laplace approximations can accurately capture most posterior summaries at a fraction of the cost of MCMC, while maintaining good predictive properties. Thus, our approach offers a scalable, uncertainty-aware framework for the generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields.

title: Galilean invariance of Hamiltonian guiding center theory
abstract: Galilean invariance is a desired property for classical non-relativistic theories. Guiding center theory describes the slow drift motion of charged particles in strong magnetic fields. While one can guarantee a Hamiltonian formulation to all orders, it was previously unknown whether such a theory can possess Galilean symmetry. We show that specific first- and second-order guiding center models are Galilean invariant. Furthermore, we prove that one can ensure Galilean invariance to all orders.

title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
abstract: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.

title: An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion
abstract: The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars. This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution (CEE), when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag. However, this inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly. Here, we present observations of AT 2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy, that originates from the CEE of a ~7M$_{\odot}$ asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with its companion. Extensive pre- and post-eruption spectroscopy is best explained as a ~0.7M$_{\odot}$ companion inspiraling within the convective AGB envelope that powers a seven year period of gradual brightening - the first direct observations of frictional drag energy dissipation induced by CEE. The subsequent merger of the companion with the primary core within a few (<10) orbits powers the ejection of the outermost ~10% of the stellar envelope at speeds ~10x the primary escape speed, and empirically constrains the fraction of dissipated orbital energy available to unbind the convective common envelope, $0.01\lesssim α\lesssim 0.4$. This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys.

title: Interference-Aware Tone Selection for Bluetooth Channel Sounding
abstract: Bluetooth Channel Sounding enables distance estimation using phase measurements across multiple frequencies. However, coexistence with Wi-Fi and other 2.4 GHz radios can fragment the available frequency band, making reliable ranging difficult when only a limited number of tones can be selected. Drawing on sparse antenna-array theory, we show that interference avoidance alone is insufficient: the spacing of selected tones can introduce repeated peaks in the ranging response, leading to estimation errors. We propose a lightweight, interference-aware tone-selection method that jointly considers frequency occupancy, tone spacing, and frequency span. Our method constructs a 15-tone map using a three-step rule without ranging measurements, ground-truth distance, or online candidate-map search. We evaluate the method using simulations of 900 indoor environments, a public Bluetooth Channel Sounding dataset, and measurements from commercial Nordic nRF54L15 hardware. Compared with random interference avoiding baseline, our proposed method improves ranging success percentage by 39 points under mixed interference, 29 points on the public dataset, and 82 points in hardware experiments. These results demonstrate the importance of tone selection for practical Bluetooth Channel Sounding.

title: A Graph-Theoretic Framework for Identifying Mathematical Programming Decompositions
abstract: We develop a framework for identifying combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints that can be used to formulate mathematical programming decompositions. A mathematical program is represented by a graph which accounts for the structural and functional relationship between variables and constraints. Graph projections are used to focus on variable- or constraint-based decompositions. A series of coarsening operations is used to generate a reduced graph based on the original or projected graph. On the reduced graph, we use integer programming to identify different combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints. Specifically, variables and constraints are identified as complicating based on their structural role and/or their functionality (contribution to nonlinearity) in the mathematical program. The framework allows us to assess the viability of different decomposition types (variable, constraint, cross) and identify multiple potential decomposition formulations of the same type (e.g. different combinations of complicating variables for Benders decomposition). The systematic nature of our framework facilitates broader studies into the efficacy of different decompositions across a range of problems including energy markets, process design, and machine learning.

title: Reliability by Architecture: Agentic Workflows for Validated Multi-Physics Simulation from Natural Language
abstract: Preparing, executing, and validating strongly coupled multi-physics simulations require expert time. Agentic workflows use large language models (LLMs) to coordinate them from natural-language descriptions, but reliability requires checks of physical consistency and fidelity to the problem description. Our agentic harness implements explicit task allocation: LLMs interpret user requests and simulator diagnostics, generate input components not covered by predefined construction rules, and propose repairs, while deterministic routines construct supported components and check inputs, edits, and results. We evaluate CO2-storage problems using the multi-physics simulator GEOS, from compositional flow to flow-poromechanics with frictional fault contact. In 80 attempts on two flow problems, grounding raises the proportion of structurally valid inputs from 5/20 to 20/20, but acceptance reaches 20/20 only with complete rule-based input preparation. With identical inputs, local repairs correct three seeded defects while preserving valid inputs. Supporting tests identify simulations passing physics checks despite differing from the problem description or reference results.

title: AllotNet: an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Choice Model for Moral Judgement in Humanitarian Aid Allocation, Validated against a Planted Synthetic Population
abstract: Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, and the decision of who is helped first when there is not enough for everyone is moving into software. A leading published machine-learning targeting system excluded 53 per cent of eligible households as deployed. If the rule of distribution ends up in code, it should carry the judgement of many cultures, and the machine should execute while a person judges. AllotNet is an interpretable mixture-of-experts conditional logit for the allocation judgements elicited by Allot, a pre-registered six-language instrument: eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria, weighted by a gate over participant context, with a damped residual, an encoder for household intake, an outcome head and a budget-constrained planner that builds a review queue and never rejects anyone. A model of human judgement has no answer key on real data, so we wrote one first: a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions and 104 million responses (98 million usable choices), generated by the production code path from a ground truth hidden from the loss. All sixteen pre-specified checks passed: criterion ranking $ρ= 1.000$, hidden segments recovered (ARI 0.671), outcome head at 99 per cent of the noise ceiling, planner at 99.4 per cent of oracle. The caveats are reported with them: two checks are weaker than their titles, and a live-generation failure cost 260,712 seeds. The model has 23,550 parameters, is trained quantisation-aware for NVFP4 with its interpretable core in fp32 (welfare-rank parity $ρ= 0.9937$ at W4A16 on the shipped bundle; one parity threshold was relaxed post hoc), and ships as a 125 KB bundle with C11, Java, Rust and Python runtimes. Nothing has been trained on real data yet; at the study's real scale a hierarchical Bayesian mixed logit is the registered comparator.

title: Formalizing local gauge freedom via bi-equivariant groupoid algebras
abstract: Gauge degrees of freedom appear in many different contexts. Here, we describe their emergence in the context of architected metamaterials built from self-coupling blocks with internal symmetries. Quantifying the dynamics requires choices of local frames and the many available options constitute the local gauge degrees of freedom of the problem. In the absence of internal symmetries, the dynamical matrices generating the dynamics are all built from the left regular representation of a groupoid C*-algebra canonically associated to the architecture. If the resonators display internal symmetries, we show that the mentioned groupoid C*-algebra accepts a natural 2-action by the group of internal symmetries and that the local gauge freedom can be encoded in a bi-equivariant sub-groupoid algebra generated from the mentioned 2-action. The latter is shown to be the smallest C*-algebra containing all dynamical matrices that can be engineered in a laboratory, for a given architecture and discrete group of internal symmetries.

title: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

title: mmTherm: Absolute 3D Human Pose Estimation from Low-Resolution Thermal Images and mmWave Radar
abstract: Absolute 3D human pose estimation (HPE) aims to recover both a person's body pose and their global position in 3D space. Privacy-preserving millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides distance and direction measurement capabilities, but its sparse point clouds make HPE under-constrained. Low-resolution thermal imaging can provide complementary observations of body direction and structure. However, our evaluation shows that a strong feature-level fusion baseline loses much of its localization and HPE advantage when generalizing to unseen subjects, with radial localization becoming less accurate than a radar-only baseline. Motivated by this finding, we introduce mmTherm, a lightweight framework that explicitly incorporates the complementary geometric properties of thermal imaging and mmWave radar. It combines body structure and joint directions estimated from thermal images with range information from radar to localize the body and reconstruct its 3D pose. Experiments on OctoNet show that mmTherm reduces cross-user absolute joint error by 33% and root localization error by 38% relative to the strongest corresponding baselines, while requiring substantially fewer parameters and less computation at inference.

title: Unique-maximum colourings of planar graphs with respect to neighbourhoods
abstract: A colouring of the vertices of a graph by positive integers is a unique-maximum colouring with respect to open (resp. closed) neighbourhoods if the maximum colour appears exactly once in the open (resp. closed) neighbourhood of every vertex. Fabrici, Lužar, Rindošová and Soták (Discrete Appl. Math. 324 (2023) 80-92) conjectured that four colours suffice for closed neighbourhoods in planar graphs. We prove this conjecture by colouring a suitable independent dominating set with the three largest colours. They further conjectured that six colours suffice if the colouring is also proper. We disprove this conjecture by a planar graph which needs seven colours, and we show that seven colours always suffice. For open neighbourhoods, we show that eight colours suffice, even for proper colourings, which improves the previous bound of ten. In the proper case, our graph again needs seven colours. If the colouring need not be proper and the graph has no vertices of degree 2, then six colours suffice.

title: Graphene Transfer for Vertical Amorphous-Selenium Photodetectors: Fabrication, Optical Transmission and Operation at 77 K
abstract: Graphene can serve as a VUV transparent electrode in vertical photodetector devices. Using an optically transparent graphene as a top-electrode of amorphous selenium (a-Se) photoconductor requires transfer process compatible with the thermal and chemical sensitivities of a-Se thin films. The baking and polymer-removal steps of conventional commercial Trivial Transfer graphene procedures are undesirable because heating can promote selenium crystallization and prolonged solvent exposure can cause delamination. We implement two alternatives: PMMA-free transfer of nominal 50-layer graphene and transfer of nominal 10-layer graphene using an approximately 80 nm PMMA support removed in acetone at 40C. Raman G and 2D bands identify graphene after transfer. Separate graphene/MgF2 specimens are characterized by dark-corrected transmission measurements over 120-325 nm and compared with earlier single-layer and nominal 6-8-layer Trivial Transfer spectra. The completed graphene/a-Se/Cr devices produce bias-dependent voltage transients under pulsed 415 nm illumination at 293 K and 77 K. These results establish an a-Se-compatible fabrication route for graphene-electrode devices and demonstrate vertical device operation at both room and cryogenic temperatures. The completed devices provide a platform for detection-efficiency studies, and direct VUV photoresponse measurements now underway.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001).
