In addition to transient broadband compact binary coalescence GW signals, we apply it to long-duration (continuous), quasi-monochromatic GW signals, for which the relative motion of source and lens makes the amplification factor time-dependent over the observation. The implementation is publicly available in the Python package GWLENS.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Location Encoding Methods for Species Distribution Modelling
abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of species is a key question in ecology. A variety of solutions, from statistical, traditional machine learning, through to deep learning-based methods have been proposed. These methods take sparse observations for a species of interest as input and aim to generate dense spatial outputs indicating the spatial range of the species. Orthogonal to the choice of statistical model used is the question of what input features are most informative. Thanks to recent developments, the number of options has greatly expanded, with choices spanning different climate variables, learning-based encodings, earth embedding models, or raw transformed geographic coordinates. In this work, we introduce a standardized evaluation framework and quantify the effectiveness of different location encodings in the context of species range estimation, both at the local and global scale.

title: Robust, Lightweight Locally Differentially Private Histogram Estimation and the Role of Dropout Attacks
abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) is vulnerable to output manipulation by malicious clients. Zero-knowledge proofs can enforce correct report computation, but clients may still selectively drop out after inspecting their outputs. Prior work combines zero-knowledge proofs with homomorphic encryption to hide reports from clients and prevent selective dropout, but incurs substantial computational cost. We instead develop a three-message lightweight verification framework for robust histogram estimation that uses proofs of plaintext evaluation to restrict output manipulation to selective dropout. Across the evaluated settings for PI-RAPPOR and Hadamard Response, mean per-client online latency remains below 500 milliseconds. We further establish tight error bounds showing that, for RAPPOR, PI-RAPPOR, and Hadamard Response, restricting malicious clients to selective dropout reduces attack-dependent error by a factor proportional to the square root of the domain size compared with output manipulation. Additionally, when client protocols cannot be modified, we propose server-side consistency checks for RAPPOR and Hadamard Response. These checks improve robustness without client-side cryptography and can be applied post-hoc to collected reports, offering an alternative under different deployment constraints. Experiments demonstrate that both verification and consistency checks substantially reduce attack error for certain mechanisms, with consistency checks yielding errors intermediate between those obtained with verification and those under unrestricted output manipulation.

title: Instanton tunnelling as a verifiable benchmark for digital quantum simulation: circuit structure, classical simulability and hardware reproducibility
abstract: We use instanton-mediated tunnelling in the quartic double well as a benchmark for digital quantum simulation that is checkable against an exact answer at every step. The instanton enters through the classical analysis; the hardware tests the dynamics of the lattice model. A unary (single-excitation) encoding maps N lattice sites to N qubits, with the single-excitation dynamics as a reference that remains classically cheap at any N. For a second-order Trotter circuit with adjacent, equal-angle XX/YY pairs on each bond, we prove that the Schmidt rank across any cut is at most four at every gate boundary and at most two after each pair, independently of N. Matrix-product-state simulations of this gate list reproduce the exact splitting up to N = 48. For this bond-wise formula the admissible Trotter step shrinks roughly as N^-2, so one tunnelling period costs about N^3.3 two-qubit gates; a kinetic/potential splitting keeps the step near 0.065 up to N=128, so this scaling belongs to splitting the kinetic term bond by bond. At a coarser, separately bounded step we measure the full transfer at N=8 on two superconducting processors, recovering the lattice splitting to a few percent and its dependence on the barrier height, which at this resolution is set by the lattice rather than by the instanton. Over 9 repetitions, runs taken minutes apart agree to shot noise, while runs hours to weeks apart differ by up to 6.1%, also on a fixed set of qubits; with sessions as the sampling unit, the processors differ in the damping, while a difference in the splitting is not established. Normalising by the measured single-excitation population extends the usable depth about 4-fold but does not improve the splitting. A Gaussian start state, which needs no diagonalisation, reproduces the splitting of the eigenvector-based start to within 1.6 percentage points.

title: LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA stochastic constraints on first-order phase transitions: A tale of priors
abstract: We re-examine the methodology for constraining cosmological first-order phase transitions from gravitational-wave searches using Bayesian statistical analysis. Specifically, we use results from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA searches for a stochastic gravitational wave background during observing runs O1--O4a. We explore multiple prior choices across three categories of fit parameters: geometrical parameters, thermodynamical parameters of phase transitions, and the parameters of an Abelian Higgs particle physics model. Our key finding is that the constraints on most parameters describing gravitational waves from a phase transition depend strongly on the prior. Consequently, the data do not yet allow to derive robust constraints on these parameters. Besides, even if a parameter is meaningfully constrained, the upper limit can vary significantly with the prior range. We provide practical recommendations for assessing the robustness of parameter estimates and guidelines for rigorously testing prior independence in future analyses.

title: Transferring an analysis of human brain organization to language models
abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.

title: Early spectra of AT2017gfo from scaled 3D merger ejecta: mass--velocity distribution, 3D structure, and treatment of line opacity
abstract: We present ARTIS radiative transfer calculations for neutron star merger ejecta with line-by-line opacities, wavelength-calibrated lanthanide data, and time-dependent r-process compositions and thermalisation, testing how the early kilonova depends on the mass-velocity distribution, dimensionality, and line treatment. We rescale 3D dynamical ejecta from a merger simulation in density and velocity to approximate AT2017gfo. Mass scaling alone provides good agreement with the bolometric light curve but inconsistent spectra. With velocities additionally halved, the model also reproduces the observed spectra at 1.4, 2.4, and (albeit less accurately) 3.4 days. The Sr II triplet contributes most to the 10500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ peak, and La III and Gd III to the 13500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ shoulder. Although hydrodynamically not fully self-consistent, this model is to our knowledge the first kilonova model based on calibrated atomic data that reproduces the light curve and main spectral features of the early AT2017gfo, suggesting that total (dynamical plus post-merger) ejecta with higher mass, lower velocity, and similar composition compared to our dynamical ejecta could explain AT2017gfo. A 2D azimuthal average mixes lanthanide-poor with lanthanide-rich regions, smooths the density, and makes the averaged model three times fainter at 1 day and redder throughout than the 3D model, highlighting the importance of 3D modelling. We compare the line-by-line macroatom treatment with expansion-opacity and line-binned schemes with thermal redistribution, using identical atomic data. Luminosities agree to $\lesssim 10$ per cent after 1 day, but the expansion-opacity scheme, unlike converged line-binned schemes, overestimates the spectral flux by up to 20 per cent, which can bias inferred abundances.

title: Capacity-Aware Redistribution Control for Mitigation of Cascading Failures in Networks
abstract: This paper studies the control of irreversible cascading failures in networks with finite node capacities. Each node carries a nonnegative divisible quantity, referred to as load, and fails irreversibly when its load exceeds its capacity. The network dynamics are represented by topology-dependent row-stochastic matrices. When nodes fail, these matrices must be updated. However, directly deleting rows and columns corresponding to failed nodes can reduce the total load in the network. We therefore introduce a topology update that preserves unit row sums and quantifies any unserved load explicitly. We derive the resulting load-balance relation and a necessary and sufficient condition for lossless redistribution after simultaneous failures. Based on these results, we formulate a two-stage optimization problem: the first stage minimizes unserved load, and the second stage minimizes the highest capacity utilization among the surviving nodes. Simulations on grid and Barabasi-Albert networks show that, unlike the standard equal and residual-capacity redistribution approaches, the proposed method prevents secondary failures in all tested cases, with a tradeoff against served load on scale-free networks.

title: Unified Theory for Momentum-Space Nonsymmorphic Symmetry of Spin Space Groups
abstract: Projective crystal symmetry provides a route to nonsymmorphic symmetry structures in momentum space, but a general theory for their realization in spin space groups has been lacking. We show that a nonsymmorphic momentum-space action is possible only when the unitary translation subgroup is combined with rotations about a common axis for a coplanar or noncoplanar spin space group of spin-$1/2$ systems. Its factor system originates entirely from the double cover $\mathrm{Spin}(2)\to SO(2)$, yielding a general formula for the fractional reciprocal-lattice translations and hence for the point-group action on the Brillouin zone. We further prove that a momentum-space nonsymmorphic group is realizable by a spin space group if and only if its Brillouin-zone action contains a two-point orbit. Consequently, 842 of the 1,357 nonsymmorphic magnetic space groups are realizable by spin space groups. Applying this theory, we construct a database covering all 67,475 SSGs that can be queried bidirectionally: from an SSG to its momentum-space magnetic group, or from a given momentum-space magnetic group to all SSGs that realize it. Together, these results establish the momentum-space symmetry foundation for a systematic band theory of SSGs in spin-$1/2$ systems.

title: The Gas-Phase Metallicity and Nitrogen abundances in typical galaxies at $z\sim5$
abstract: The relation between stellar mass and gas-phase metallicity (MZR) is a key tracer of the baryon cycle in galaxies. JWST now gives access to rest-optical emission lines at z > 3, enabling unprecedented constraints on the chemical enrichment and the conditions of the interstellar medium of galaxies in the early Universe. In this work, we present the MZR at $z=3.8-6.6$ from stacked NIRCam/grism spectra of 1748 H$α$-selected star-forming galaxies compiled over an area of 320 arcmin$^2$. The simple H$α$ flux-limited selection allows us to measure representative [NII]$λ$6584/H$α$ and [SII]$λλ$6716,6731/ H$α$ ratios in stacks spanning $\rm log(M_\star/M_\odot)=8-10.2$, extending the upper mass range of previous high-redshift MZR measurements by $\sim1$ dex. Gas-phase metallicities are derived from these ratios using strong-line calibrations recently derived from high-redshift galaxies. The[NII]-based MZR has a slope $γ= 0.42^{+0.10}_{-0.07}$ and $12+\rm log(O/H) = 7.94^{+0.06}_{-0.09}$ at $\rm log(M_\star/M_\odot) = 9$, in broad agreement with recent empirical studies and hydrodynamical simulations. The [SII]-based relation yields a consistent slope and a $\sim0.3$ dex higher normalization, within the systematic uncertainties of strong-line calibrations. From the resolved [SII] doublet we infer a median electron density of $n_e = 184^{+226}_{-169}\,\rm cm^{-3}$. Combining [NII] and [SII], we indirectly estimate the N/O ratio and find that it follows the trend expected from primary and secondary nitrogen production, with no evidence for nitrogen enhancement in the HII region emission that dominates our galaxies. Our results provide a benchmark for the chemical enrichment and ISM conditions of typical star-forming galaxies at $z\sim5$ across a wide mass range.

title: Hydrodynamics of robotic micro-swimmers in confinement
abstract: Inspired by seminal work by E.M. Purcell, we discuss the problem of predicting and optimizing the performance of autonomous robots swimming in confinement. Our approach is based on the explicit numerical resolution of the fluid flow induced by the swimmer, and it is validated experimentally on a cm-size prototype composed of a cargo head and a rotating propulsive tail. Using hydrodynamic scaling, we predict the performance of replicas of our prototype scaled down to mm- and sub-mm-size to test the feasibility of autonomous micro-robots navigating in narrow vessels. The main result of our theoretical, computational, and experimental analysis is that, while hydrodynamics seems to place no fundamental obstruction to the vision of autonomous micro-robots navigating in narrow lumens inside the human body, it does provide useful and strict guidelines for rational design at different length scales.

title: Stratonovich approximation for halo bias: An efficient framework within excursion set theory
abstract: We develop an efficient framework for calculating halo multiplicity functions and bias parameters in the excursion-set approach based on the previously presented Hertz and Stratonovich approximations for the first-crossing distribution. The framework enables efficient evaluation of first-crossing distributions for a broad class of moving barriers and filter functions, from which halo biases can be calculated within the peak-background split formalism. We compare halo multiplicity functions and biases obtained from these approximations with those computed from first-crossing distributions obtained from numerically generated ensembles of excursion-set trajectories. We find close agreement between predictions based on the Stratonovich approximation and numerical results across a range of barrier parameters and filter choices, demonstrating that the approximation captures the impact of non-Markovian correlations on first-crossing statistics while substantially reducing the computational cost compared to trajectory-based calculations. Overall, this framework provides a flexible and computationally efficient tool for analyzing halo statistics in cosmological applications.

title: H3Remover: Reinforcing Video Object Removal without Paired Data
abstract: Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. To limit unintended scene changes, a background-geometry reward encourages preservation of relative depth ordering. To preserve background appearance without retaining unwanted shadows or reflections, an appearance reward constrains RGB changes in source-derived protected regions while exempting targets and estimated effects. Frozen HPSv3 complements these constraints with perceptual-quality feedback for synthesized content. Evaluation regions remain fixed across candidates, and DiffusionART optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen. Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over original H3, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.

title: Charge at regular centers in curvature-coupled electrodynamics
abstract: An electric or magnetic flux through shrinking symmetry spheres ordinarily produces an $r^{-4}$ Maxwell stress and a singular center. We examine how this obstruction changes when the Maxwell invariant is multiplied by an arbitrary scalar-curvature response $h(R)$. For real, static, spherically symmetric solutions, the difference between the radial and temporal gravitational equations gives a linear equation for a composite response variable. Combined with the trace equation, it bounds the response-weighted Maxwell source whenever the Kretschmann scalar is bounded, without assuming a limit or derivative bounds for the Ricci scalar. Magnetic and electric displacement charges cannot coexist, and neither charge is possible if $h$ remains bounded and bounded away from zero. On either surviving charged branch, the Ricci scalar converges and the weighted source tends to zero. Magnetic charge requires $h=o(r^4)$, whereas electric displacement requires $r^4|h|\to\infty$. Exact solutions show that these thresholds are sharp and realize the $r^6$ magnetic and $r^{-6}$ electric rates for a smooth geometric center. We also classify the zero-response sector, where an electric field may survive even though its displacement charge vanishes.

title: Investigating the Impact of SAX J1808.4-3658's Very Bright Thermonuclear X-ray Burst on the Accretion Disc with NICER
abstract: We analyse a bright thermonuclear X-ray burst from the accreting millisecond X-ray pulsar (AMXP) SAX J1808.4-3658, the brightest burst detected by \textit{NICER} to date, to explore interactions between thermonuclear burst radiation and the accretion disc. This burst features a remarkable soft (<1.5 keV) excess in its spectra. For the first time, we simultaneously detect a reflection signal and the signature of an evolving persistent component, with our fits producing a peak persistent scaling factor $f_{a,1} = 59.6\pm0.6$. We find a high peak reflection fraction ($f_{r,1} = 0.82\pm0.15$) and a peak bolometric burst blackbody flux below Eddington (0.68$L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$) despite signatures of photospheric radius expansion. We detect a raised $N_\mathrm{H}$ ($\approx$34% above persistent emission) and raised disc blackbody temperature ($\approx$15% above persistent emission) during the burst's tail. This is the first time that spectroscopic evidence consistent with burst-induced disc heating has been found. We interpret that disc heating could cause the disc to puff up and inhibit burst photons, explaining the high reflection fraction and below-Eddington burst luminosity during the burst peak. We find an increasing count rate starting from $\approx$150s before the burst onset. Spectral analysis revealed a thermal component that evolves towards hotter temperatures closer to the onset of the burst. This is the second detection of this phenomenon from an AMXP. Lastly, we find that both the double-peaked structure and the "pause" in the rise are energy-dependent.

title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

title: A Generative Model for Higher-Order Network Dynamics
abstract: Conventional network representations inferred from multivariate time series describe statistical relationships between pairs of components, even when the underlying dynamics involve group interactions that cannot be represented by pairwise interactions alone. Several multivariate information-theoretic measures have been proposed to characterise dependence beyond pairs. However, due to a lack of systems with known generating mechanisms, these measures have not been carefully validated or compared for empirical use. To address this, we here introduce a generative model of stochastic network dynamics with pairwise and higher-order interactions specified by the user. The higher-order interactions are represented by directed hyperedges, and the model provides a controlled benchmark for evaluating information-theoretic measures. Removing only the higher-order term gives a pairwise-only reference. The experiments test whether a measure detects changes induced by the higher-order term relative to this reference and recovers the participating nodes and their source-target roles. A separate experiment tests discrimination between a product coupling and a specified nonlinear pairwise control, with equal root-mean-square coupling magnitude under the pairwise-only reference. Several measures detected sufficiently strong higher-order interactions across the tested network topologies and coupling functions. In the separate discrimination experiment, the measures also separated the product coupling from the specified nonlinear pairwise control. Recovery, however, became harder as the number of candidate interactions grew. The framework therefore provides a testbed where the link between higher-order signatures and mechanisms can be tested, rather than assumed, before measures are applied to empirical data.

title: Structure-Preserving PHS RBF-FD Methods for Schrodinger Equations
abstract: We develop and analyze a structure-preserving polyharmonic-spline radial-basis-function finite-difference (PHS RBF-FD) method for the two-dimensional Schrödinger equation with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. The method combines a 29-point complete-shell stencil with odd boundary reflection to construct a symmetric discrete Laplacian. Unlike conventional nearest-neighbor RBF-FD discretizations, whose independently selected stencils do not generally preserve global symmetry, the proposed construction admits an exact discrete sine eigenbasis. We derive a Fourier-symbol representation and establish a sufficient criterion for strict negative definiteness, verified for the \(r^7+\mathbb P_4\) and \(r^{11}+\mathbb P_5\) formulations using validated coefficient calculations. The resulting symmetric spatial operator preserves discrete mass and energy under exact semidiscrete evolution, while fully discrete conservation depends on the time integrator. Numerical experiments examine kernel selection, dispersion, convergence, symmetry defects, and computational cost. Comparisons with conventional RBF-FD and fourth-order finite differences include exact Fourier modes and a variable-potential Schrödinger problem with an independently refined spectral reference. The \(r^{11}+\mathbb P_5\) formulation provides favorable accuracy in the tested problems while maintaining the desired spatial structure. The analysis establishes a connection between boundary treatment, global operator symmetry, and structure preservation in localized PHS discretizations.

title: A provably efficient classical algorithm for simulating OTOC$^{(1)}$ in 1D
abstract: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are quantities of broad interest in many-body physics due to their connection with information scrambling and quantum chaos. Recently, estimating higher-order OTOCs in random quantum circuits was proposed as a promising avenue for quantum advantage, yet the classical hardness of this task remains poorly understood. Even for first-order OTOCs, where growing evidence suggests classical tractability, no efficient classical algorithm with rigorous guarantees has been established to date. In this work, we introduce "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, at arbitrary depths and with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. We also conduct numerical experiments comparing our simulation results to exact computation on up to $512$ qubits for Clifford circuits with $768$ $T$-gates and up to $22$ qubits for Haar-random circuits. We emphasize that our results do not directly apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which is the subject of recent quantum advantage proposals. Nevertheless, our work provides a rigorous step towards understanding the classical complexity of OTOC estimation and represents a family of non-trivial quantum circuits for which a provable, polynomial time algorithm is now known, establishing foundations for understanding these widely used diagnostics of quantum chaos.

title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.

title: Towards modelling redshift uncertainties in the photometric void size function
abstract: We present an extension of the theoretical formalism for the Void Size Function (VSF) to incorporate photometric redshift uncertainties, combining the excursion set with the theory of Lagrangian density peaks. Photometric redshift scatter induces anisotropic line-of-sight smoothing of the density field, which modifies the variance of the field and suppresses the abundance of large voids. We model this effect by damping the variance of the smoothed density field in the theoretical model, and we test it on AbacusSummit halo lightcones with true redshifts and with mock photometric redshifts generated with a Gaussian scatter. The predicted damping of the variance agrees with the one measured in the halo distribution to 1% and the suppression of the VSF due to photometric redshift scatter is well reproduced by the modified model, with recalibrated barrier parameters, for sigma_z <= 0.015 and for voids larger than 40 Mpc/h (about 2.5 mean tracer separations). This work is a first step towards modelling the VSF in modern photometric surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the Euclid mission.

title: AggCLIP: Aggregating CLIP for Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection
abstract: Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection (ZSMAD) aims to identify both appearance and geometric defects in novel categories without relying on target-specific training data, making it especially valuable in real-world scenarios constrained by data scarcity, privacy concerns, or high annotation costs. While recent approaches successfully adapt vision-language models like CLIP to achieve this open-vocabulary generalization, they still face significant challenges: (i) severe geometric information loss during 3D-to-2D point cloud rendering; (ii) spatially noisy 2D feature maps produced by raw CLIP patch embeddings, compounded by shallow late-stage modality fusion; and (iii) severe cross-modal semantic misalignment due to decoupled processing streams. To address these limitations, we propose AggCLIP, a novel framework that adapts frozen CLIP representations for ZSMAD by explicitly incorporating local geometric structure and visual spatial context. Specifically, to accurately localize fine-grained defects, we design a Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module that refines back-projected 3D point features via density-adaptive neighborhood weighting, alongside a Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) module that smooths multi-scale 2D patch embeddings using a lightweight trainable adapter. Furthermore, to prevent semantic drift between modalities, we introduce a Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss, which aligns the abstract concepts of normality and abnormality across the point cloud and RGB streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed AggCLIP framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies benchmarks under both one-vs-rest and cross-dataset zero-shot settings, notably surpassing the strongest competitive methods by up to 2.9% in pixel-level AUPRO.

title: Equal Steps, Unequal Curvature: Where Muon's Update Goes Wrong
abstract: Muon updates each hidden weight matrix along the polar factor of its momentum, the steepest-descent direction under the spectral norm. That choice fixes two allocations without consulting the loss: every singular direction of the momentum receives the same step, and in a non-square matrix each neuron's step is set by its leverage score. Whether they are good is a question about curvature, which steepest-descent arguments do not answer; we measure it. Using held-out gradients and Hessian-vector products, we decompose Muon's step by singular-value band and by neuron group and compute each group's second-order optimal multiplier. In a 124M-parameter decoder trained on FineWeb-Edu, the multipliers rise monotonically from the top singular directions to the tail: Muon over-steps the high-curvature top of its spectrum. We prove in Lean when such a diagnostic licenses an intervention at Muon's own update norm. On the measured curvature, the criterion predicts, and held-out losses confirm, that moving step length off the top helps mid-training and early in the cooldown, but not at its end. We then test interventions under per-step norm matching, tuned baselines and paired seeds. Orthogonalizing Q, K and V separately rather than as one fused matrix lowers the loss by 0.0250 nats and accounts for all of the gain of block-wise variants. A matmul-only, rotation-equivariant spectral tilt $σ^{-1/4}$ applied in the cooldown lowers the loss of this stronger baseline by a further 0.0120 nats, additively with NorMuon (0.0158 nats together, three seeds; the baseline needs about 4.3% more tokens to match), and by 0.0188 nats at 355M parameters (three seeds). Energy-matched Schatten-1 weight decay adds a further 0.0052 nats. Geometrically principled changes that do not act on the measured miscalibration, namely exact polar factors, steepest-descent input whitening and top-heavy decay, do not help.

title: Broximal Gradient Descent in General Norms: Convergence without Fejér Monotonicity
abstract: We study Broximal Gradient Descent in a general norm for smooth optimization over a closed convex set. Each update minimizes the linear model over the intersection of the feasible set and a norm ball. Unlike the Euclidean case with suitably restricted radii, the distance to a solution can increase, even when the squared norm is strongly convex. We instead use a comparator inequality and an observable stationarity certificate. For convex objectives, prescribed radii yield value convergence, including escape when the infimum is unattained, and a last-iterate $O(K^{-1/3})$ bound without a distance-bound assumption. A level-set distance bound gives an all-iteration $O(1/K)$ rate with calibrated radii and an asymptotic $O(\log K/K)$ rate with radii using no problem constant. Strong convexity and power growth give explicit faster envelopes and convergence of the iterates. Without convexity, a constrained Polyak--Łojasiewicz inequality gives linear convergence with prescribed radii. An observable radius-halving rule needs a valid smoothness constant but neither the PL modulus nor an initial gap bound; warm starting gives logarithmic total oracle complexity in inverse accuracy. The analysis separates established local-oracle ingredients from the control of level sets, radius calibration, and accuracy-based oracle counts.

title: Conceptual full-vehicle modeling of a modular all-wheel-drive robotic ADS test platform as a foundation for a digital twin architecture
abstract: This paper presents the development of an initial full-vehicle simulation model of the PixKit modular electric test platform in IPG CarMaker. The objective is to create a physics-based and extendable model structure that can serve as a low-level foundation for future digital twin applications. The reference vehicle is a skateboard chassis combining unconventional vehicle characteristics such as four independent wheel-hub motors and rear axle steering capable of high steering angles. Since complete measurement data of the vehicle is not yet available, the model parameterization is based on a combination of manufacturer documentation, derived values and engineering assumptions. The modeling approach focuses on the system-level integration of the main vehicle subsystems rather than on a fully validated representation. The resulting model was assessed through basic driving scenarios with different steering inputs and configurations. The simulations showed stable model behavior and physically plausible interaction between the subsystems. The all-wheel-drive configuration produced symmetric wheel responses in longitudinal driving, while counter-phase rear axle steering increased the yaw response and reduced the simulated turning circle diameter compared with front axle steering only. The circular driving scenario further indicated bounded roll and slip behavior. Overall, the implemented CarMaker model provides a traceable and functional simulation basis for the PixKit vehicle. It can support future model refinement, calibration with real vehicle data and development with the goal of creating a validated digital twin architecture.

title: Complete quasinormal modes of Type-D black holes. III. Reissner-Nordstrom spectra from zero to extremal charge
abstract: Earlier calculations left open how gravitational quasinormal modes (QNMs) of charged black holes recover the Schwarzschild spectrum and how the modes near algebraically special frequencies relate to the exact special solutions. We extend our Kerr analysis to Reissner-Nordström black holes by analytically continuing the ingoing horizon solution and locating the zeros of the incoming amplitude at infinity. For each of $\ell=2$ and $3$, we trace the first 42 overtone families from the Schwarzschild limit to extremality. The charge trajectories distinguish crossings of the negative imaginary axis from turns near it and separate the unconventional Schwarzschild modes from neighboring branches. At zero charge the polar algebraically special mode is a QNM. At extremal charge the exact axial special modes are total-transmission modes. Of the 84 families, 75 approach distinct extremal frequencies with finite damping, and nine approach zero frequency with vanishing excitation. At exact extremality we also compute, for the first time, gravitational QNMs on the unconventional Riemann sheet reached across the negative imaginary axis. At intermediate charge, the clearest resonant enhancement of both excitation factors occurs for the $\ell=3$ overtone pairs $(22,23)$ and $(23,24)$.

title: Zonotopic Analysis of Quantization Error in Neural Networks
abstract: Quantized neural networks achieve computational efficiency by reducing precision, but bounding their quantization error remains a challenge due to discrete rounding and clamping operations. We present a zonotope-based abstract interpretation framework for quantized ReLU feed-forward network verification, introducing a unified round-clamp abstract transformer that jointly handles both operations. We extend this framework to constrained zonotopes, which add linear constraints to tighten bounds, and derive sound quantization error representations. We establish soundness and affine-strip optimality of the round-clamp abstract transformer, as well as convex-hull optimality of its complete constrained formulation. On the ACAS Xu benchmarks, our constrained zonotope method reduces average error-bound widths by approximately 70-85% and runtimes by 65-80% compared to QEBVerif's symbolic DRA propagation at the two smallest tested perturbation radii (r=3 and r=6). These improvements are not uniform across bitwidths, and symbolic DRA achieves tighter bounds at larger radii. Our plain zonotope method delivers competitive sound bounds nearly 300 times faster on average.

title: A Principled Approach to Concurrency, Nondeterminism, and Asynchrony in Choreographies
abstract: Choreographic programming (CP) describes a distributed system as a global program and compiles it into communicating network programs via endpoint projection (EPP). Asynchrony captures the independent progress of communicating processes, while nondeterminism captures the range of behaviours that can arise from their interactions. However, the integration of both features into a theory of CP is absent. We present Nyarlathotep, the first asynchronous nondeterministic CP framework. We define its operational semantics of choreographies and networks using labelled transition systems. Besides asynchrony and choreographic nondeterminism, Nyarlathotep supports expressive features including general branching, out-of-order execution, and general recursion with parameterised procedures that processes can enter independently. We prove EPP sound and complete, establishing strong behavioural equivalence between the semantics of choreographies and their projected networks. We prove that projected networks are communication-safe and deadlock-free. We mechanised all our results in Lean 4.

title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels. We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content. We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.

title: Infinite-dimensional invariant tori for the perturbed modified KdV equation
abstract: In this paper, we consider the perturbed modified KdV equation $u_t=-u_{xxx}+6u^2u_x+\partial_x(u^5)$ on the circle, without external parameters. We prove that it admits plenty of almost periodic solutions.

title: The state of nuclear data for fusion activation simulations
abstract: This report compares decay-heat calculations made with four nuclear data libraries, TENDL-2025, ENDF/B-VIII.1, JEFF-4.0 and JENDL-5, against the JAEA FNS decay-heat benchmark. The main comparison uses the 2000 campaign, in which 73 foils were irradiated for five minutes in a mostly 14 MeV neutron field and their decay heat was measured for about an hour. The 1996 seven-hour campaign, with 29 foils and cooling times of up to 400 days, is compared separately and is not included in the rankings. Over the 69 elemental foils solved by all four libraries, the median deviation from the measurement (the mean absolute C/E deviation of each foil) is JENDL-5 17 percent, TENDL-2025 19 percent, JEFF-4.0 22 percent and ENDF/B-VIII.1 44 percent. No library is best everywhere: JENDL-5 on 24, JEFF-4.0 on 18, TENDL-2025 on 17 and ENDF/B-VIII.1 on 10 of the foils. For each element the report breaks the heat down by product and lists the nuclear data on which the libraries differ, and the final sections propose measurements, including enriched-isotope irradiations, that would resolve the largest differences.

title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning
abstract: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.

title: Generation of neutron Bessel beams
abstract: Matter waves can exhibit structured wavefields analogous to those of light, offering new means of controlling the spatial and angular-momentum degrees of freedom of massive particles. Bessel beams are a fundamental class of structured waves that exhibit non-diffracting propagation, self-healing, and well-defined orbital angular momentum (OAM). Here, we experimentally realize neutron Bessel beams by imprinting a nanoscale conical phase gradient onto a neutron wavefront. By incorporating azimuthal phase gradients, we generate zeroth-, third-, and sixth-order Bessel beams, demonstrating direct control of both the OAM and radial structure of a massive particle. We also propose a neutron Bessel-grating interferometer, complementary to established optical and electron interferometric methods, in which varying the radial grating period by approximately 100 nm yields a controlled Gouy phase shift of $π$. These results establish neutron Bessel beams as a new platform for diffractive neutron focusing and provide an experimental foundation for theoretical studies of Bessel beams in neutron scattering, decay, and OAM characterization.

title: Half-Line Hardy-Szegő Point Processes: Fisher-Hartwig Asymptotics and Sparse Conditioning
abstract: A horizontal window extending from a fixed positive height to infinity has infinite area but a finite expected number of Hardy-Szegő zeros. We study its zero count as the horizontal length $L$ grows. Unlike for fixed bounded-height windows, the logarithmic moment generating function has a new $θ^2\log L/(2π^2)$ term; we also identify its holomorphic order-one correction. The logarithmic term has two equal contributions: a Fisher-Hartwig jump in a canonical Wiener-Hopf model and an endpoint effect in the original Fourier-Laplace operator. This yields precise point and tail probabilities at positive count densities. We also determine the transition when a moving upper height is comparable to $L$. For sparse exact counts $n_L\to\infty$ with $n_L=o(L)$, we obtain logarithmic probability asymptotics relative to the exact void probability. We determine the void exponent and sharp asymptotics relative to the void probability for counts up to order $\log L$. Under sparse exact-count conditioning, the empirical distribution of rescaled horizontal positions and logarithmic heights converges to the uniform law on the unit square. Near distinct interior horizontal locations, the rescaled configurations converge to independent Poisson processes with uniform logarithmic-height marks.

title: Modelling population distribution across cities on spatial networks using the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems
abstract: We investigate the urban population distribution of the Italian region of Sardinia through the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems on spatial networks, interpreting cities both as agents and vertices of a graph, and representing interurban links as edges. We consider various emigration rules to model the interactions between agents, obtaining two main results: the bimodal lognormal fit of the total population distribution among cities and the Pareto fit of the tail. Overall, our model provides results consistent with the actual distribution derived from ISTAT data of Sardinia; furthermore, the bimodal lognormal fit generally follows the distribution tail more accurately than the Pareto one, although the two coincide in the first half.

title: Light fermions can trigger a Brout-Englert-Higgs effect
abstract: The Brout-Englert-Higgs effect produces the masses of the Standard Model particles. However, the cause of this effect is unknown. Beyond-the-Standard-Model theories aim to find the source of this effect, for example using a composite Higgs and dynamically generating its vacuum expectation value. In this paper, we show evidence from lattice simulations with vectorially coupled fermions and without Yukawa couplings that the Brout-Englert-Higgs effect could be triggered by the light masses of fermions. This suggests that an explanation entirely within the Standard Model could be possible. Moreover, our results are consistent with weak couplings and fermions can only impact the Higgs potential at NNLO. This implies a so far unidentified mechanism in an SU(2) scalar-fermion-gauge system that produces a non-zero vacuum expectation value. In addition, we find that the transition from a QCD-like behavior to a Higgs-like behavior happens when the fermion mass falls below twice the W/Z mass: a threshold that is integer valued but not connected to other critical physical behavior.

title: ChainIT Transaction Truth: Stablecoins, Web3 Wallets, and Multi-Rail Commerce. A Zero-Trust Control Plane for Verified Identity, Organizational Authority, Runtime Compliance, Secure Wallet Execution, and Immutable Settlement Evidence
abstract: Stablecoins can move value continuously across programmable networks, and Web3 wallets can authorize those transfers with cryptographic signatures, but neither capability, standing alone, establishes a complete commercial transaction. A blockchain may prove that a transaction satisfied protocol rules, and a wallet may prove that sufficient signing authority existed; neither proves who initiated the transaction, for which legal entity, under what current authority, against which current compliance evidence, on what exact instruction, or with what settlement and accounting outcome. We describe the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture, a zero-trust control, execution, and evidence architecture that places verified individual and organizational identity, the organizational authority record and authority policy of the ChainIT Authority Protocol, transaction-specific runtime compliance decisions, exact-digest approval, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use Execution Authorization Credential in front of wallet execution, and that records settlement, reconciliation, and lifecycle evidence after the transaction. The architecture separates five boundaries: control of a key is not identity, identity is not organizational authority, authority is not compliance, compliance is not execution authority, and network confirmation is not complete commercial settlement. We describe wallet and custody profiles, including a multi-party computation (MPC) profile in which custody security is kept independent of business authority, stablecoin and Web3 evidence domains, layered finality, the U.S. stablecoin regulatory context as of September 2026, and a phased deployment in which pilot success requires that the control invariants hold under attack and failure.

title: Optical readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors with SiPMs
abstract: Scintillation light readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) is used for imaging and track reconstruction applications including in optical Time Projection Chambers (TPC). Typically, high resolution CCD or CMOS imaging sensors are used and PMTs can be employed to obtain auxiliary timing information. We report on the optical readout of MPGDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) which enables limited spatial resolution. Arrays of SiPMs were used to read out Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs) and Glass Micromegas amplification stages. Center of gravity reconstruction of hit positions yields a spatial resolution of approximately 1.35 mm for signals shared across multiple SiPMs. High gain of the amplification stage as well as the SiPMs enables good signal sharing and is advantageous for position reconstruction.

title: Metadata-Driven AI: An Architectural Pattern for Sustainable Data Analysis with LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. We describe the pattern together with a simple cost model, a measurement of how little information crosses the boundary on public datasets, and a benchmark showing that a small, locally hosted model can serve as the generator. We illustrate the pattern on three applications, each built on a different implementation of it: geospatial photovoltaic prospection over live public APIs, extraction of portfolio positions from bank statements, and a conversational assistant over smart-city dashboards.

title: Gradient-Based Defensive Poisoning Against System Identification Attacks on Cyber-Physical Systems
abstract: AI-driven attacks learn the models of cyber-physical systems (CPS) by passively observing controller and plant signals, then use this knowledge to act covertly. Because covertness depends on the accuracy of the identified model, degrading that accuracy is a viable countermeasure. This work applies Adversarial Machine Learning as a defense, injecting small perturbations into the measurements the attacker observes to degrade an artificial neural network (ANN)-based system identification (SI) attack. The perturbations are derived from input gradients of several independently trained identification models, aggregated into a generalized perturbation, and confined to the transient regimes that carry most of the dynamic information. A sparsity parameter further restricts them to the most influential samples, with negligible cost in effectiveness. On a simulated DC motor networked control system, the proposed perturbations induce larger prediction errors than stochastic poisoning of equal root-mean-square magnitude, and the advantage widens as the magnitude grows. This limits the defense's operating range, which is intended for decoy environments such as CPS honeynets. Additional results indicate that the designed poisoning signals can also degrade N4SID-based system identification, providing evidence of their transferability beyond the ANN-based models originally targeted.

title: Data-Driven Factored Abstractions of Stochastic Systems
abstract: Formal verification and correct-by-design policy synthesis for stochastic dynamical systems face significant scalability challenges due to the curse of dimensionality. These challenges are exacerbated when the system dynamics are unknown and abstractions must be constructed from data. This paper introduces a data-driven framework for constructing factored interval Markov decision process (fIMDP) abstractions from noisy transition observations. Assuming conditional independence of successor coordinates and known coordinate-wise Lipschitz bounds on the dynamics, the framework estimates marginal transition probabilities rather than joint probabilities, resulting in an exponential reduction in the number of probability entries to be estimated and stored. We establish finite-sample confidence guarantees that the abstraction captures the concrete transition probabilities uniformly over each abstract region, enabling certified lower bounds on satisfaction probabilities for $ω$-regular specifications. Experiments on benchmark systems, including pendulum swing-up, unicycle control, and a four-dimensional planar robot model, demonstrate improvements in certified satisfaction probability lower bounds of up to 25 percentage points compared with a state-of-the-art flat IMDP abstraction method. Our framework required up to 23x less memory and was consistently faster in constructing the abstraction.

title: Rapid Equation of State Inference from Multiprobe Datasets
abstract: Fully constraining the neutron star equation of state (EoS) requires combining observations from various channels that probe different density regimes. We perform a joint multimessenger inference of the equation of state using gravitational-wave observations from binary neutron star mergers, NICER mass-radius measurements of X-ray pulsars, and radio timing measurements of massive pulsars. We constrain the parametrized equation of state and perform Bayesian model selection among a set of candidate equations of state. The joint analysis produces a radius of $R_{1.4} = 11.93^{+1.02}_{-0.83} \, \rm km$ for a canonical $1.4 \, M_\odot$ neutron star, and a maximum non-rotating neutron star mass of $M_{\rm max} = 2.31^{+0.23}_{-0.23} \, M_\odot$ with $90\%$ credible intervals. Gravitational-wave and NICER observations constrain the equation of state at low to intermediate densities, while massive pulsar observations constrain it at high densities by requiring the equation of state to support the neutron star masses. We find no simple correlation between the stiffness of an EoS and Bayesian evidence because the observations probe the pressure at different density regimes. By combining constraints on the equation of state with Bayesian model selection using multimessenger data, our analysis connects macroscopic neutron star measurements to microscopic properties of candidate nuclear matter models.

title: Uniformly positive entropy and mixing in minimal systems
abstract: Every minimal system with uniformly positive entropy of order two is topologically mixing. In a minimal system, mixing along an infinite set $A\subset\N_0$ is equivalent to $\dist(T^nU,T^nV)\to0$ along $A$ for all nonempty open $U,V$, and to unbounded complexity of each standard binary open cover along every infinite subset of $A$. For $A=\N_0$ it is also equivalent to $Δ^*$-transitivity. A local distance condition characterizes finite cyclic decompositions with mixing return maps. Such a decomposition exists precisely when, for each infinite $S\subset\N_0$, the closure of some proximal cell along $S$ has positive measure for some invariant probability. In a minimal weakly mixing system, for fixed infinite $S$, these cells are either all dense or all have closures of measure zero for every invariant probability. We also give proximal-cell criteria for Furstenberg families and mild mixing.

title: Deep learning spacetime from entanglement dynamics
abstract: In the eternal AdS black hole, the entanglement of the thermofield double state is geometrically realised by the Einstein--Rosen bridge, in line with the ER=EPR conjecture. Hartman--Maldacena surfaces threading this bridge pass behind the event horizon, so the time-dependent entanglement entropy $S(t)$ of a pair of half-lines, one on each boundary, probes the black hole interior. We turn this relation around and ask how much of the bulk spacetime can be reconstructed from $S(t)$, using a neural ordinary differential equation that learns the metric directly from the entanglement data. We show that $S(t)$ depends on the geometry only through a single function, the local surface gravity expressed in terms of the timelike Killing norm. This is enough to fix a metric with one unknown function: for charged BTZ black holes, the network reconstructs it throughout the region probed by the surfaces, including part of the interior, and the learned metric also yields the Hawking temperature and the location of the critical surface that bounds the accessible interior. With two unknown functions, however, it is not: physically distinct geometries whose two-dimensional $(t,z)$ sectors are related by diffeomorphisms produce the same $S(t)$. Finally, although the null energy condition is not imposed, the network reproduces data obeying the causal bound $v_E\le 1$ on the entanglement velocity, but not data that violate it. Our results thus offer a data-driven perspective on how spacetime, including the black hole interior, emerges from quantum entanglement, and delineate which features of the geometry entanglement alone can determine.

title: Physics-based Tabulation Approach for Rotating Detonation Engines
abstract: High-fidelity simulations of rotating detonation engines remain computationally expensive due to the strong coupling between compressible flow dynamics and stiff chemical kinetics. The coexistence of deflagrative and detonative combustion, along with shock interactions and rapid thermodynamic changes, further challenges conventional reduced-order chemistry models. This work presents a multi-mode tabulation framework that replaces detailed chemical kinetic integration with precomputed thermochemical states and source terms while accounting for variations in the local thermodynamic state. The key novelty lies in a unified treatment of distinct combustion regimes, wherein homogeneous reactor solutions describe deflagrative combustion and post-detonation reactions up to the Chapman-Jouguet (CJ) point, while an equilibrium isentropic expansion model captures supersonic relaxation beyond the CJ state. The framework is evaluated against detailed chemistry across progressively complex configurations, including homogeneous ignition, one-dimensional detonations, and a two-dimensional rotating detonation engine (RDE). The tabulated model accurately reproduces ignition delays and captures the initiation and sustained propagation of detonation waves across varying mixture compositions. Furthermore, the framework reconstructs the complete thermodynamic evolution along an RDE streamline, including post-injection expansion, detonation, post-detonation expansion, and oblique shock interactions, directly from conserved flow variables. These results demonstrate the capability of multi-mode tabulation to represent coupled combustion, shock, and expansion processes within a single thermodynamically responsive framework, offering a promising route toward computationally efficient simulations of detonative combustion across a broad range of applications.

title: Multiplicity of positive solutions for degenerate nonlocal $p$-Laplacian problems without monotonicity of the normalized reaction
abstract: We study degenerate nonlocal Dirichlet problems driven by the $p$-Laplacian, with diffusion depending on weighted sums of integral powers of the solution. Under explicit sign, spectral and size conditions, we obtain two positive solutions for each bounded positivity interval of the diffusion coefficient with zero endpoint values. Neither monotonicity of the normalized reaction $f(x,t)/t^{p-1}$ nor uniqueness of the frozen problem is required. The proof combines Schauder's theorem on a product space of a scalar parameter and a function with subsolution bounds and an energy estimate. The multiplicity result also persists under uniformly small continuous perturbations of the nonlocal functional, including perturbations that do not preserve order.

title: Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability
abstract: Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.

title: Real Frøyshov invariants and lattice homology
abstract: For a class of almost rational plumbing 4-manifolds equipped with smooth involutions, we give a description of the Real Frøyshov invariants of their boundaries in terms of lattice homology. Our approach uses the $S^1$-stable equivalence between Seiberg-Witten Floer spectra and lattice spectra constructed by Dai-Sasahira-Stoffregen, and the $\operatorname{O}(2)$-equivariant versions of these spectra developed by Kang-Park-Taniguchi. As applications, we derive a formula for these invariants for every $\operatorname{spin}^c$ structure on the double branched covers of even torus knots $T_{2p,q}$, and determine the smooth nonorientable $4$-genus of an infinite family of torus knots $T_{4,q}$.

title: A New GUT
abstract: We present a new class of 4-dimensional Grand Unified Theories where the gauge sectors of the standard model have a novel embedding in the unified group that does not factor through an $SU(5)$ subgroup. The smallest example has gauge algebra $\frak{su}(12)$ and an anomaly-free spectrum that produces the three standard model generations with no additional chiral matter. The embedding predicts the axion-photon anomaly ratio $E/N=2/3$ and the weak mixing angle $\sin^2θ_W=1/2$ at the unification scale. Gauge-mediated proton decay proceeds through flipped-$SU(5)$-like operators and the minimally charged smooth monopole carries two Dirac charge units. The global gauge group can be $SU(12)$ or $SU(12)/\mathbb{Z}_2$, with the former allowing color singlets of half-integer electric charge. We develop a GUT bootstrap to constrain $SU(n)$ embeddings with three generations and no additional chiral matter. For unified fermions in up to two-index representations, we prove that all new embeddings arise from the $SU(8m+4)$ family, including flavor unified models for $m \geq 2$.

title: Predicting Species Splits: A Challenging Fine-Grained Benchmark for Category Discovery
abstract: Widely used category discovery benchmarks have become increasingly saturated and often fail to reflect real-world discovery settings, making long-term evaluation of new methods difficult. We introduce PS-SPLIT, a large-scale fine-grained benchmark for category discovery, motivated by taxonomic splitting: the real-world process by which what was once considered a single species is found to comprise multiple distinct ones. PS-SPLIT contains 79K globally distributed, high-quality, community-collected bird images spanning 771 species, derived from 257 recent real expert-verified taxonomic splits, with associated geographic metadata and full taxonomic hierarchy. The visual differences between categories arising from real taxonomic splits can be very subtle, often requiring significant human expertise to tell apart, making PS-SPLIT a challenging benchmark which we hope will assist in advancing fine-grained category discovery research. Based on taxonomic splitting, we introduce the task of discovery by category splitting, where the goal is to determine which known categories should be subdivided into new finer-grained subcategories. We adapt four generalized category discovery methods to this setting, evaluate existing methods, and show that there is substantial room for future progress.

title: Fluctuations and Correlations of Conserved Charges in Isobar Collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV with the STAR Detector
abstract: We report measurements of second-order cumulants and correlations of experimentally accessible baryon number, electric charge, and strangeness proxies in Ru+Ru and Zr+Zr collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$~GeV with the STAR experiment. The results exhibit similar centrality dependences in the two isobar systems within uncertainties. The baryon-strangeness correlation $C_{BS}$ is compared with lattice-QCD and UrQMD calculations. Motivated by recent lattice-QCD predictions for QCD matter in an external magnetic field, several ratios of conserved-charge correlations are studied as functions of centrality. In peripheral collisions, the measured ratios exhibit the same ordering as the lattice-QCD prediction. A qualitatively similar hierarchy is also found in UrQMD, although the model underpredicts the observed peripheral-to-central enhancement. These results motivate further quantitative studies of possible magnetic-field contributions and other sources of the observed centrality dependence.

title: On the cosmic window for neutrino self-interactions
abstract: Neutrino self-interactions ($ν$SI) beyond the Standard Model have arisen as a promising probe of new physics in cosmology. In this Letter, we show that $ν$SI emerging in the low-energy limit of renormalizable theories implies resonant mediator behavior. We identify two regions for $ν$SI: (i) neutrinos become tightly coupled with background evolution; for the first time, we establish how this evolution modifies the Boltzmann hierarchy equations (BHEs), and (ii) resonant $ν$SI dominates the dynamics with negligible background evolution, relevant for mediator masses $\sim 10^{-6}-1$ MeV. In region (i), before matter-radiation equality, neutrino free-streaming is determined by the effective four-fermion interaction, known as the heavy-mediator limit (HML); we explore the impact of background evolution on this scenario, and from our modified BHEs, we show that self-interacting dark radiation scenarios require larger couplings than previously estimated to mimic $ν$SI. Region (ii) shows that the simplest realization of $ν$SI mediated by a (pseudo)scalar particle leads to an extra radiation contribution of $ΔN_{\rm eff}^{\rm CMB} \approx 0$, instead of the commonly quoted $\simeq 0.12$, at the CMB epoch. Overall, we highlight that our findings should be considered in any plausible scenario involving $ν$SI.

title: Dual Gauss-Thakur sums for Drinfeld modules
abstract: We define dual Gauss-Thakur sums for Drinfeld modules, building on constructions of Gauss-Thakur sums due to Thakur, in the case of the Carlitz module, and Gazda and Maurischat, for general Anderson $t$-modules. Using results of Ferraro, we demonstrate that these sums can be obtained by evaluations of dual special functions at elements of finite fields. Our main results are matrix identities assembled from Gauss-Thakur sums and dual Gauss-Thakur sums in terms of multiplication coefficients for the Drinfeld module and its adjoint. We further prove determinant identities and explore connections with special Goss $L$-values and Drinfeld modular forms.

title: Can Bandits Learn to Share a Channel? Distributed Multi-Armed Bandits for Slotted ALOHA
abstract: Slotted ALOHA networks constitute a playground for research on machine learning (ML)-based channel access schemes. We consider ML agents deployed in such networks and operating under severe constraints: fully distributed (independent operation), fully online (no pre-training), aperiodic (no fixed schedule), and with no explicit coordination (no signaling). We ask whether a multi-armed bandit (MAB), a minimal reinforcement learning agent, can learn the optimal policy for a capture-free slotted ALOHA system. We evaluate several MAB algorithms on aggregate network throughput and per-node fairness. Our best-performing agent is based on a Softmax bandit, which we call SALSA (Softmax ALOHA Learning for Shared Access). SALSA learns a per-node transmission policy close to optimal, with throughput near the theoretical maximum for fair random access. We achieve performance comparable to a competing state-of-the-art solution, but without requiring a priori knowledge of the network size.

title: A variational approach to an anisotropic nonlocal porous medium equation with drift
abstract: We study nonlocal porous-medium equations driven by anisotropic Riesz-type repulsive interactions and an external confining potential. The pressure is determined by convolution with an interaction potential of the form $$ W(x)=|x|^{-s}Ω\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right), \qquad d-2<s<d, $$ where $Ω$ is a smooth, even, and strictly positive angular profile. For quadratic confinement and $s\in(d-2,d)\cap(0,5]$, under suitable positivity assumptions on the anisotropic kernels, we prove that the unique energy minimizer is the only steady state among bounded continuous probability densities. We then establish the long-time convergence of global weak solutions to this equilibrium, both locally and globally in Hölder norms. To obtain these results, we derive uniform $L^p$, $L^\infty$, and Hölder estimates, adapting the regularity theory for fractional porous-medium equations to the anisotropic setting. We also construct global weak solutions through a minimizing-movement scheme in Wasserstein space, establish the corresponding energy-dissipation inequality, and prove a Talagrand-type transport inequality.

title: Scalable Non-Parametric Bayesian Inference of Free Energy Landscapes and Emission Functions from Observations
abstract: Free-energy landscapes govern processes from protein conformational change to climate oscillations, but are typically observed only indirectly, through observables such as FRET intensity or optical-tweezer transmittance. Neither the landscape shape, nor the emission function mapping latent state to signal, is usually known, and distinct states may produce the same signal. We therefore infer landscape and emission function jointly and non-parametrically, using the exact non-linear Bayesian filtering likelihood, to fully use the information contained in observable trajectories that are often noisy, scarce and costly to acquire. A novel parallel-in-time algorithm makes this tractable: it is up to 27 times faster than sequential filtering on one GPU, scales near-ideally across GPUs, and, given enough resources, has runtime independent of trajectory length. We demonstrate the method on a single-protein optical tweezer recording, where distinct conformations produce the same signal, and beyond biology on the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and financial market volatility.

title: Unbounded traces, Connes' index theorem for measured foliations, and the Godbillon-Vey invariant in KK-theory
abstract: We prove that unbounded positive traces define KK-elements with real coefficients. Such traces naturally arise from invariant transverse measures on foliations (Connes, 1979) and, more generally, on Lie groupoids (Crainic--Mestre, 2019). As an application, we build a canonical KK-element with real coefficients whose associated map of K-groups is the Godbillon-Vey invariant as constructed by Connes. In the process, we show how Connes' index theorem for measured foliations can be deduced from the Connes-Skandalis longitudinal index theorem, using cyclic cohomology.

title: A stratified version of geometric realizations
abstract: Given a simplicial set $X$, let $\operatorname{B}({X})$ denote its poset of nondegenerate simplices.
