We define a natural stratification $\left\vert{X}\right\vert\rightarrow\operatorname{B}({X})$. When $X$ is locally finite, we prove that this stratification is conical. Moreover, if $X$ is finite, we prove that the exit path category $\operatorname{Exit}^{\operatorname{B}({X})}(\left\vert{X}\right\vert)$ satisfies the geometric realization formula $\mathop{\operatorname{colim}}\limits_{σ:Δ[p]\rightarrow X} \operatorname{Exit}^{\operatorname{B}({p})}(Δ^p)\simeq\operatorname{Exit}^{\operatorname{B}({X})}(\left\vert{X}\right\vert)$ where the colimit is indexed by the category of simplices of $X$.

title: DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings
abstract: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. We formalize these metrics in a unified integral form and show that the weight of a local error decays as the $(k+q)$-th power of its size, where $k$ is the dimension of the integration domain and $q$ is determined by the penalty function. Guided by this analysis, we propose DrawScore, which projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines, as in engineering drawings, and applies a saturating penalty along the projected curves, so that the weight of a local error decays only linearly. Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders, and on outputs of existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs that IoU rates as nearly perfect. DrawScore further improves generation as a reinforcement learning reward and, for CAD generation from engineering drawings, serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth or an additional reward model. Our code is available at https://github.com/UESTC-Simon/DrawScore.

title: The Limit Is in the Input, Not the Model: State-Dependent Command Safety in Natural-Language Interfaces to Industrial Controllers
abstract: Language models judging commands to industrial controllers may not receive machine state, the equipment's current condition. The same command can require opposite safety decisions in different states, so an incorrect answer may reflect missing information rather than poor reasoning. We propose an answerability audit: does the model receive the information needed to decide? The audit records the model's inputs and pairs the same command with two states requiring opposite answers. The paired score counts a pair only when both answers are correct. We add rules, then state values, to the model's input. In an author-built test of 15 pairs from three systems with four language models, none reliably distinguished the paired cases without state, even with rules. With state, scores ranged from 0 to 13 correct pairs out of 15; three models improved. With text alone, one model always allowed commands and another always denied them. Their overall (raw) accuracies differed by 32 percentage points; both scored 50% balanced accuracy, which weights safe and unsafe cases equally, and no correct pairs. A rule evaluator matched all 15 pairs by applying the same rules that supplied the expected answers; this is not an independent safety test. The audit complements systems that check actions against safety rules: it checks whether the model receives the information needed for those decisions. This helps evaluators separate missing-input problems from model errors. These small-sample scores do not establish general model reliability.

title: Endpoint behaviour of vertical and horizontal Riesz transforms for the flow Laplacian on homogeneous trees
abstract: We study endpoint estimates of Riesz transforms on a homogeneous tree equipped with its canonical flow measure $μ$. We prove that the known boundedness from $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)$ to $L^1(μ)$ of the vertical Riesz transform can not be strengthened to boundedness on $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)$ itself. We also prove that the adjoint vertical Riesz transform is not of weak type $(1,1)$. For the scalar horizontal transforms defined by nonzero bounded coefficients with zero sum on each child set, we establish $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)\to L^1(μ)$ boundedness and show that failure to preserve cancellation on atoms prevents boundedness on $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)$. We then introduce a horizontal derivative based on deviations from sibling averages. Its associated Riesz transform retains the $L^p(μ)$ bounds for $1<p<\infty$ and the weak type $(1,1)$ estimate, and is bounded on $H^1_{\mathrm{at}}(μ)$ itself. These mapping properties parallel those of horizontal Riesz transforms in the continuous setting, supporting our construction as a natural discrete analogue. These results distinguish vertical and horizontal behaviour at the endpoint and identify cancellation on sibling sets as a mechanism for Hardy-space boundedness.

title: Hi Gemini, Who Should I Vote For? The Benefits (and Problems) of Using LLMs As Voting Advice Applications
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can provide voters information about political issues, party positions, and even advise on which party to vote for. However, no previous study explores whether off-the-shelf LLMs could be used as voting advice applications (VAAs) to improve voter-party congruence. In this article, we address this gap by examining how Gemini 3 Flash advises a sample of 6,022 German survey respondents on which party to vote for, based on their policy preferences and priorities alone. In brief, we find that for most respondents, following the LLM's advice would benefit voter-party policy alignment (i.e. congruence), with a significantly stronger remedial effect among voters with low levels of political interest and formal education. However, our analysis also reveals concerning biases in the LLM's recommendations. For instance, the LLM suggested voting for the AfD at approximately 1.5 times the frequency of a standard salience-weighted proximity model. In addition, the LLM hardly ever advised voting for either Die Linke or the BSW. We conclude that while LLMs can approximate the behaviour of VAAs, users should be aware that the LLM's recommendations are still biased in ways that are extremely difficult to trace.

title: Discovery of HEC14: an ultra-faint stellar system in M31's outer halo at the globular cluster-dwarf galaxy boundary
abstract: We present the discovery of HEC14, an ultra-faint stellar system near M31, visually identified in the Pan-Andromeda Archaeological Survey and characterised with deeper OSIRIS+@GTC imaging. HEC14's colour-magnitude diagram shows a clear red giant branch and a well-populated blue horizontal branch, indicating old (>10 Gyr), metal poor stellar populations. We find 912$^{+88}_{-80}$ kpc to be the best-fitting heliocentric distance to the satellite, consistent with M31's outer halo. With $M_{V} \sim -5.00^{+0.51}_{-0.44}$ and a half-light radius of $r_{\rm h} \sim 31^{+13}_{-9}$pc HEC14 lies in the size-luminosity gap between globular clusters and dwarf galaxies. The satellite therefore sits in the extended clusters (EC) regime, making it one of the faintest ECs discovered yet in M31. HEC14 is a new member of M31's halo EC population, whose origins remain unclear two decades after their discovery. We serendipitously find that HEC14's size and luminosity match theoretical predictions for dwarf galaxies with globular cluster-like sizes. Star formation history and/or spectroscopic studies are required to determine whether HEC14 (and possibly all ECs) is genuinely an extended globular cluster or a compact dwarf galaxy.

title: Regularity and stabilization of integral closures of powers of homogeneous ideals
abstract: In this paper, we establish explicit polynomial bounds for the regularity defect and the stabilization index of integral closures of powers of arbitrary homogeneous ideals over fields of any characteristic. Specifically, let $I \subseteq K[x_{1}, \dots, x_{n}]$ be a nonzero proper homogeneous ideal generated in degrees at most $d$. We prove that $\reg \overline{I^{s}} \le ρ(I)s + d^{(n-1)2^{n}}$ for every $s \ge 1$, where $ρ(I) \le d$ denotes the eventual slope of $\reg \overline{I^{s}}$. Furthermore, the stabilization bound is polynomial in $d$ for a fixed number of variables $n$. In characteristic zero, an upper bound for the first Hilbert coefficient yields a significantly sharper exponent. Our approach relies on exact equigenerated reductions, free lattice constructions within normalized Rees algebras, monic Frobenius presentations, and Tor-module regularity controls, complemented by generic source hyperplanes that reduce the stabilization behavior to the eventual nonvanishing of graded components.

title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
abstract: Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program. In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection. We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous $Z$- and $X$-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

title: Moment approximations in optimal transport: geometric estimates and a semiclassical limit
abstract: We study finite moment approximations of linear optimization problems over measures. Under suitable assumptions, we establish the existence of discrete minimizers with a controlled number of support points, duality and $Γ$-convergence as the moment approximation is refined. This framework accommodates several transport problems, in which marginal constraints are replaced by finitely many moment constraints. For moment functions localized at scale $r_n$, we prove an estimate controlling $W_\infty$ by $W_p$ up to an additive error of order $r_n$, which also applies to discrete measures. For repulsive costs, we show that minimizers remain separated from the diagonal, uniformly in the number of moments, and we derive consequences for dual potentials. Finally, under a moment-correction assumption, we prove that the fermionic minimum energies converge in the semiclassical limit to the moment-constrained Coulomb transport value for a fixed family of moment functions.

title: Stealing Exact Training Data from Other Clients during Federated Learning
abstract: Malicious adversaries can employ gradient inversion attacks to reverse-engineer private data using the model updates of a round in Federated Learning. While there have been developments in gradient inversion for text, exact text recovery by a malicious client has so far remained infeasible, as FedAvg entangles the gradient contributions of many clients and obscures the signal of any individual sentence. We introduce a novel attack pipeline that unwinds this entanglement progressively through an iterative loop, in which the gradient contributions of sentences recovered exactly in one round are subtracted from the aggregate, exposing the remaining sentences for recovery in the next iteration. We show, for the first time, exact sentence recovery, with 100% precision, and on aggregates containing up to $4\times$ more tokens than the model's hidden dimension, we recover up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly, a regime where existing attacks recover none exactly.

title: An $\infty$-category approach to $A_\infty$-algebras and $A_\infty$-categories
abstract: $A_\infty$-algebras over a commutative ring $R$ are generalizations of $R$-algebras in which multiplication is only associative up to higher homotopies. Similarly, $A_\infty$-categories over $R$ are generalizations of $R$-linear categories in which composition of morphisms is only associative up to higher homotopies. They are important in the definition of Fukaya categories in Symplectic Geometry, and in other areas of mathematics. By $\infty$-categories we mean quasicategories, a class of simplicial sets which are a model for $(\infty,1)$-categories, used in the work of Jacob Lurie. We define and study $\infty$-categories of $A_\infty$-algebras and $A_\infty$-categories. Our approach is unusual in that rather than defining them by localization, we construct our $\infty$-categories completely explicitly as simplicial sets. Our $\infty$-categories are intended for applications to Fukaya categories in Symplectic Geometry. Given a suitable symplectic manifold $(X,ω)$, one should construct its Fukaya category ${\mathscr F}(X,ω)$, a (filtered) $A_\infty$-category, and its derived Fukaya category $D^b{\mathscr F}(X,ω)$, a triangulated category (or better, a stable $\infty$-category). Typically ${\mathscr F}(X,ω)$ depends on many arbitrary choices. Our $\infty$-categories give a clean way to explain in what sense ${\mathscr F}(X,ω)$ and $D^b{\mathscr F}(X,ω)$ are independent of these choices.

title: Regge Dilaton Gravity from Feynman Diagrams
abstract: Baratin and Freidel showed that closed Feynman diagrams in three and four Euclidean dimensions can be expressed as expectation values of observables in a Regge-type topological model \cite{baratin_hidden_2007, baratin_hidden_2007-1}. We extend their analysis to two dimensions with spherical, flat, or hyperbolic background geometry. Specifically, we show that the reduced Feynman amplitude of any closed (planar) scalar graph can be represented as an observable insertion in the partition function of either a discretized BF theory, whose gauge group is the isometry group of the background, or a homogeneous Regge discretization of linear dilaton gravity.

title: Combinatorial Bloch-Gieseker inequalities on toric surfaces
abstract: We give a combinatorial proof of the Bloch-Gieseker inequalities in the special case of ample toric vector bundles on toric surfaces via a new rearrangement inequality for planar curves. Using this we establish the Hodge package for combinatorial analogues of cohomology rings of ample projective bundles over toric surfaces which don't appear to arise from matroidal constructions.

title: Spectrally Correlated Frequency Spreading Codes for FRESH Filtering-based Interference Cancellation
abstract: Frequency shift (FRESH) filters can achieve co-channel interference cancellation by exploiting spectral correlation statistics of both the desired and interfering signals. In orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) signals, spectral correlation can be introduced in a structured way by symbol repetition across subcarriers. While this repetition generally requires duplicating symbols by an integer multiple of 2+ times (significantly impacting spectral efficiency), in this work it is shown that applying an incomplete spreading code, that trades spectral efficiency, to the desired signal can control its spectral correlation properties at redundancy factors less than 2. The distribution of the spectral correlation across frequencies determines the level of protection against interference at a given frequency. We introduce the design of frequency spreading codes that provide uniform spectral correlation distribution across frequencies, which provides equal interference cancellation capability independent of the center frequency of the interfering signal. The introduced spreading code can achieve arbitrary code rates while possessing two important properties: 1) semi-orthogonality and 2) spectral correlation uniformity. We evaluate the BER performance at very low signal-to-interference levels SIR$=0, 5 $ dB comparing spreading, LDPC, and LDPC+spreading at equal code rates.

title: Pole parameters of the $f_2(1270)$ and $f_2'(1525)$ from a coupled-channel analysis of the radiative $J/ψ$ multipoles
abstract: We determine the pole parameters of $f_2(1270)$ and $f_2'(1525)$ from the combined fit to the isoscalar $D$-wave $ππ$ phase shift, the $ππ\to K\bar K$ modulus, and the BESIII $J/ψ\toγπ^0π^0$ and $γK_SK_S$ data: all three $2^{++}$ multipoles $E1$, $M2$ and $E3$, and the $M2$-$E1$ phases. The hadronic amplitude is a two-channel $K$-matrix with two poles and all parameters free, so that no resonance information is taken from the Particle Data Group. The radiative decay amplitudes are written as a coupled-channel Muskhelishvili-Omnès representation, with the Omnès matrix generated by that hadronic amplitude. The left-hand cuts, which carry the production dynamics, are approximated by a linear subtraction polynomial in the physical region. The model-independent kinematic constraints among the $J=2$ helicity amplitudes are implemented explicitly. The fit describes all $358$ points with $χ^2/N=1.29$ and gives $\sqrt{s_p}=(1267.5\pm1.3\pm2.6)-i\,\frac{1}{2}\,(175.5\pm2.4\pm7.4)\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for the $f_2(1270)$ and $(1514.8\pm2.8\pm1.5)-i\,\frac{1}{2}\,(80.4\pm3.4\pm4.8)\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for the $f_2'(1525)$, where the first uncertainty is statistical, from a parametric bootstrap with the data errors rescaled by $\sqrt{χ^2/N}$ of each set, and the second systematic, from $17$ variations of the analysis.

title: Singularities of ideals with minimal tangent space dimension in the Hilbert scheme of points on a threefold
abstract: We classify all singular monomial ideals in the Hilbert scheme of $d$ points on $\mathbb{A}^3$ whose tangent spaces have the minimal dimension $3d+6$. There are two families called the opera houses and rotating staircases, and we give their combinatorial and algebraic descriptions. All the opera houses are in one linkage class, and their singularities are smoothly equivalent to the vertex of a cone over the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(2,6) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{14}$ in its Plücker embedding. The rotating staircases split into many linkage classes and we give some examples.

title: Improving Zero-shot 3D Semantic Mapping in Offroad with Geometric Priors
abstract: Semantic 3D mapping is a powerful representation that enables platform agnostic mobile robot navigation in challenging offroad conditions. Current vision foundation models can accurately predict semantics zero-shot on structured scenes but performance is compromised in natural environments. On the other hand, 3D point clouds encode valuable information for discriminating semantics in scenarios where vision foundation models fail. In this work, we propose fitting a sphericity-elevation distribution for each semantic class to act as geometric anchor. Only the points with the most confident vision foundation model predictions are considered when fitting to produce high quality geometric prior distributions. The geometric prior is fused with the vision foundation model prediction to produce the final semantic mapping. The proposed prior improves SAM3 baseline by +6.3 in mIoU and +8.9 in accuracy on the RELLIS-3D dataset, and by +1.7 in mIoU and +2.1 in accuracy on the WildScenes dataset. The source code will be made public upon paper acceptance.

title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

title: Deep Multiwavelength Constraints on the Host Galaxies and Black-Hole Growth of Dwarf AGNs
abstract: We present a multiwavelength population study of 56 X-ray-detected dwarf galaxies ($M_* < 3 \times 10^9 M_\odot$), comprising 31 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and 25 galaxies (not satisfying AGN classification) in the Chandra Deep Fields North and South. Utilizing ultra-deep Chandra observations together with high-resolution JWST and HST imaging, we investigate the demographics, host-galaxy properties, environments, and cosmic evolution of accreting black holes in low-mass galaxies out to $z\approx4$. We find no statistically significant differences in either the local environments or non-parametric morphologies of X-ray AGNs relative to mass- and redshift-matched inactive dwarf galaxies. These results suggest that AGN activity in dwarf galaxies does not generally require ongoing major mergers or strong large-scale disturbances. Using a single power-law model for the specific accretion-rate distribution, we infer a positive cosmic evolution of dwarf-galaxy black-hole growth. Both the observed AGN fraction and the long-term average black-hole accretion rate increase toward higher redshift and show a positive stellar-mass dependence. Many dwarf AGNs exhibit weak optical and near-infrared AGN signatures, consistent with moderate accretion rates and, at high redshift, potentially enhanced obscuration. The small number of detected systems at $z>2$ limits definitive conclusions, but their hard X-ray colors suggest that obscuration may play an increasingly important role in the dwarf AGN population in the early universe. Our results support a picture in which black-hole growth in dwarf galaxies proceeds through largely stochastic or secular processes while gradually increasing in prevalence toward cosmic noon, providing new empirical constraints on the low-mass end of black hole-galaxy coevolution.

title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Québec French
abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Québec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Québec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.

title: The Asymptotic Capacity of the Grabbag Channel With and Without Feedback
abstract: The grabbag channel models communication through a randomly mixed store. At each use, an input ball of one of $K$ colors is inserted into a bag containing $M$ balls, and one of the resulting $M+1$ balls is selected uniformly, observed, and removed. We show that, when $2\leq K\leq M+1$, both the capacity without feedback and the capacity with noiseless strictly causal output feedback are at most $9.77(K/(M+1))^{2/3}$, and that, when moreover $M+1\geq2^{22}$, both are at least an absolute constant times $(K/(M+1))^{2/3}$. Hence, both capacities are of order $(K/M)^{2/3}$, and of order $M^{-2/3}$ for every fixed $K$. The converse is a single bound on the information that a feedback code conveys in $n$ uses, valid for every initial state. For each initial state, it bounds the information in each output by the change of a potential of the posterior law of the state given the earlier outputs, defined through noisy cube roots of the color counts. A budget on the true state bounds the total cost of the uses in which the inserted color is rare. The lower bound uses a statistic of two output histograms whose expectation does not depend on the unknown initial composition, an outer code, and words with prescribed compositions. We also show that the channel is indecomposable and relate its capacities to the finite-state-channel information formulas.

title: Coherent-Response and Thermal-Fluctuation Information in Cavity-Magnon Magnetometry
abstract: Magnetic sensing with cavity--magnon systems typically relies on the coherent response, while field-dependent fluctuations are treated as measurement noise. Here, we show that the variance of a measured microwave quadrature provides a distinct source of magnetic-field information. For repeated phase-sensitive measurements of a calibrated quadrature, we derive the Gaussian likelihood and show that its Fisher information separates exactly into two terms. The coherent-displacement term depends on the field derivative of the quadrature mean, and the thermal-fluctuation term depends on the field derivative of its variance. Both terms are accessible from the same measurement record, but their optimal operating conditions differ. For the amplitude quadrature, the dimensionless coherent response factor reaches its global maximum at cooperativity $C=2$, corresponding to a coupling strength $g=\sqrt{2κ_aκ_m}$, and at linewidth-normalized detunings $δ_a=δ_m=\pm 1$. In the near-resonance approximation, the reduced variance-information term is globally maximized at cavity--magnon frequency matching, $Δ_a=Δ_m$, and approaches a finite limit at large cooperativity. We map the relative contributions of the two terms across drive frequencies, drive strengths, and temperatures. Strong coherent driving favors displacement-based sensing, whereas at finite temperature the variance contribution can dominate under weak driving and remain finite even when the coherent-displacement contribution vanishes. These results establish a measurement-specific framework for cavity--magnon magnetometry and identify operating regimes for exploiting the quadrature mean, its variance, or both.

title: Task-Oriented Network Ranging via Joint Graph and Schedule Design
abstract: Measuring inter-node distances is the basis for network localization, whereas acquiring node positions does not require a fully connected graph of distances. Existing complete-ranging protocols for network localization require every node pair to exchange signals, which prolongs the ranging cycle. In this paper, we propose sparse signal-multiplexing network ranging (S-SM-NR), a task-oriented framework that adapts the transmit-listen schedule to the ranging task required by network localization. First, we establish the S-SM-NR framework by formulating the joint design of the task graph and the transmit-listen schedule. Then, we analyze the minimum round count required by S-SM-NR and establish a connectivity condition for network localization. Subsequently, we develop a closed-form joint design that constructs the sparse task graph and the balanced transmit-listen schedule. In particular, the joint design can achieve the minimum round count under the complete physical connectivity. Finally, simulations show that the proposed S-SM-NR scheme reduces the occupied-round count and improves the localization accuracy by shortening the ranging cycle.

title: A simplicial model for manifold calculus through the configuration category
abstract: Let $M$ be a closed $d$-dimensional smooth manifold and $X:Δ^{op}\rightarrow\operatorname{Fin}$ a finite simplicial set whose geometric realization is homeomorphic to $M$. Given the $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}\mathrm{isk}_{/M}$ of disks embedded in $M$ and the path components functor $π_0:\mathcal{D}\mathrm{isk}_{/M}\rightarrow\operatorname{Fin}$, we construct a cofinal functor $Γ_X:Δ^{op}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\mathrm{isk}_{/M}$ such that $X=π_0\circΓ_X$. This result provides an alternative construction of a simplicial model developed by Boavida de Brito, Lambrechts, Pryor and Songhafouo Tsopméné to compute the space-valued presheaf $\operatorname{Emb}(-,M):\mathcal{D}\mathrm{isk}^{op}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}$. We also extend the result to manifolds with a $G$-structure and discuss applications to manifold calculus, factorization homology, and a possible generalization to manifolds with boundary.

title: Efficient orders for reciprocal matrices with block structure
abstract: We consider block partitioned reciprocal matrices. For these matrices, we characterize the efficient vectors whose subvectors, corresponding to principal blocks, are positive multiples of given efficient vectors for those blocks. This generalizes a prior, scalar oriented, extension theorem. Conditions are presented that guarantee the existence of efficient vectors that preserve ordinal relations associated with cross-block comparisons. The notion of order transitivity is also generalized to block reciprocal matrices. For such matrices, it is then shown that efficient vectors, with no rank reversals in positions corresponding to off-diagonal blocks, exist. The notion of uniformly ordered reciprocal matrices (all efficent vectors exhibit the same order) is also generalized in the block reciprocal setting. This class is characterized via known matrix bounds for the consistent matrices associated with efficient vectors. We also provide a graph-theoretic characterization of the existence of a positive vector that is efficient for all completions of a given partial reciprocal matrix. Based on this, we apply some of our results on ordering to such matrices.

title: Chemotactic aggregation as cue-mediated adaptation toward Nash equilibrium in a spatial patterning game
abstract: Chemotactic cells generate their own chemical gradients to form spatial patterns that support collective functions ranging from cooperative metabolism to immunity. Despite progress in understanding the optimality of chemotaxis in imposed chemical gradients, it remains unclear how close decentralized cell populations can come to maximizing the population-wide benefit of spatial organization through individual movement and local modulation of chemical gradients. We employ mean field game theory to characterize efficient spatial patterns achievable by decentralized populations as Nash equilibria: each agent optimizes its positioning given the spatial density of the other cells, whereas the population density is determined by the positioning of all individuals. We derive coupled dynamics of population movement and cue modulation that drive adaptation toward these equilibria and verify its structural correspondence to established phenomenological models of chemotactic pattern formation. We apply our framework to self-organized aggregation and numerically demonstrate that the dynamics can form multiple equilibrium patterns, some of which are comparable to the population-level optimum under moderate incentives to aggregate. We also show that the relative timescales of cue modulation and movement influence pattern selection and population-level efficiency: slower cue modulation can yield more coherent and efficient equilibrium patterns. Our framework thus highlights fundamental limits on collective optimization in decentralized cell populations, and suggests a functional role for timescales in self-organized coordination through environmental feedback.

title: Can Omni-modal LLMs Understand Spoken Intentions?
abstract: Omni-modal large language models (omni-modal LLMs) can respond to spoken requests directly through voice and video calls. Such requests rely on the scene shared by the user and the assistant, so the same utterance may call for different help or for no response. Most audio-visual benchmarks provide questions as separate text input, and interactive benchmarks mostly score a response as a whole. It thus remains unclear whether a model recognizes when the user is asking for help, and whether its reply meets the user's need once the request is recognized. We propose O-IN-Bench to evaluate how well omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions. A model watches a complete video with native speech and outputs one text response, or [SILENCE] when no response is needed. O-IN-Bench contains 1,000 Chinese and English samples in five categories and 16 subcategories. Contrastive pairs combine the same request with different scene conditions to test whether the response changes with the context. A sample-specific rubric judges language, intent, and content separately, and O-IN-Engine verifies each rubric against the video. Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, the best overall score is 59.6, achieved by Gemini3.7-Flash. Gemini3.7-Flash passes 74.4% of the intent judgments but only 42.6% of the content judgments. When the speech is a conversation between peers rather than a request to the assistant, even strong models often keep responding. When a reply must satisfy several people, the best score is only 25.9. These results indicate that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities, and O-IN-Bench measures each of them.

title: The Long and Winding Pore: Tuning Porosity in Templated Nanoporous Carbons
abstract: Disordered materials pose a recurring challenge for molecular simulation: realistic structural models are often generated through thermal protocols in which several structural descriptors emerge simultaneously and cannot easily be varied independently. Nanoporous carbons constitute a particularly relevant example: pore size, wall order, curvature, and network tortuosity generally emerge as outcomes of the thermal preparation protocol, rather than being independently prescribed structural parameters. Moreover, for practical applications, models of porous materials should ideally exhibit a percolating pore network, capable of supporting end-to-end transport of adsorbed species through the material. To this end, here we introduce a hierarchy of templating strategies, built around a common melt-quench-anneal protocol driven by a machine-learned interatomic potential for carbon, that progressively separates these variables. A rigid cylindrical template interacting with the environment through a tunable Lennard-Jones potential provides independent control over pore size and local wall organization, while leaving the structural disorder of the surrounding carbon matrix essentially unchanged. Generalizing the template to a spring-connected, tortuous backbone further allows pore geometry and curvature to be prescribed without qualitatively altering the local templating mechanism established for the straight pore. Finally, making the template mobile lets the growing carbon network reshape it in turn, which sharpens pore boundaries and allows sub-nanometer pore sizes to be targeted precisely, as needed for applications such as supercapacitor electrodes. Ultimately, this approach enables systematic studies of structure-property relationships in porous materials for applications such as energy storage, desalination and gas capture.

title: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?
abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.

title: The computational complexity of Undirected Vertex Geography with maximum height 3
abstract: The impartial game Undirected Vertex Geography is known to be polynomial time solvable. The variant in which vertices are assigned heights with maximum value m that reduce by 1 whenever the token is moved from that vertex, denoted UIRm, is known to be polynomial time solvable when m=2 and PSPACE-complete when m=4. We solve the open question of the computational complexity of UIR3 by a reduction from Directed vertex geography, and show that the complexity holds when the underlying graph is planar and (a) has degree at most 3, (b) is bipartite with maximum degree 4, or (c) is bipartite with maximum degree 5 and only has heights of 1 and 3.

title: The magical memory cost of entanglement spectrum compression
abstract: How much quantum memory is needed to faithfully retain the entanglement spectrum of a bipartite pure state after separating out Bell pairs through local unitaries? We derive the exact tradeoff between Bell-pair yield, residual memory, and reconstruction fidelity under local unitaries, defining an operational measure of entanglement-spectrum complexity. Smoothed entanglement spread bounds this memory cost from below, while diverging nonlocal magic forces unbounded memory at any fixed positive fidelity. Chaotic circuit dynamics exhibit a transient memory peak whose height increases with system size, followed by declining cost despite continued entropy growth. A large typical Haar-random state requires only an accuracy-dependent memory, whereas stationary fermionic Gaussian states retain a growing cost with size. In the circuits studied, the multiscale spectral structure associated with entanglement catalysis also has a practical consequence for matrix product state compression, yielding a multiplicative overhead not captured by the conventional entropy-based bond dimension estimate.

title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

title: Flexibility for the Monge-Ampere system implies flexibility for isometric immersions into Riemannian manifolds
abstract: We prove that any flexibility result for the Monge-Ampère system implies the corresponding flexibility result for the isometric immersion system, with the same Hölder regularity. We treat the general isometric immersion system, in which both the source and the ambient metrics are arbitrary Hölder regular, in arbitrary dimension and codimension. Combining this implication with existing results for the Monge-Ampère system, we obtain new ${C}^{1,α}$ flexibility statement for isometric immersions with arbitrary source and ambient metrics. To our knowledge, these are the first such results for non-Euclidean ambient metrics.

title: Low-dimensional optimal stopping with rank-dependent loss
abstract: Sequential selection problems with independent observable scores and rank-dependent objectives are not reducible, in general, to dynamic optimisation over a state space of fixed dimension. We consider optimal stopping problems with truncated loss structures through the lens of the planar Poisson process, where self-similarity removes the time variable and the state is reduced to the $m$ lowest scores observed so far, rescaled to the initial time. For $m=1$ the optimal rule stops at the first record below a hyperbola, which is found by a sliding-window argument. For $m=2$ we derive the equations for the boundaries of the stopping sets of $1$-records and $2$-records, solve them explicitly on a part of the state space, and express the optimal values by quadratures. The value function and the optimal strategy are characterised by a static integro-differential equation. The optimal strategies are compared with simple low-parameter rules, which are close to optimality.

title: The Structural Number of Parties: An Electoral-Outcome-Independent Baseline for Comparing Party-System Scale
abstract: How many parties can a country structurally sustain? Standard measures such as the effective number of parties (ENP) cannot answer this question. They are descriptive and post hoc: they summarize competition only after an election, and they depend on electoral returns that are often missing, interrupted, or unreliable in many developing democracies, particularly in Africa. They also offer no common scale for comparing the size of party registers with realized electoral fragmentation. We introduce the Structural Number of Parties (SNP), an outcome-independent baseline derived from two universally available quantities: population size and territorial area. Building on the logic of the seat product model and the cube-root law of assembly size, the SNP gives an ex ante benchmark that can be computed for any country and year, including where electoral data are absent. Applied to African states, the SNP enables a structural gap diagnosis that distinguishes under-fragmented systems, marked by hegemonic-party dominance, from over-fragmented ones, marked by excessive atomization. The framework thus provides a transparent and reproducible tool to inform institutional reform and the rationalization of party systems across the continent.

title: Interpersonal trust, institutional trust and trust in technology in Air Traffic Control
abstract: Air traffic control (ATC), the safe, orderly and efficient management of planes through controlled airspace is a complex task. In this article, we explore the roles that different kinds of trust play in ATC. Our study provides the essential foundations for examining the conditions that need to be satisfied if Air Traffic Controllers are to establish and sustain trust relationships with technical innovations, such as agent-based systems, and so ensure their safe and dependable embedding within ATC work.

title: The Lyapunov and uniform spectra
abstract: The \textit{Lyapunov spectrum} of a linear cocycle (or vector bundle) is the set of Lyapunov vectors with respect to all ergodic probability measures for the base topological dynamical system. This spectrum disregards trajectories that are atypical from the measure-theoretic viewpoint, and so it is in general insufficient to determine important properties of the cocycle, such as existence of dominated splittings. We resolve this deficiency by introducing a larger set which we call the \textit{uniform spectrum} of the cocycle. This definition is akin to Misiurewicz and Ziemian's rotation set. We prove several properties of the Lyapunov and uniform spectra, including relations between them. Motivated by a theorem of DeWitt and Gogolev, we consider Hölder-continuous cocycles over hyperbolic homeomorphisms and then provide bounds for the uniform spectrum in terms of the Lyapunov spectrum. We exhibit additional connections to the literature.

title: On automorphisms of symplectic varieties acting trivially on the second cohomology group
abstract: We prove that the group of automorphisms acting trivially on the torsion-free part of the integral second cohomology on a primitive symplectic variety is a locally trivial deformation invariant. We exhibit some examples of this invariant.

title: Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning
abstract: Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $μ$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.

title: DRIFT: Detachable Reasoning for Runtime-Flexible and Efficient End-to-End Driving
abstract: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. Project page: https://drift-e2e.github.io/

title: Balanced Simplicial Complexes for the $γ$-Vectors of Zig-Zag Eulerian Polynomials
abstract: In this paper, we construct a simplicial complex whose $f$-vector equals the $γ$-vector of the descent polynomial of an arbitrary canonically labeled rank-one poset. As an application, we prove Petersen and Zhuang's conjecture that the $γ$-vector of the normalized zig-zag Eulerian polynomial is the $f$-vector of a balanced simplicial complex.

title: Induction Head Origins of SLAM-ASR Speech Recognition Models
abstract: What makes a small trained map from encoder states to the embedding space of a frozen language model sufficient for competitive speech recognition? The premise of the SLAM-ASR architecture is that a frozen language model possesses linguistic knowledge rich enough to perform the recognition task. This assumption, while reasonable, provides little insight into the mechanisms underlying these models. We therefore seek the concrete internal structures on which they rely. This work shows that SLAM-ASR models rely on induction heads of the frozen language model: the same heads that copy repeated token sequences in text are also important for mapping speech embeddings to transcript tokens. Moreover, we find pairs of heads that behave as a constrained form of differential attention, cancelling attention noise and sharpening attention onto the previously generated word. Finally, we show how induction heads could be used to improve transcription quality under noisy audio.

title: Proof-Relevant Interpolation for Circular Proofs in Linear Logic
abstract: First introduced for proving Craig's interpolation theorem, Maehara's method provides a constructive, proof-theoretic procedure for extracting interpolants in sequent calculus proofs. Building on this method, Saurin developed a ``proof-relevant'' interpolation theorem for first-order linear logic, in the sense that the interpolated proof is obtained by cut-introduction steps that can be reversed via cut-elimination. In this work, we extend Saurin's proof-relevant interpolation to linear logic proofs with cuts as well as to circular proofs in linear logic with fixed-points. We specifically show how Maehara's method can be extended in a proof-relevant way to work on non-cut-free and non-well-founded (but regular) proof objects, and guarantee that the interpolation procedure preserves strong validity. We also study conditions under which one can interpolate system L terms that are not necessarily in normal form.

title: Multi-Band Galaxy Novel-View Synthesis with Radiative Gaussian Fields
abstract: We propose a novel view synthesis tool for galaxies based on Gaussian Splatting (GS). Unlike RGB data, where GS has achieved success, galaxy observations consist of multi-band signals from a massive number of bodies, contain complex patterns of cross-band interactions, and capture light propagation in highly heterogeneous media. As a result, the underlying physical process poses great challenges in model representation and optimization, which have not been investigated in existing research. To this end, we propose a physically inspired Gaussian Splatting method, GalaxyGS, which is equipped with physically meaningful components that capture both the energy emission mechanism of different astronomical bodies and the light propagation between them. In the absence of directly comparable baseline methods, we adopt a wide range of possible alternative approaches. Comparisons conclusively demonstrate that GalaxyGS is better in accuracy and physical fidelity across datasets and metrics.

title: On a Secretary Problem with Two Equal-Sized Pools of Candidates
abstract: This paper presents the solution of a secretary type problem where the decision maker observes a sequence of offers of two types. There are N objects of both types and these objects appear to the decision maker in random order. Objects can only be compared when they are of the same type. The objects of a given type that have already appeared can be ranked according to a complete order. Objects of different types are not comparable. On the appearance of an object, the decision maker must decide whether to accept that object (and thus stop searching) or irrevocably reject it (and thus continue searching). The goal of the decision maker is to accept an object that is the best of its type. The authors present the general form of the optimal policy and the asymptotical solution. The authors give a strong result describing whether an object of relative rank one should be accepted when the same number of objects of both types have been seen.

title: An Atiyah--Hirzebruch to Adams map and the hastened Adams spectral sequence for supercohomology
abstract: We construct a map of filtered spectra inducing a map from the Atiyah--Hirzebruch spectral sequence (AHSS) to the Baker--Lazarev Adams spectral sequence of a $\mathit{ko}$-module $M$. Using this and a theorem of Bruner--Rognes, we construct a hastened Adams spectral sequence (HASS) for the Postnikov truncations of $\mathit{ko}$ and the connective Adams summand. Then, motivated by questions in quantum field theory, topological phases of matter, and tensor category theory, we apply the HASS to supercohomology, the cohomology theory $I_{\mathbb{C}^\times}(τ_{\le 2}\mathit{ko})$, and observe that in examples of interest it is easier to calculate with than either the AHSS or the usual Adams spectral sequence. We include a User's Guide to the HASS and several worked examples, as well as hastened Adams charts for many commonly encountered $\mathcal{A}(1)$-modules.

title: Generalization of Text Line Segmentation for HTR in Historical Documents
abstract: In this paper we investigate the generalization capability of state-of-the-art object detection models (Hi-SAM, YOLO, and RT-DETR) for the automatic segmentation of text lines in historical documents. Generalization is needed because it is not practical for museums and archives to produce large amounts of labeled samples for each new collection. We also evaluate the few-shot setting by fine-tuning the networks with only a small number of training samples per target dataset. To this end, we use nine different datasets that differ significantly in visual layout and language. Additionally, we discuss why mean average precision (mAP), a classic evaluation metric for object detection, is insufficient for assessing the quality of a text line segmentation model. Depending on the dataset, our CRNN models achieve character error rates (CER) ranging from 2.48% to 7.07% per page for the segmented text lines. This is sufficient for reading comprehension and simple text searches. Finally, we quantify the resource and time requirements of training and inference in different use case settings. This forms the basis for more informed decisions about model and hardware choices based on available resources.

title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
abstract: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

title: How Generative Models Generate: A Concise Guide to the Generative AI Landscape
abstract: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.

title: Large deviation principles for component counts in the dense regime
abstract: This paper develops large deviation principles for component counts in dense random geometric graphs. We consider a homogeneous Poisson point process on the flat \(d\)-dimensional torus and study the number of isolated components of fixed order \(k\) at connection radii above the connectivity scale. Two types of large deviation behaviour are investigated. First, we prove a Donsker--Varadhan large deviation principle in the regime where the expected number of such components tends to infinity. Second, we study the opposite extreme regime, where this expectation tends to zero, and establish fixed order tail measure limits for the associated \(k\)-component isolation-volume point process. As a consequence, we obtain functional large deviations for the moving threshold component count process.

title: Finite-temperature effects on the single-particle Green's function of a mobile impurity in a Luttinger liquid
abstract: We consider the problem of a quadratically-dispersing quantum impurity interacting through a contact density-density term with a one-dimensional (1D) superfluid described by Luttinger liquid theory. By means of a field-theoretical approach based on the linked-cluster expansion, we quantitatively address the effects of a finite temperature of the 1D bath on the momentum-space single-particle Green's function. Through a careful identification of the resonant phonon-impurity scattering processes, we obtain asymptotic large-time estimates for the thermally-induced exponential damping of the zero-temperature signal both in the $\textit{quasiparticle}$ regime, dominated by the presence of a finite lifetime for the host impurity, and in the $\textit{infrared-dominated}$ regime, where the impurity causes a Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe of the 1D bath. In both cases, we identify a temperature-induced coherence time that sets the characteristic timescale of the exponentially-decaying finite-temperature correction to the amplitude of the zero-temperature single-particle Green's function. Moreover, we draw connections between the aforesaid thermal timescale and the microscopic parameters of the Lieb-Liniger model, which admits an effective Luttinger-liquid description, highlighting the dependence of the inverse coherence time on the intra-bath interactions across the different dynamical regimes of the impurity.

title: HandWorldBench: A Unified Benchmark for Hand-Centric World Models
abstract: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.

title: Slope stability for normal varieties
abstract: In this expository paper, we review the theory of slope stability of torsion-free sheaves with respect to nef curve classes and extend it to normal varieties.

title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

title: Infrared spectrum of the Type Iax supernova remnant Pa30
abstract: The central star of Pa30 and its nebulosity offer one of the best opportunities to study a SN Iax explosion and its remnant. Pa30 is thought to be the product of the historical supernova explosion of 1181. No infrared spectroscopy of its extremely hot central star has hitherto been reported. Here, we present a 0.75-5 $μ$m spectrum taken by the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), together with ground-based infrared spectra, at higher resolution, covering the 0.8-2.5 $μ$m region. The spectra contain very broad lines, which we have attempted to identify and model using the codes CMFGEN and CLOUDY. The CMFGEN modelling suggests that most of the lines are due to OVI. However, CLOUDY modelling, using expected theoretical abundances for the bound remnants of SN Iax explosions, provides evidence for the presence of coronal lines of Si, S, Mg, and Al arising from a shocked gas. This strengthens the suggestion that Pa30 is indeed the remnant of a SN Iax explosion.

title: A disproof of the El-Zahar--Erdős conjecture
abstract: El-Zahar and Erdős asked whether every graph of bounded clique number and sufficiently large chromatic number contains two vertex-disjoint induced subgraphs, each of large chromatic number, with no edge between them. We give a negative answer even for triangle-free graphs. For every integer $g \ge 4$, we show by a probabilistic argument that there exist graphs of girth at least $g$ and arbitrarily large chromatic number in which any two vertex-disjoint induced subgraphs that each require at least seven colors are joined by an edge.

title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks
abstract: A physics-based reduced-order model unifies curved-meniscus inertia, viscous losses and nonsmooth contact-line stick-slip in a passive port-Hamiltonian formulation for lateral sloshing in cylindrical tanks. Dirichlet-Neumann and Jacobi operators describe inertia and restoring forces, while a convex potential combines bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line dissipation. Analytical propagation between stick-slip events supports faster-than-real-time simulation of coupled spacecraft translation and sloshing. The viscous closure agrees within 5% with a reference Stokes calculation, and the model reproduces the Henderson-Miles modal measurements and the Cocciaro hysteretic decay. Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduces the root-mean-square frequency error from 24 to 4%. For flight and ground tests from the Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE), frequency errors range from 0.9 to 7.1%, while ideal contact lines underestimate the damping ratios from the MODE fits by 38-87%. One hysteresis width, calibrated on the lowest orbital water excitation, predicts higher orbital excitations and the ground test with normalised force errors of 11-35%, against 149-208% for an ideal pinned line. It predicts 8.5% resonance softening against 7.3% measured, which the tested one-parameter damping laws miss. Uncertain wetting and remaining response discrepancies motivate damping ranges in spacecraft control analyses.

title: Approximate Dynamic Programming with Basis Function Learning
abstract: This work presents a novel approach for approximating the value function in Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our approach is grounded in the approximate linear programming (ALP) framework, wherein basis functions (BFs) play an important role. Traditionally, BFs have been pre-defined, randomly generated, or restricted to specific structures, which both limits the accuracy that can be achieved and leaves no mechanism for improving a given approximation. We instead learn BFs from the model itself, by repeatedly applying the Bellman operator to the current value estimate. We introduce the Bellman operator basis function (BOBF) learning method, and prove that each learned BF improves the approximation by a quantifiable amount and that the method converges to the optimal value function. Its shrunken counterpart (SBOBF) retains this guarantee while capping the number of BFs, and therefore the computational effort per iteration. For large-scale problems, where the number of constraints is prohibitive, we develop hybrid variants (HBOBF and SHBOBF) that combine constraint sampling with BF learning, and we show that the improvement and finite-termination guarantees are preserved under explicitly stated conditions. Numerical experiments on (continuous) perishable inventory and queueing control problems demonstrate that our BF learning techniques significantly outperform existing methods in the literature.

title: Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate
abstract: System One models such as Jev return decisions through fast, parallel prediction. In this paper, we introduce Jeveration, showing that the same decision paradigm can also generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its visual-semantic knowledge for holistic image generation. The key challenge is to maintain global consistency. A single prompt admits many valid images, yet parallel predictions must converge on a coherent whole. We therefore condition all positions on a shared random state to coordinate parallel predictions, so that each draw yields a different but coherent image. Since the model tends to ignore this state under direct image supervision, we first learn a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation. Beyond text-to-image generation, we further unify image-to-image generation and dense prediction within the same architecture, so that one checkpoint supports all three tasks, each in one forward pass. Experiments show that Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms, up to 122x faster than existing unified models, while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.

title: Uneven gains in protein-RNA affinity and mutation-effect prediction
abstract: Accurate matched affinities determine mutation effects, but gains in aggregate affinity prediction may transfer unevenly to average effects, ordering and local accuracy. We evaluated eleven method families using method-specific matched populations. Controlled CoPRA reduced absolute-affinity mean absolute error from 1.2898 to 1.1431 pKd. Across 220 mutation pairs from 20 families, it generated stronger responses and improved mean-effect accuracy, with uncertain ranking gains and no decrease in mean centered local error. In an independent external test (24 quantitative pairs from three source-matched families), absolute and ordinary mutation-effect errors fell in all three families. Mean centered local error fell from 0.4198 to 0.3761 pKd, with improvements in two families and higher error in one. Error decomposition localized gains in landscape means. PRA-Pred feature tracing, fixed-weight M2-PRNet input controls and matched supervision interventions identified specific restrictions on mutation response. These results establish the need to evaluate average effects, ordering and quantitative local variation jointly.

title: An Upper Bound on the Proportional Choice Number of a Graph
abstract: Proportional choosability is a list analogue of equitable coloring introduced in 2019 that imposes both upper and lower bounds on color class sizes based on the availability of each color. The proportional choice number of a graph $G$, denoted by $χ_{pc}(G)$, is the smallest positive integer $k$ such that $G$ is proportionally $k$-choosable. A recently proposed conjecture states that for any graph $G$ with at least one edge, $χ_{pc}(G) \leq Δ(G) + \text{col}(G) - 1$, where $Δ(G)$ is the maximum degree of $G$ and $\text{col}(G)$ is its coloring number. In this paper, we prove this conjecture using a generalization of Edmonds' matroid intersection theorem due to Aharoni and Berger, in which one of the matroids is replaced with an abstract simplicial complex. As a consequence, we can completely determine the proportional choice number of every path: $χ_{pc}(P_1)=1$, $χ_{pc}(P_n)=2$ for $2 \leq n \leq 5$, and $χ_{pc}(P_n)=3$ for $n \geq 6$. This resolves a question about paths that has remained open since the introduction of proportional choosability.

title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70\% to 75\% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.

title: Comparing Lower and Upper Spectral Gaps of Nonnegative Symmetric Matrices
abstract: We establish sharp estimates comparing the lower and upper spectral gaps of nonnegative symmetric matrices. Combining these comparisons with a multiplicity argument in the spirit of Li and Liu, we improve and extend earlier spectral gap comparison bounds of Saha and Li and Liu, which provide quantitative refinements of an observation of Breuillard, Green, Guralnick and Tao relating combinatorial expansion to two-sided spectral expansion. Our graph estimates hold for nonbipartite even-walk-regular graphs, which covers the classes of graphs, including vertex-transitive graphs, (twisted) Cayley graphs, and (twisted) Cayley sum graphs, investigated in previous work. Under an additional eigenmap assumption, we also establish quantitative two-sided comparisons between the lower and upper spectral gaps. In particular, these comparisons apply to walk-regular graphs.

title: Squeezed Cooling and Lasing with Cold Atoms in Cavity-QED
abstract: A squeezed laser undergoes a lasing transition into a squeezed cavity mode, where stimulated emission generates a bright coherent field with a laser-like coherence time while maintaining one field quadrature below the vacuum noise level. Here we propose an optical implementation that needs neither a nonlinear crystal nor injected squeezed light, based on engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum, a mechanism we term squeezed cooling, yielding up to 9 dB in the intracavity field, surpassing the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators. Tuned for output instead, it reaches up to 18 dB of output squeezing. Incoherently pumping a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, emitting a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum spanning a megahertz-wide band, away from the sharp phase-diffusion peak of excess noise at the carrier frequency, and robust to relaxation oscillations. We characterize lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing, and identify the experimentally accessible regime where the system exhibits the defining features of a squeezed laser.

title: GenerativeQC: A Generative, GPU-Accelerated Quantum Chemistry Program
abstract: GenerativeQC is an open-source, GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry program that computes energies and analytic nuclear forces from Hartree-Fock (HF) and density functional theory (DFT) to closed-shell density-fitted CCSD(T) and an MP2-assisted CCSD(T)/complete-basis-set (CBS) composite. Its scientific compiler translates symbolic equations into C++ and CUDA code and uses automatic differentiation to generate the derivative and response programs that analytic forces require. A native runtime executes these programs together with hand-written iterative solvers and integral routines. Across HF and DFT benchmarks for eight methods on water clusters of up to 96 atoms, GenerativeQC is faster than GPU4PySCF in all 128 comparisons on an RTX 5090 GPU and in all but two comparisons on an H100 GPU.
