Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.

title: The limits of inertia bounds on graph powers
abstract: We investigate the tightness of inertia and inertia-type bounds related to graph powers. This class of graphs appears in several contexts, such as the theory of distance-regular graphs, quantum information theory and coding theory. They are a priori not covered by previous separation constructions involving locally sparse graphs, see Kwan and Wigderson (2024), or Alon's pseudorandom graphs, see Elphick, Tang and Zhang (2025). Instead, we apply the latter's lower bound for complements of pseudorandom graphs to random graphs and random Cayley graph constructions, whose graph-power structure is ensured by additive combinatorial arguments. From this we are able to conclude that also for graph powers there can be a large gap between inertia bounds and the actual independence number. For the inertia-type bound, which is based on polynomials, we achieve even larger separation by considering sequences of graphs whose spectrum converges to a continuous distribution. Our methods draw from several areas of mathematics, ranging from additive combinatorics and probabilistic methods, to character sums over finite fields and arithmetic geometry.

title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part II: The momentum convection term
abstract: The two-phase Volume-of-Fluid solvers of OpenFOAM overpredict the horizontal water velocity near the crest of a water wave, and the error grows as the wave propagates. Part I of this series removed the spurious air velocities caused by the gravity term but left this error unchanged. Here we show that it is caused by the momentum convection term. Its mass flux is computed in the interface advection step from the velocity at the start of the time step, whereas the convected velocity is taken at the end of the step, because convection is discretised implicitly. In a progressive wave, where the horizontal and vertical velocities are 90 degrees out of phase, this time lag produces an upward flux of horizontal momentum, proportional to the time step, which accumulates in a spurious current near the surface. The same mismatch makes the response to a force depend on the density at the wrong time level. Explicit convection removes the lag and makes the response consistent with the gravity force, but requires the convected face velocity at the interface to be taken from the upwind cell. Only then is the new velocity of a cell a weighted average of old velocities, whatever the density ratio. We demonstrate both requirements with prescribed flows and with the full solver. For a progressive wave, explicit convection with upwind face velocities at the interface reduces the overprediction of the crest velocity from 26-31 % to within 1 % and removes the near-surface current. The resulting solver, fluxinator, is meant for maximum Courant numbers of 0.1 and below, where it keeps the wave height within 1.5 % over 15 periods on meshes with six or more cells per wave height. Because the spurious velocities that limit the time step are removed, it needs 34-42 % less wall-clock time than interFoam for the tested wave.

title: Choosing What to Observe: Budget-Paired Counterfactual Audits for Credible Evaluation of Visual Agents
abstract: Visual agents that read dense documents must ration a finite observation budget across candidate regions, yet answer accuracy conflates where an agent looks, how it adapts to the reads that remain, and how it an?swers once observation stops. We introduce budget-paired counterfactual audits, an evaluation protocol that holds public evidence and region bindings fixed while perturbing only the remaining budget or de?clared task parameters, and credits every acquired history with exact continuation values. The resulting accounting decomposes lost expected accuracy into stepwise acquisition loss and terminal decision loss, separating planning from fixed-role heuristics. Across forty paired routing anchors, five open-weight

title: The Ceresa Cycle on $X_0^+(p)$
abstract: We consider the curve $X_0^+(p)$ with prime $p$, which is the quotient of the modular curve $X_0(p)$ by the Fricke involution. We describe how one can explicitly calculate the shadow of a Hecke operator on $X_0^+(p)$, which is a rational divisor on $X_0^+(p)$ whose nonvanishing is an obstruction to the Ceresa cycle of $X_0^+(p)$ being torsion in the Chow group of the Jacobian of $X_0^+(p)$. We also provide an implementation of this procedure in PARI/GP and SageMath and use this on all primes below 5000.

title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

title: Kinetic study of Reaction-Control-Jet Interference in Rarefied Hypersonic Crossflow
abstract: A 1975 wind-tunnel study at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) of a helium jet blowing from a flat plate into a Mach 11 to 12 air crossflow at three freestream densities is revisited using two- and three-dimensional Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) computations at Knudsen numbers 0.021 to 0.125. The planar slot used in two-dimensional model computations reproduces the shock topology, the sign and two-lobed structure of the interference pressure and its trend with rarefaction, and its plate-alone boundary layer is consistent with the three-dimensional one and with a similarity solution with slip and temperature jump. However, two-dimensional simulations overpredict the peak interference pressure about twelvefold at every condition and carry it farther upstream. A resolution sweep at the most rarefied condition converges the planar interference to within 1% of its extrapolated limit. Three-dimensional DSMC reproduces the measured interference pressure at all three densities, within 25% at the lobe peak and 3 mm in its position, although two- and three-dimensional simulations overpredict the plate-alone wall pressure by 50 to 75%. Continuum breakdown around the jet persists even at the lowest Knudsen number examined. Fully three-dimensional kinetic simulations are underway to extend the present validation to a comparison of jet strength and forces over wider Knudsen number ranges, and to an examination of lateral relief as a reason for the discrepancy.

title: Pair Siegel-Veech constants for branched covers of tori and Veech surfaces
abstract: For a locus $\mathcal{E}$ of branched covers of tori satisfying a monodromy assumption, we show there exists an explicit constant $c_A(\mathcal{E})$ so that the number of pairs of saddle connections on surfaces in $\mathcal{E}$ of length at most $R$ and cross product at most $A$ grows like $c_A(\mathcal{E})R^2$ for every Diophantine surface in $\mathcal{E}$; this constant is moreover piecewise linear in $A$. In particular, this covers the case of billiards on rectangles with a barrier. Similar pointwise results are shown for Veech surfaces. The proof uses work of Margulis-Mohammadi on the quantitative inhomogeneous Oppenheim conjecture.

title: MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
abstract: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs. We present MicroAssert, a microarchitecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions through structured contracts and deterministic verification primitives. Coverage-guided feedback further improves verification completeness by progressively expanding proof-relevant RTL coverage. Evaluated on five open-source RISC-V CPUs against three existing assertion generation approaches, MicroAssert achieves 100% syntax correctness and complete branch, statement, and toggle coverage, with an average proven rate of 74.82% and Proof Core coverage of 90.96%. Mutation testing further demonstrates its advantage, achieving an average error detection rate of 28.73%, 1.99 to 3.51 times higher than existing methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of microarchitecture-aware assertion generation.

title: TangentPDE: Learning Local Operator Responses with Sparse Finite-Difference Supervision
abstract: Neural PDE operators are often optimized through state reconstruction, which largely constrains operator values at observed inputs but does not fully characterize their sensitivity to local perturbations. A more faithful approximation of operator behavior requires not only accurate state predictions, but also correct variations along local perturbation directions. We present TangentPDE, which uses finite differences to approximate directional derivatives and constructs task-relevant finite-step responses from the state outputs of a reference solver at sparse paired inputs. Its objective jointly constrains state fidelity, response-direction alignment, and response-magnitude calibration, thereby learning both operator values and their local variations. Because the response labels are constructed solely from state outputs at paired inputs, the method requires neither explicit derivative labels, linearized or adjoint PDE solves, nor full Jacobians, and remains applicable to nonlinear solvers without derivative interfaces. Building on this, we additionally propose a selectively executed adaptation mechanism to strengthen local operator representations under finite-difference supervision. Budget-matched and correspondence-perturbed controls isolate the effect of relational supervision from improvements attributable to additional state observations or increased data volume. Designed as a plug-and-play training framework, TangentPDE integrates with diverse neural-operator backbones. Across four PDE systems and 20 task-backbone settings, TangentPDE lowers the three-seed mean state error in 18 settings and the corresponding Rollout@20 error in 18, while intrinsic finite-step response gains are strongest on DiffReact and remain task- and backbone-dependent elsewhere.

title: Rotating black hole thermodynamics at NNLO in higher-curvature gravity
abstract: We investigate higher-curvature corrections to black-hole thermodynamics in quasitopological gravity using perturbative Euclidean-action methods. Static, spherically symmetric black holes provide a benchmark for the action expansion, while our main application concerns five-dimensional, asymptotically flat, rotating black holes with equal angular momenta. For Einstein gravity supplemented by Gauss--Bonnet and cubic quasitopological interactions, we compute the Gibbs free energy through next-to-next-to-leading order, retaining both quadratic and cubic corrections. The result retains the full dependence on the background spin parameter, without a slow-rotation expansion, and extends to arbitrary couplings of quadratic and cubic curvature invariants. We derive the corrected mass, entropy and angular momenta, and show how rotation affects the size and sign of the corrections.

title: Cameron--Martin theorem for SLE welding measures
abstract: For $κ\in(0,4]$, we prove a Cameron--Martin theorem for the welding law induced by SLE$_κ$ loop measure. Under simultaneous left and right composition $h\mapstoφ\circ h\circψ^{-1}$, the transformed law is mutually absolutely continuous with respect to the original law exactly when both maps belong to the Weil--Petersson group, and is mutually singular otherwise. Thus the Weil--Petersson group is the quasi-invariance group of the welding law under composition on either side. We also prove that it is its own normalizer in the group of orientation-preserving circle homeomorphisms. For Weil--Petersson pairs, we derive an explicit Radon--Nikodym derivative in terms of a relative action well defined for SLE weldings and prove that it belongs to $L^{1+\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ depending on the pair.

title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.

title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.

title: From geometric curvature to effective backgrounds: a dictionary for Dirac fermions in one, two and three spatial dimensions
abstract: Dirac equation on curved backgrounds can be rewritten as a flat-space equation in which geometry appears as a tensorial Fermi velocity together with a set of background fields. We derive this correspondence from a single Clifford-algebra identity and follow it through one, two, and three spatial dimensions. Once the spin connection is written in terms of Ricci rotation coefficients, only two contractions can occur. The trace produces a term with the index structure of a vector potential in every dimensionality; it enters with an imaginary factor i and is precisely the term that keeps the operator Hermitian when the Fermi velocity depends on position. The totally antisymmetric contraction produces an object that depends on the number of indices available to the Levi-Civita symbol: a trace on a line, a pseudoscalar mass on a surface, and an axial vector potential in a volume. Neither contraction is invariant under local rotations of the frame, and we give the transformation laws. On a surface, the curl of the trace term can always be removed by a frame rotation, while its divergence is proportional to the Gaussian curvature. We apply the correspondence to a Gaussian bump, where the local density of states at the center falls below its flat value and obeys a closed form at low energy; to a wire, where a nonuniform lapse binds states inside the gap and a nonuniform velocity cannot; to stationary frames on a surface, where a circulating drag shifts the Dirac mass locally with either sign; and to twisted and rotating frames in a volume, where the axial term takes the form of a chiral chemical potential produced by the frame alone, or separates Weyl nodes in a rotating sample. We separate the geometric contribution from the lattice pseudogauge field that dominates the response of strained samples

title: Gauss--Bonnet theorem for o-minimal surfaces with isolated singularities
abstract: We study the relationship between topology and curvature of surfaces definable in an o-minimal structure. Our main result is a Gauss--Bonnet-type formula for closed (not necessarily compact) definable surfaces with finitely many singular points, expressing the Euler characteristic in terms of the total Gaussian curvature, the local densities at the singular points, and the density at infinity. As consequences, we obtain an inequality for definable minimal surfaces with isolated singularities and, for complex algebraic curves, a formula and an inequality relating the Euler characteristic, the total curvature, the multiplicities at the singular points and the degree.

title: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

title: Monoculture Robust Learning
abstract: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $ρ$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $ρ$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $γ$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = Ω(\log(1/γ))$.

title: Hurst Exponent Estimation with Quantum Wavelets
abstract: How accurately can the Hurst exponent $H$ of fractional Brownian motion be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, when every measurement interrogates the same realization? We extend the $ε$-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform in three directions: we remove the endpoint jump of circular filtering, derive the sampling distribution of the estimator, and compare readouts at equal query budgets. A one-qubit mirror extension removes the jump and keeps every coefficient that straddles a fold of the same order as an interior coefficient, for any compactly supported filter and circular shift. The transform for any such filter is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of its filter bank, and the energy share of a level is the success probability of one multiply-controlled reflection, which is both the controlled unitary of a Hadamard test and the oracle of amplitude estimation. For filters with at least two vanishing moments we prove a root-$N$ central limit theorem for the log-energy contrasts, independent of the limiting path norm, so the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal for deterministic query budgets under which the success count at every level diverges. For sparse counts we give a working multinomial--lognormal likelihood, exact in its readout model for direct measurement, and check its coverage by simulation. For paths of length $512$, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of $3$--$10$ for $H\ge0.5$, and with exact shares the nondecimated db2 estimator is $6$--$14\%$ above the root Cramér--Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of the leading qubits at every budget. At $H=0.9$ and $2^{20}$ queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE $0.0347$, against $0.0451$ for direct measurement and $0.0295$ with exact shares.

title: Teleoperated Haircutting with Delay Compensation and Passivity-Based Control for Unilateral Internet Teleoperation under Real Communication Uncertainties
abstract: Robotic haircutting requires accurate motion execution and reliable communication to safely reproduce the operator's commands. Internet-based teleoperation is a key enabling technology to remotely perform precise manipulation tasks such as haircutting. However, communication uncertainties, including variable transmission delays and packet jitter, degrade synchronization between the master and slave systems and affect tracking performance. This paper presents a unilateral Internet teleoperation framework for robotic haircutting that takes into account experimentally measured communication uncertainties. Three delay-compensation techniques, namely Zero-Order Hold (ZOH), First-Order Hold (FOH), and Low-Pass Filtering (LPF), are evaluated together with a classical proportional-derivative (PD) controller and a passivity-based synchronization controller. Unlike conventional studies based on synthetic delay models, the proposed framework is validated using communication data acquired from a real cloud-based teleoperation platform, where both packet delay and effective delay are characterized. The results demonstrate that combining delay-compensation techniques with passivity-based synchronization improves the robustness of unilateral Internet teleoperation under realistic communication uncertainties, providing a reliable control framework for robotic haircutting applications.

title: Bar formation and secular evolution in live Milky Way-like galaxies
abstract: Context. Bars and their boxy/peanut (B/P) shapes drive the secular evolution of disc galaxies, redistributing angular momentum and reshaping the radial and vertical structure of stellar discs. Bars occur in bulgeless to bulge-dominated hosts. Bars are known to grow and slow down, but how this relates to host galaxy structure remains poorly understood. Aims. We investigate how the formation and evolution of bars and B/P structures depend on the initial stellar mass and bulge fraction of Milky Way (MW)-like galaxies, and explore the links between disc kinematic settling, bar formation, resonance structure, and vertical thickening. Methods. We analyse fifteen isolated MW-like hydrodynamical simulations run with AREPO for 3 Gyr, spanning three stellar masses and five bulge fractions, with live stellar, bulge, and dark matter components. We measure bar properties via Fourier decomposition, locate resonances from circular and epicyclic frequencies, and quantify B/P evolution from the vertical stellar distribution. Results. Bar formation timing depends strongly on galaxy structure. Low-mass galaxies generally form bars only after global disc kinematics have settled, whereas the most massive systems can form bars while the orbital distribution is still evolving. All bars slow down and grow in strength and size, and remain in the slow-bar regime. B/P structures form shortly after the bar and keep growing, appearing much earlier in more massive and disc-dominated galaxies. Only one model shows a clear buckling event; the rest form B/P bulges through smooth secular evolution. Conclusions. Initial stellar mass and bulge fraction strongly regulate the timing of bar and B/P formation. We find a coherent evolutionary sequence linking bar growth, bar slowdown, and B/P assembly, whose timing is set by the initial disc structure rather than by its global kinematic settling.

title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
abstract: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

title: CREST: A Hardware-Aware GNN-Based Framework for High-Fidelity and Robust Superconducting Quantum Compilation
abstract: Quantum compilation on superconducting processors requires selecting a connected execution region whose topology and calibrated properties suit the input circuit. This choice constrains subsequent routing and influences the noise encountered during execution, yet aggregate hardware-quality metrics alone may not reliably predict the execution fidelity of a given circuit. Calibration updates can also change region suitability and trigger the rebuilding of calibration-dependent resource structures. We present CREST, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework that evaluates circuit-region compatibility before routing. It encodes gate dependencies and logical-qubit interactions alongside each candidate region's connectivity and current calibration attributes; bidirectional cross-graph attention relates the two representations, while real-device execution outcomes supervise candidate ranking. The trained scorer is reused with updated calibration attributes. Evaluations on 324 circuits from seven datasets on TianYan-176 show that CREST improves mean measurement-distribution fidelity by 19.03% over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest mean fidelity on every dataset. Furthermore, using updated calibration attributes, the same trained model maintains the highest overall mean fidelity across six measurement dates without retraining. With a unified model of circuit-region compatibility, CREST improves execution fidelity across diverse workloads and sustains that advantage as hardware calibration changes.

title: Ground, Iterate, Trace: Decomposing AI Research Ideation
abstract: Large language models have been widely used to generate plausible research ideas, yet it remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how generated novel proposals arise from prior scientific work. We introduce the Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic framework combining literature grounding, iterative development and explicit conceptual operators. CAR constructs a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved literature and equips an ideation agent with graph-retrieval tools and four operators: bisociation, analogy, exploration and elaboration. Each operator call is checked against structural acceptance conditions and recorded, producing a trace of intermediate transformations and declared literature sources. We evaluate CAR with two language-model backbones across 40 LiveIdeaBench research topics and two execution benchmarks. CAR achieves significantly higher methodological novelty (MN) than single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist. Its methodological novelty does not differ significantly from the Research Ideation Agent, while its feasibility scores are higher on both backbones. With a shared experiment executor, CAR achieves the highest pairwise win rate among the evaluated AI methods on FML-bench-Lite and BioXArena. In a ten-condition ablation study, MN point estimates favor CAR over one-step proposal on both backbones, but no MN contrast survives correction for multiple comparisons. The results do not establish a consistent quality benefit from explicit operators beyond free-form iteration. CAR makes the sequence of operations and declared literature sources inspectable, separating judged idea quality from procedural traceability.

title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

title: Improved Asymptotic Approximation Guarantees for Continuous-Review Lost-Sales and Dual-Sourcing Inventory Models
abstract: We study continuous-review inventory models with unit Poisson demand and deterministic lead times: single sourcing with lost sales and dual sourcing with backlogging. Xin [Operations Research. 70(1):111--128 (2022)] establishes an asymptotic approximation factor of 1.79 for each model in its proportional-growth regime. Under the same assumptions, we obtain a factor of 1.248977 for the better of base-stock and constant-order policies for lost sales and a factor of 1.599528 for the better of dual-index and tailored base-surge policies for dual sourcing. The benchmark is the optimal long-run average cost over all policies using only current and past information. For lost sales, lead time and the lost-sales penalty grow proportionally. For dual sourcing, the lead-time difference grows proportionally to the express premium, the extra unit cost of faster supply, while express lead time and backorder penalty remain fixed. For sufficiently large fixed backorder penalties, the dual-sourcing factor improves to 1.248977. The improvements follow from stronger lower bounds on the optimal cost. We retain intermediate constraints on mean inventory for lost sales and use events determined only by future demand to bound backlog costs for dual sourcing.

title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits
abstract: Symmetry-preserving (SP) variational quantum circuits restrict evolution to physically relevant sectors of Hilbert space, but symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee accessibility within those sectors. We show that a restricted generator set can possess a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks. The associated block populations are conserved and impose a kinematic upper bound on the fidelity with a target state. We then invert this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: candidate SP generators can be screened before variational optimization by asking whether they break the residual commutant, which invariant blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. For two orthogonal residual blocks we prove that a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra. We further derive a complex escape criterion: if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. A connected residual-block graph yields a natural multi-block generalization and suggests minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit design. We demonstrate this design principle in the XXZ and Hubbard models, where residual-algebra screening identifies SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions. These examples establish a unified route from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to predictive quantum circuit design.

title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.

title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.

title: AMISS: An Integrity Framework for Magnetic Navigation
abstract: Magnetic Navigation (MagNav) is a promising alternative to traditional systems like Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), offering resistance to jamming or spoofing attacks to which the latter are vulnerable. MagNav matches scalar magnetic measurements over time against a known map of Earth's magnetic anomaly in order to position a vehicle. MagNav is therefore sensitive to the quality of these maps, especially to errors in the survey data that the maps are derived from. In order to be a reliable and mature navigation technology, MagNav must satisfy integrity requirements for mitigation of such faults. To this end, a solution-separation monitoring algorithm is developed that performs a role equivalent to Advanced Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (ARAIM) in GNSS, which detects faults as well as generates worst-case bounds (protection levels) on estimation error for faults too small to be detected. It is shown how these integrity methods can be developed in a \emph{windowed-in-time} sense, where subsets of measurements over a time window are compared with each other in order to detect outliers that can potentially result from errors in the map. The applicability of the approach is demonstrated using results obtained using synthetic aircraft data with injected faults.

title: ProvCards: Artifact-Oriented Provenance for Heterogeneous Scientific Workflows
abstract: Reproducibility in scientific workflows is hindered by heterogeneous components and execution environments, as well as fragmented provenance capture. Although existing approaches offer established semantics and workflow-specific solutions, provenance remains difficult to capture, exchange, and compose across workflow boundaries. We present ProvCards, an artifact-oriented approach that treats provenance as a first-class artifact grounded in the W3C PROV Data Model. Individual workflow components can generate cards that are stored, exchanged, reused, and composed independently of any workflow system or centralized execution context. ProvDecks group related cards into portable scopes while preserving their identities. ProvGraphs provide derived views for provenance reconstruction, querying, visualization, and analysis. Together, these representations support coherent, task-specific provenance views across heterogeneous components, facilitating traceability, reuse, and reproducibility. We implement ProvCards using a graph-based infrastructure and evaluate them in a scientific data-processing workflow. The results demonstrate independent provenance capture at the component level, composition across component boundaries, and reconstruction for querying and analysis. ProvCards provide a portable, composable, and incrementally extensible foundation for provenance management in heterogeneous scientific workflows.

title: Efficient search for microlensed gravitational-wave signals with matched filtering and a two-image statistic
abstract: Gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences can be microlensed by compact objects along the line of sight, producing frequency-dependent waveform distortions. As standard matched-filter searches rely on unlensed templates without accounting for lensing effects, microlensed signals can lose signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) through template mismatch and suffer further losses from signal-consistency tests. We quantify both effects for the $\texttt{PyCBC}$ search using microlensed injections in simulated data. The two losses occupy different regions of lens parameter space in the geometric optics representation: template mismatch is governed by the relative magnification of the two images, while the consistency-test penalty is governed by their time delay. We show that a microlensed signal lies in the two-dimensional subspace spanned by a template and its time-shifted copy, allowing the relative magnification and Morse phase to be maximized over analytically, leaving only the time delay to search. The resulting statistic requires no extension of the template bank and reduces the median loss in re-weighted SNR from $10\%$ to $1.6\%$, and the $90^\mathrm{th}$ percentile from $41\%$ to $9\%$. At a false-alarm rate of one per day, the relative detection volume improves by about $6\%$ across all injections, and by a factor of $1.9$ for the $10\%$ of injections most affected by lensing. In addition to increased detection capacities, we also show how the detection statistic can be used to establish the lensed nature of the trigger. Therefore, the work proposed here lays the foundation for an effective search and identification of microlensed signals in gravitational-wave data.

title: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators
abstract: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.

title: Beyond hidden zeros and uniqueness in Tr$(ϕ^3)$: Block and rod zeros in any Tr$(ϕ^m)$
abstract: Hidden zeros have proven powerful tools for reconstructing amplitudes in Tr$(ϕ^3)$, a theory of colored scalars with cubic interactions. We show that these structures extend to any Tr$(ϕ^m)$ theory. For odd $m$, we construct \emph{block zeros} from orthogonal sums of consecutive momenta, generalizing the original cubic hidden zeros. For every $m\geq4$, including even $m$, we describe a second family of nonlinear \emph{rod zeros} through a rod packing problem. In Tr$(ϕ^4)$ this construction reduces to a simple rank-one condition on a matrix of momentum contractions. We connect this new zero to the classic threshold nullification zeros of Voloshin, where certain amplitudes in massive $ϕ^4$ theory vanish when all produced particles are at rest. Finally, we demonstrate the reconstruction power of these zeros. Assuming locality, we prove that the rod zeros uniquely fix all Tr$(ϕ^m)$ tree amplitudes for $m\geq4$ up to normalization. We also conjecture that the block zeros enforce both locality and unitarity for any Tr$(ϕ^m)$ theory with odd $m$.

title: When Time-Reversible Sensor Records Require Hidden Dissipation
abstract: A binary sensor record can be time reversible yet require dissipation in every compatible finite-state Markov model. For a four-state sensor with correlated dwell times, two observed switching statistics give an exact equilibrium criterion and, when equilibrium is excluded, a positive lower bound on entropy production independent of hidden-state number. An explicit four-state construction provides an upper bound on the minimum dissipation. For a noisy Poisson sensor, the bounds differ by less than a factor of two and vanish at a kinetic matching point while the sensor remains dissipative.

title: "I Don't Think It's a Scam": A First Look at Family Intervention Barriers in Elder Abuse Discussions on Reddit and Baidu Tieba
abstract: When older adults trust scammers despite warnings, families face obstacles to intervention. Complainants aged 60 and older reported \$4.9 billion in losses in 2024 to the U.S. Internet Crime Complaint Center. To investigate family intervention barriers to elder scams, we collected 2M Reddit posts from May 2021 to June 2026 and 2B Baidu Tieba posts from 2007 to 2026. The final corpora contain 13,082 Reddit posts and 3,933 Baidu Tieba posts, labeled using platform-specific codebooks, manual reference annotations, and LLM coding. Through a mixed-methods analysis, we find that scams often extend beyond a single incident and are reported alongside debt problems and broken family relationships. In 68.0\% of Reddit posts recording reactions, older adults showed resistance or continued involvement; in Baidu Tieba family-confrontation posts, 41.9\% showed continued belief. Relatives identified fraud in 74.4\% of Reddit posts and narrated cases on Baidu Tieba, but without the victim's consent, relatives may lack the legal authority to intervene. In Reddit posts recording reactions, account locks or credential changes appeared in 8.9\% under resistance or continued involvement, compared with 33.3\% under acceptance. Measures such as phone or network monitoring and financial takeover were reported more often under resistance. Recovering funds is very limited in posts recording follow-up results of fraud; Baidu Tieba users reported that police classified older adults' voluntary transfers as civil disputes.

title: New Observational Insights into Generalised Axion-Like Dark Energy
abstract: We consider a quintessence model based on a generalised axion-like scalar field potential, originally introduced as a phenomenological framework to describe the late-time accelerated expansion of the Universe. The model exhibits a tracking regime that alleviates the coincidence problem and naturally leads to a phase of late-time acceleration driven by an effective cosmological constant, without requiring fine-tuning of the scalar field initial conditions. In this work, we confront the background cosmological evolution of this model with current observations by performing a parameter inference analysis using cosmic microwave background distance priors, baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, Type Ia supernovae, the SH0ES distance ladder, cosmic chronometers, and gamma-ray bursts. This analysis allows us to assess the observational viability of the model, its ability to reconcile different cosmological datasets, and its statistical performance relative to $Λ$CDM.

title: Toward high-throughput, low-latency structural biology using light, Part I: Protein-ligand pose determination
abstract: We demonstrate for the first time that an optical spectroscopy - electron-vibration-vibration two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy (EVV 2DIR) - has sufficient structural competence to enable the reconstruction of the three-dimensional geometries of drug-protein binding at the level needed for practical drug discovery applications. Klug et al. previously demonstrated experimental detection of drug binding to a kinase using EVV 2DIR. Here we use a quantum mechanical approach to calculate and assign elements of EVV 2DIR spectra for the spectral region 1200-1800 cm$^{-1}$ / 1100-1800 cm$^{-1}$ of 92 protein-ligand complexes. This dataset includes ligand-target poses drawn from existing crystal structures and ligand-target poses created by docking and cofolding models. We find that binding-dependent spectral features are robust, interpretable, and consistent across poses in a given binding mode, and distinct for each unique hydrogen bonding geometry. We construct a spectral distance metric to distinguish poses that conform to the ligand-target hydrogen-bonding pattern of the crystal structure from those that do not. These results show that, given a set of predicted ligand-target poses containing the correct geometry, the hydrogen-bonding pattern of the valid pose may be rapidly identified by comparing simulated and experimental EVV 2DIR spectra. Finally, we discuss the practical implications for a new, high throughput structural biology for drug discovery that will be the subject of forthcoming manuscripts, noting that the base technologies to perform EVV 2DIR quickly and efficiently already exist and will enable a novel structure to be determined in only minutes for each sample. Moreover, this can be achieved without the need for crystallization, isotopic labeling, or low temperatures, non-destructively using picogram quantities of material.

title: Mine Locally, Verify Globally: Exact Recovery, Compilation, and Distortion of Mined Temporal Rules
abstract: Specification mining extracts temporal rules that describe relationships between events in recorded system traces. Applying these rules in distributed monitoring systems is more difficult because observations come from different nodes, whose clocks may not be synchronized, and events may be lost or reordered during transmission. In this paper, we study how to aggregate the coverage of mined rules across observers, determine whether their temporal windows are needed during monitoring, and characterize their detection under event loss. Our evaluation uses IPv6 packet traces collected from 21 receivers across four continents. We show that local mining followed by global confirmation recovers centralized rule coverage under suitable conditions while substantially reducing communication overhead. In contrast, merging traces with unaligned clocks can distort coverage by introducing incorrect temporal matches. A window-gain criterion identifies rules that require temporal state, while our loss analysis and broker experiments demonstrate why contiguous losses can be more damaging than independent losses. The results identify separate requirements for aggregating observations, selecting monitor state, and handling event loss.

title: A Geometric Calderón Problem for Differential Forms
abstract: We establish boundary determination and global partial-data uniqueness for Karpukhin's Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator on differential $p$-forms. We derive an explicit recursion for its full symbol and determine the full boundary jet of the metric, modulo conformal gauge in the critical dimension $n=2p+2$. For $p\geq1$, partial data determine metrics that are analytic in the interior and near the measured boundary subset, up to isometry or conformal equivalence. The global uniqueness relies on a new projection-kernel embedding that detects the unobserved boundary through rank loss and small eigenvalues. We also establish global partial-data uniqueness for smooth metrics with harmonic curvature, using elliptic-transport unique continuation and, in the critical dimension, conformal-geodesic coordinates. A Weyl nondegeneracy condition further upgrades conformal equivalence to isometry.

title: ShadowTransfer: A Geographic Transfer Benchmark for Overhead Shadow Detection
abstract: Overhead aerial imagery feeds dense-prediction pipelines that are routinely trained in one geographic region and deployed in another, yet no benchmark measures how shadow detection models transfer across regions. Existing overhead shadow datasets either lack a geographic transfer protocol or rely on automatically generated labels. We introduce ShadowTransfer, a benchmark of 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities at two native resolutions, paired with a leave-one-city-out evaluation protocol. Under vanilla training, holding out the test city costs 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU across four architectures, the gap remains significant when the training set grows from 225 to 900 images, and six of eight adaptation methods degrade more than vanilla training on average. We propose a three-probe framework that diagnoses where and how the transfer breaks: the failure operates in feature space, beyond the reach of pixel-histogram matching, shows up as a confidence collapse on shadow pixels while background confidence stays intact, and is recoverable by retraining different architectural components depending on the model: encoder for some, decoder for others. These findings replicate on INRIA building footprints, suggesting they describe geographic transfer beyond shadows. Guided by the diagnosis, we build Spectral Information Bottleneck (SIB), a plug-in module with one component per finding. Across the 9 (architecture, held-out city) cells, SIB has the smallest mean gap to the within-city upper bound of the ten methods we evaluate (6.42 mIoU), level with FDA. The benchmark, LOCO protocol, code, and trained models are released to support reproducible evaluation of geographic transfer in overhead dense prediction.

title: Batch-Dynamic Coreness and Applications with Logarithmic Work via Balanced Pressures
abstract: We give a parallel algorithm that maintains a one-sided $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation of all core numbers under batches of edge insertions and deletions. For fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the expected amortized work is $O(\log n)$ per edge update, and each batch has deterministic polylogarithmic depth. This improves on the previously known $(4+\varepsilon)$-approximation and $O(\log^2 n)$ amortized work bounds. This approximation factor approaches the factor-two limit for polylogarithmic update and query time under the OMv conjecture. Our algorithm is based on assigning each vertex a "pressure" and splits each edge's unit load smoothly between its endpoints according to their pressures. After each batch of updates, our dynamic algorithm adjusts the pressures of vertices in parallel to restore balance between the pressures and loads. We show that by maintaining balanced pressures we can obtain good approximations of core numbers. Our construction also gives a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of the densest-subgraph value with logarithmic expected amortized work and supports batch-dynamic maximal matching, clique counting, forest decomposition, and coloring in low-arboricity graphs with improved or matching work bounds. We give a practical implementation of our batch-dynamic coreness algorithm and find that it is able to achieve smaller empirical error than the state-of-the-art parallel batch-dynamic implementation, while running faster. On six real-world graphs, it runs $32\times$ faster than that implementation in geometric mean and $4.1\times$ faster than a state-of-the-art heuristic baseline. On three graphs with up to 1.8 billion edges, it is $9.2\times$ faster than the heuristic baseline.

title: Infinite cascades for the defocusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the square torus
abstract: For each $1<s<2$ we construct a solution of the defocusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the square two-torus with initial data in $H^s$ whose $H^s$ norm tends to infinity as $t\to+\infty$. The growth can be arbitrarily slow. More precisely, the squared norm agrees, up to a bounded error at all positive times, with the number of selected axial frequencies $K_j$ for which $K_j^s\le t$. The central construction couples a finite tree of orthogonal frequency pairs to a periodic one-dimensional solution of the same equation. Each transfer leaves a nonvanishing Fourier coefficient on the horizontal axis. Control on an entire half-line allows successive transfers to retain the coefficients produced earlier.

title: Shadowing Property for Linear Operators on Banach Spaces
abstract: This note is dedicated to the study of the shadowing property for (bounded linear) operators on Banach spaces. We combine the spectral characterization of the shadowing property, recently established by Dragičević and Pituk, with tools from local spectral theory, to obtain new results and simpler proofs of known results on shadowing for operators. We also prove that the shadowing property always implies the average shadowing property and the asymptotic average shadowing property for invertible operators on Banach spaces. Furthermore, we investigate the shadowing property for some specific classes of operators, such as weighted composition operators and adjoints of multiplication operators on certain spaces of holomorphic functions.

title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation
abstract: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.

title: Prediction and Screening of $η$-carbide-type Nitrides for Ammonia Synthesis
abstract: Synthesis of ammonia is of critical importance to applications in energy, industrial chemistry, and especially agriculture, and is accomplished industrially using the carbon- and energy-intensive Haber-Bosch process. η-carbide-type nitrides such as Co3Mo3N have gained attention in recent years as alternative ammonia synthesis catalysts with the potential to lower these energy demands. Co3Mo3N is experimentally observed to undergo a reversible phase transition from Co3Mo3N to Co6Mo6N, offering a chemical looping-based NH3 synthesis route that has not been fully explored. In this work, we present a first-principles exploration of phase change in the Co3Mo3N/Co6Mo6N system as a prototype η-carbide-type nitride and fit a cluster expansion to predict the energy of Co3Mo3Nx systems. We use our results to identify the phase energy difference as a useful screening criterion for the phase change process. We then apply this methodology to screen a broad range of η-carbide-type nitrides that combine group 4-6 transition metals with Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, or Zn. We report strong periodic trends in phase energy difference, which increases with decreasing period and group number of the group 4-6 transition metal and with distance from group 9 for the other metal. We identify Co3W3N, Fe3W3N, and several quaternary nitrides as promising candidates for NH3 synthesis via a phase change mechanism.

title: Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator
abstract: We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances. We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied to the ions. In addition, we demonstrate individual addressing of dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.

title: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound
abstract: An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform $O(λ^2)$ bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where $λ$ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains $O(λ^2)$ accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.

title: Stock bubbles in limited participation models with power utilities
abstract: We prove that the equilibrium state-price deflated cum-dividend stock-price process in Guasoni, Larsen, and Leoni (2025) is a strict local martingale. Our result is based on proving that the unrestricted trader faces an endogenously complete model.

title: Sharp Bounds for Selector Advice and Oblivious Equilibrium Search
abstract: Ko's tournament argument recognizes a P-selective language with quadratic advice. We determine the leading coefficient in the selector-query model. On $n$-bit inputs, $n^2/4+O(n)$ ordinary advice bits and $n$ nonadaptive comparisons suffice. Some cuts require $n^2/4-O(n\log n)$ bits even for randomized decoders with adaptive access to individual-degree-two extensions. At degree one the exact fixed advice width is $n+1$. Assuming exponential hardness in $\mathrm E$ against SAT-gate circuits, the quarter bound holds in deterministic polynomial time for every P-selective language. The same fixed point determines the cost of searching for an approximate equilibrium before seeing the payoffs. In an $N$-action symmetric constant-sum game with payoffs in $[0,1]$, let $P$ be the best worst-case probability that one game-independent proposal is an additive $ε$-Nash equilibrium. For each fixed $0<ε<1/2$, \[ -\log_2 P=(1+o(1))\, \frac{(\log_2 N)^2}{4[1-H_2(1/2+ε)]}. \] The algorithm draws uniform actions and proposes their empirical distribution for both players. The lower bound allows arbitrary mixed profiles and $N^{o(1)}$ adaptive payoff inspections before the proposal. For all symmetric two-player games, including general-sum games, the sharp exponent is $(\ln 2/8+o(1))(\log_2 N)^2/ε^2$ when $ε\to0$ and $\log(1/ε)=o(\log N)$. For security strategies in arbitrary zero-sum games the exponent is four times larger, and sampling an optimal strategy attains it. The common mechanism counts successful tuples. A fixed point makes them capture constant sampling probability while controlling a power moment of their distribution.

title: The role of externally-driven density fluctuations in the enhancement of beam spray
abstract: Speckled laser beams, commonly used to ionize and heat plasma for inertial confinement fusion and high-energy-density experiments, are shown to drive long-wavelength plasma-density fluctuations that induce beam spray in other laser beams. Experiments show that a 1053 nm beam undergoes increased beam spray when 351 nm speckled heater beams are on. These observations indicate that the high-intensity speckles sustain an increased level of steady-state density fluctuations. Modeling of these fluctuations predicts amplitudes that are orders of magnitude larger than the level of thermal fluctuations. Beam propagation simulations show increased beam spray due to self-focusing and filamentation when heater-driven density fluctuations are included.

title: PrismRestore: A Compact Restoration Toolbox for Agentic Image Restoration
abstract: Agentic image restoration composes operations to handle mixed degradations, yet its toolbox often requires storing multiple restoration networks. We propose PrismRestore, which constructs a compact bank of callable restoration actions from a single frozen all-in-one model. Our approach builds on task-dependent yet overlapping channel responses in the shared model. An offline task-prior search uses activation and gradient statistics to group channels with similar response profiles, then searches task-specific modulation coefficients over non-representative channels while leaving representative channels unmodulated. The resulting prior bank enables explicit action selection and composition without additional restoration backbones or task-specific adapter modules. A state-conditioned policy learns to compose these actions using Group Relative Policy Optimization. Its objective separately normalizes fidelity and perceptual feedback within groups of trajectories sampled for the same input, and combines terminal evaluation with return-to-go derived from stepwise quality changes. Experiments on synthetic composite-degradation and real-world multi-task benchmarks show improvements over the evaluated all-in-one baselines and restoration quality competitive with multi-model agents. PrismRestore achieves these results with a single restoration backbone and faster inference than the evaluated agentic baselines.

title: Locally infrared finite two-loop amplitudes for multi Higgs production in association with one jet
abstract: We study the two-loop amplitudes for multi-Higgs production through a massive top-quark loop in association with one jet. We consider the quark-antiquark channel with a final-state gluon, $q\bar q\to g+nH$ although our construction applies to crossed channel as well. We utilize (non-local in momentum space) Ward identities to factorize longitudinal and gauge degrees of freedom through exact identities between Feynman graphs without reference to an infrared region. In the genuine two loop topologies, we replace the internal gluons by their physical degrees of freedom and show that the resulting amplitude is free of collinear singularities. The only remaining infrared divergence is a soft singularity that can be identified with a change of reference gauge vector. We construct explicit soft counterterms for these singularities, obtaining a locally infrared-finite representation. We verify that the factorized longitudinal degrees of freedom reproduce the remaining infrared poles of the original Feynman graphs. Our formalism requires no counter-terms for collinear finiteness or for manifesting Ward identities in various regions since we perform a decomposition of covariant gauge Feynman graphs. We expect its extension to more complicated processes to eliminate all collinear singularities--particularly in the initial state.

title: Unified Law for Visual Tasks (The Four Laws of Computer Vision)
abstract: In this paper, we propose a Unified Law for Visual Tasks, which could be further divided into Four Laws of Computer Vision, with the goal of enabling a single framework or method to uniformly train on and perform nearly all visual tasks. Our starting point is an inspiration and hypothesis: if the world information is encoded into image, which we call World Snapshots, then image processing is world processing, and image generation is World Snapshot generation. Furthermore, if all visual and visualization tasks can be reformulated as generation tasks, then a unified method, World Snapshot Models (WSMs), can perform the vast majority of visual tasks, much as large language models have largely unified natural language processing. This paper validates these laws across more than 1,000 trained and evaluated visual tasks (defined by distinct input-output mappings) and presents a unified training framework for future visual-task research and applications.

title: Hardness of "Infinite Energy" Puzzles
abstract: Infinite Energy (by Light Potato, 2025) is a single-player puzzle in which one wires a network of sockets so that, after every power source is unplugged, energy keeps circulating and leaves every board energized. We study several variants of the game and the complexity of deciding whether an instance can be won. The variants can be played at https://infinite-energy-peer-review.netlify.app, which also has worked examples of the reduction techniques. The colorless game, with connectability given by an arbitrary matrix, is NP-hard (by reduction from Hamiltonian Path) and lies in PSPACE. We give a seven-socket instance winnable only by charging a temporary battery loop and then breaking it, so the natural "charge and keep" strategy fails. We reduce NP-membership to one conjecture: that every winnable instance has a winning play in which no socket is charged twice. Two variants bound the complexity more tightly. The unconstrained variant, in which connectability is unrestricted, is $\mathsf{TC}^0$-complete under $\mathsf{AC}^0$ Turing reductions (hence in L). The geometric variant, in which connectability is set by proximity of points in $\mathbb{R}^k$, stays NP-hard for every fixed $k \ge 2$ via reduction from Hamiltonian Path over grid graphs. The one-dimensional case is open. The colored variant is NP-hard, though a matching upper bound remains open.

title: Zero-Temperature Energetics of a First-Order Surface Phase Transition from Diffraction
abstract: First-order phase transitions are governed by the balance between zero-temperature energy, thermal vibrational energy, and entropy, yet these contributions are rarely accessible experimentally. Here, we establish a diffraction-based route to determine them for the prototypical Si(111)-In atomic-wire system. From the temperature-dependent Debye-Waller attenuation of reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) intensities we extract distinct Debye temperatures for the low-temperature $(8{\times}2)$ ground state and the high-temperature $(4{\times}1)$ phase. The softer vibrational spectrum of the high-temperature phase yields the entropy gain that stabilizes this phase above the critical temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$. Evaluating the thermodynamic balance between internal energy and entropy at $T_\mathrm{c} = 125\,\mathrm{K}$ yields a zero-temperature energy difference of $ΔE_0 = 138\,\mathrm{meV}/(8{\times}2)$, including the difference in vibrational zero-point energies of the two phases, thus providing direct access to hidden thermodynamic parameters of a first-order surface phase transition.

title: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2
abstract: We construct a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order in which every online rule earns strictly less than $1/2$ of the expected offline optimum. A common partition, revealed at the third arrival, gives the first three buyers one unit of welfare per item. If the rule uses three distinct partitions, either an item allocated early contributes zero or the fourth buyer's expected value for the remaining bundle is one less than its size. We compute the optimal online and offline welfare exactly and show that a $1/2$ guarantee always holds with at most three buyers.

title: Strong Epsilon-Near-Zero Confinement and Interface-Controlled Dynamics in Inverse-Designed Transparent Conducting Oxide Cavities
abstract: Achieving optical modulation that is both strong and ultrafast remains a central challenge in time-varying photonics. Here, we theoretically demonstrate that combining inverse-designed cavities that utilize transparent conducting oxides (TCOs) operating at the epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) point with boundaries that support carrier transport can meet this requirement. This is achieved by leveraging ENZ-enhanced optical absorption and electron heating with interface-engineered carrier relaxation. A multilayer inverse-design framework, combined with a structural disorder-aware correction loop, is developed to preserve robust resonant absorption in ultrathin TCO films under realistic material disorder. Relative to conventional TCO cavity geometries, the inverse-designed structures exhibit stronger light confinement, greater electron temperature modulation, and markedly faster recovery. Beyond cavity design, interfacial barrier engineering and adjacent-layer doping emerge as effective degrees of freedom for co-designing spectral and temporal dynamics.
