We characterize exactly when a mechanism has a finite EA-QDP parameter, and show that the optimal parameter $\varepsilon^*_{\mathrm{EA}}$ of any quantum mechanism can be computed by a semidefinite programming problem (SDP). Building on this, we quantify the extra privacy leakage caused by entanglement and show that it can be bounded by choosing appropriate mechanisms, with the depolarizing channel being our recommended choice. Finally, we demonstrate both the attack and its countermeasure on simulated and physical quantum hardware, and the experimental results agree with our theoretical predictions.

title: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.

title: Hindsight Self-Distillation: Teaching Robots to Act from the Present
abstract: A robot must choose an action before it can see the outcome. In a recorded demonstration, later camera frames show what happened after the robot moved. Hindsight Self-Distillation (HSD) uses these later frames to teach a policy what to extract from current images. During training, a teacher sees both the current and later frames, while a student sees the current frames. They share a visual encoder and an action predictor. Each branch summarizes its images with a small set of feature vectors. These visual summaries supply all visual input to the action predictor. The teacher learns from demonstrated actions. For each noisy action sequence, the student learns from either the demonstration or the teacher's denoising prediction. It also learns to match the teacher's visual summaries. We analyze which aspects of the teacher's predictions the student can recover from its inputs. At deployment, the student encodes the current images once and reuses its summaries at every denoising step. HSD achieves average success rates of 98.50\% on LIBERO and 92.31\% on RoboTwin 2.0.

title: ECHO: In-Context Behavior foundation model for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) acquire diverse skills through large-scale motion imitation and massively parallel reinforcement learning, yet broad behavioral capability does not ensure precise execution across physical conditions. Without distinguishing the underlying dynamics, policies may favor conservative compromises over environment-specific precision. We introduce ECHO, an in-context BFM that turns interaction experience into environment-specific control, separating general behavioral capability from dynamics-specific execution. Mixed and Annealed Sampling first establishes a behavior prior in a single pretraining stage by balancing targeted practice with broad motion coverage. Building on this prior, Context Representation and Residual Adaptation learns structured dynamics representations from interaction histories to guide residual corrections to the frozen prior, enabling adaptation without test-time parameter updates. Extensive experiments show that ECHO outperforms all baseline methods across diverse motions and physical conditions. Moreover, deployment on the Unitree G1 demonstrates whole-body teleoperation spanning extreme acrobatics and terrain interaction, alongside payload adaptation in manipulation and whole-body control. Page is available at https://mwondering.github.io/echo-bfm/

title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures
abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.

title: RouteVerify: Routing Interventions for Step-Level Verification in Mixture-of-Experts Models
abstract: Routing states in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps. If changing routing also changes a model's step-level verification judgment, it is tempting to conclude that the judgment follows what routing encodes. We test this inference with RouteVerify, a controlled intervention study that replaces selected internal activations from one solution trace with activations from another, while keeping the evaluated input unchanged. Across nine MoE checkpoints, we compare three intervention interfaces: router logits, MoE outputs, and post-MoE residual states. We vary the layers and token positions at which activations are replaced. We measure changes in a verification margin that quantifies the model's preference for INCORRECT over CORRECT. We also evaluate the same input with activations from correct versus erroneous steps to test whether the resulting judgment depends on the source step's correctness. We report four linked results. First, probes on router logits separate correct from erroneous steps in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88). Second, replacing router logits across all routed layers changes the judgment in all nine checkpoints, and by more than a norm-matched random replacement. Third, this change rarely depends on whether the source step is correct. At one layer, routing from erroneous steps and from correct steps produces indistinguishable margins in all nine checkpoints. Under all-layer routing, their difference is resolved and positive in only one. Fourth, the same difference is positive for local residual replacements in eight of nine checkpoints, so the measure does detect such dependence where it exists. Correctness is therefore readable from routing, and routing replacements move the judgment, but the movement rarely follows correctness.

title: Sonic Palette: Predicting Dynamic Color Themes from Music
abstract: We present Sonic Palette, a music-driven framework for predicting time-varying color themes from audio. Rather than treating music-to-palette generation as a static problem, our method formulates music--color correspondence as a cross-modal sequence prediction task that models how palette-level visual attributes evolve over time in response to music. Specifically, Sonic Palette uses a music-conditioned autoregressive Transformer to predict frame-wise color themes, each represented by five dominant colors, from input audio features. To support this task, we curate a dataset of paired audio--color sequences derived from 265 full-length official music videos. We further visualize the predicted color themes through a palette-guided recoloring process that preserves image structure while revealing temporally varying color appearance associated with the music. Quantitative results show that Sonic Palette predicts color themes that more closely match the ground truth, while subjective results indicate more natural temporal color transitions and stronger perceived music--color atmosphere alignment, highlighting its potential for music-driven visual design, computational art, and creative visual authoring.

title: Asymptotic behavior of solutions to the one-dimensional $p$-system with time-dependent non-smooth damping
abstract: This paper is concerned with the asymptotic behavior of solutions to the Cauchy problem for the one-dimensional $p$-system with time-dependent damping. When the damping coefficient $b(t)$ behaves like $(1+t)^{-λ}$ with $0\leλ<1$, the solutions are expected to converge to a diffusion wave. For $b(t)=(1+t)^{-λ}$, previous studies have established convergence to a diffusion wave together with convergence rates using the energy method, provided that the initial perturbation and the wave strength are sufficiently small. In this paper, we introduce two auxiliary functions and reformulate our problem into two perturbation problems adapted to the structure of the system. This enables us to prove a result analogous to those obtained in previous studies, without assuming the differentiability of $b(t)$. The auxiliary functions are given by the differential equations $1+g'(t)=b(t)g(t)$ and $1-h'(t)=b(t)h(t)$, respectively. Our result shows that it suffices to assume $b\in C([0,\infty))$, $b(t)\asymp(1+t)^{-λ}$, and $|g'(t)|\lesssim(1+t)^{-(1-λ)}$ to obtain convergence to a diffusion wave.

title: Symmetry of pole order spectra and freeness of plane curves
abstract: Let $C:f=0$ be a reduced plane curve of degree $d$ having only weighted homogeneous singularities, and let $\mathrm{Sp}_P^0(f)$ be the pole order spectrum of the top cohomology of its Milnor fiber. Writing $\mathrm{Sp}^0_P(f)=\sum_q m_q\,t^{q/d}$, we show that $m_q-m_{2d-q}=n(f)_{q-3}-n(f)_{q+d-3}$ for every integer $q$, where $n(f)_k$ is the Hilbert function of the Jacobian module $N(f)$. Consequently, $\mathrm{Sp}^0_P(f)$ is symmetric with respect to $α\mapsto 2-α$ if and only if $C$ is free. For a free curve with exponents $(d_1,d_2)$ we give a closed formula: $\mathrm{Sp}^0_P(f)-t^{-1}\mathrm{Sp}^1_P(f)$ depends only on $(d,d_1)$. This explains the symmetry of pole order spectra of reflection line arrangements, an open problem raised in Dimca's monograph on hyperplane arrangements.

title: Quantitative approximations for finite-state mean-field configuration models
abstract: We establish quantitative approximations for the empirical measures of finite-state mean-field particle systems in a general framework. The scales of the empirical drift and covariance distinguish the ODE and critical diffusion regimes and determine the corresponding time rescaling. In the ODE regime, we obtain quantitative central limit approximations in the $1$-Wasserstein distance and a Bernstein-type concentration inequality. The concentration bound has no dimensional prefactor. Its explicit time dependence also identifies growing intervals on which the ODE approximation remains accurate. In the critical regime, we prove a quantitative nonlinear diffusion approximation in the $1$-Wasserstein distance. We apply our quantitative approximation results to noisy voter systems, Moran models with mutations and selections, heat-bath Glauber dynamics for the $p$-spin Curie--Weiss model, and autocatalytic reactions with mutations.

title: Coxeter Group Symmetries of Frieze Patterns
abstract: Coxeter group symmetries of frieze patterns are investigated through their relation to $2\times n$ matrices and the associated Plücker coordinates. For odd order $n$, the symmetric group acts on the set of friezes, while for even $n$, the dihedral subgroup acts. We further show that a larger group acts when $n = 6$.

title: Phase transitions in self-gravitating objects and black holes: Common properties and interpretations
abstract: We develop a simple analytic two-component model that links the thermal evolution of self-gravitating systems to black-hole thermodynamics. The model consists of a monatomic nonrelativistic ideal gas and an effective barotropic support calibrated by the specific heat $\hat c_V^{\rm J}(Θ)$ of a Jüttner gas. From the partition function we obtain an exact modified Bessel expression for $\hat c_V^{\rm J}(Θ)$ and supply compact Padé approximants with good accuracy across all temperatures. These inputs yield a closed virial-capacity formula, which we use to determine where the heat capacity changes sign as the support pressure becomes competitive with the thermal pressure. We then contrast this behavior with Schwarzschild anti-de Sitter black holes. Despite the disparate microphysics, both systems exhibit a switch in heat-capacity behavior governed by competing pressure contributions. The surrogate model provides compact analytic insight into stability thresholds in self-gravitating systems and their black-hole analogues.

title: GeoPillars: A Large-Kernel Pillar Detector for Single-Sweep LiDAR Under Point Sparsity, and a Decomposition of Its Gain
abstract: GeoPillars is a pillar-based 3D detector for single-sweep LiDAR under a hard budget of eight points per 0.4 m pillar, a budget that discards 46.6% of in-range points. It adds geometric pillar features, grouped vector attention within each pillar, a learned absolute positional prior on the bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid, a large-kernel backbone, auxiliary surface-normal supervision and a full-resolution detection head. Trained on 123k synthetic CARLA scans and evaluated on cars, it reaches 81.33 BEV AP@0.7, 13.76 points above CenterPoint at the same input budget and 1.91 points above CenterPoint at its native, denser budget. These are in-distribution figures, because the validation split is per-frame rather than scene-disjoint. A rung-by-rung decomposition shows that the new components explain little of the gain. Raising the detection-head resolution alone recovers 10.19 of the 13.76 points, the joint change of encoder, backbone, neck and positional prior adds 3.37, and the normal-supervision branch adds 0.20, which is within run-to-run variation. With heading reversals folded out, orientation error is similar for all seven models, although GeoPillars reverses headings about half as often as a resolution-matched baseline. It is also the slowest of the seven models. Evaluated zero-shot on 6,743 real nuScenes keyframes, no model transfers, and each retains 3.7% to 12.2% of its CARLA accuracy. A collection defect left LiDAR intensity constant, so every model learned from geometry alone. Code and checkpoints are publicly available.

title: Collision-Free Is Not Enough: Passage-Conditioned Navigation for Wheeled-Legged Robots
abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10° off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.

title: From Attention to Semantics: Detecting and Mitigating Sound Event Hallucinations in Large Audio-Language Models
abstract: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) excel at diverse audio tasks, yet remain prone to hallucinating sound events absent from the input. Prior work links such hallucinations to insufficient audio attention. However, we find that real and hallucinated events can receive comparable audio attention mass while attending to different audio positions. To examine whether the attended representations support the generated events, we adapt LatentLens to retrieve neighboring contextualized text representations. The retrieved contexts reveal semantic support for real events, but a semantic mismatch between hallucinated events and their attended audio representations. Directly masking the corresponding audio regions can suppress hallucinated events at the cost of real content. We are motivated by these findings to introduce an explainable and training-free detect-then-mitigate framework for effectively hallucination detection and mitigation that aggregates semantic support and applies differential audio masking to protect regions associated with events predicted to be supported. Extensive experiments on three LALMs and two datasets demonstrate that our method significantly improves hallucination detection and hallucination mitigation performance.

title: On the Reliability of CyberGym Evaluation: Task Material Consistency and Reference-Target Identity
abstract: CyberGym evaluates vulnerability reproduction by checking whether a proof-of-concept input (PoC) crashes a vulnerable program version but not a fixed version. Interpreting this differential pass as successful reproduction requires consistent task materials and evidence that the PoC triggers the intended defect. We examine these requirements through a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of the final PoCs from one complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run. Taking the defect associated with each reference crash report as the target, the audit assigns inconsistency labels to 338 tasks (22.4%) after correcting two labels identified by stratified blind review. The largest categories are coverage inconsistency (205 tasks) and descriptions and patches that jointly point to another defect (110 tasks). We assess PoC identity using an execution check, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review. Of the 1,286 differential passes, the procedure assigns 89 non-target and 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts; requiring a target hit lowers the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%. Non-target verdicts also occur in tasks with no material inconsistency found: 39 of 1,052 differential passes (3.7%). Although the identity verdicts require independent validation, these findings motivate separate checks of task-material consistency and submission identity when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores.

title: Kernel Compensation and Quasi-Newton Iteration for Nonlinear Non-Hermitian Eigenproblems in Photonic Crystals
abstract: We extend the kernel-compensated eigensolver developed in our previous work from Hermitian to non-Hermitian nonlinear eigenproblems arising in dispersive photonic crystals. A mimetic finite-difference discretization preserves the discrete curl--divergence complex, and three-dimensional discrete Fourier transforms provide matrix-free realizations of the curl and divergence blocks. The isotropic inverse dielectric coefficient is stored through the material-edge indices, so its value and derivatives can be updated without assembling a Maxwell matrix. Kernel compensation is characterized by a fixed unitary block diagonalization, which remains exact for the nonlinear problem. At each outer step, a right Generalized Davidson iteration solves the non-Hermitian linearized eigenproblem. The exact derivative of a simple eigenvalue branch is expressed through its left and right eigenvectors. To avoid a second eigensolve, we replace the left eigenvector by the available normalized right eigenvector and obtain a right-Rayleigh quasi-Newton update. We prove that the exact left--right Newton iteration is locally quadratically convergent at simple roots, whereas the proposed iteration with exact inner eigenpairs has an explicit linear error factor and is at least quadratic when the derivative defect vanishes. A spectral regularity estimate bounds the gradient appearing in the derivative defect.

title: Current-driven resistive switching in high-field heavy fermion metal UTe2
abstract: In UTe$_2$, superconductivity persists up to 70 T for fields tilted by roughly 20-40° from the b axis toward c. Its normal state is a field-polarized (FP) state, which emerges above a first-order metamagnetic transition when the field component along b exceeds $\sim$35 T. Despite being the parent of this high-field superconductivity, the FP state remains poorly understood, including whether it shares underlying physics with the low-field paramagnetic (PM) state from which it is abruptly separated. Using microstructures fabricated by focused ion beam, we reach current densities of 30-60 kA/cm2 and observe a current-induced high-resistivity state in both the PM and FP regimes over a wide range of field angles in the bc plane. Above a critical current density of order 10 kA/cm2, the resistivity sharply rises to values comparable to those near the critical end point of the metamagnetic transition. The critical current density increases with temperature, opposite to the trend expected from Joule heating, ruling out a thermal origin. The emergence of the same instability on both sides of the metamagnetic transition reveals an unexpected commonality between the FP and PM states. More broadly, the observation of a current-induced transition in a heavy-fermion metal exposes the multitude of nearby electronic states in correlated electron systems and shows that electric current, like magnetic field and pressure, can switch between them.

title: When Safety Rationales Hallucinate: Diagnosing and Grounding Multimodal Safety Guards
abstract: Multimodal safety guards increasingly generate rationales alongside safety predictions, yet whether these rationales are reliable remains largely unexplored. We systematically study *rationale hallucination* from two perspectives: visual rationale hallucination, where rationales contain unsupported visual facts, and safety attribution hallucination, where grounded content is assigned an incorrect safety interpretation. Across rationale-generation methods, multiple vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, we find that rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently diminish with higher classification accuracy or increased model scale. Further analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows that hallucination is concentrated in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. Based on these findings, we propose *Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning* (TCG-RL), which rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference. TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance. By revealing the gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, our study motivates a shift in multimodal safety guarding from outcome-only evaluation toward safety decisions that are both accurate and verifiably grounded.

title: The distribution of greatest common divisors of binomial coefficients and their upper indices
abstract: For positive integers $n,d$, let $A_d(n)$ denote the number of integers $0\le k\le n$ such that $\gcd\bigl(n,\binom nk\bigr)=d$, and put $S_d(x)=\sum_{n\le x}A_d(n)$. We prove that, for each fixed integer $d\ge2$, \[ S_d(x)\sim\frac{d-1}{d}\,\mathfrak c\,\frac{x}{\log x}\qquad(x\to\infty),\qquad \mathfrak c=1.526453\ldots \] The key step is to extend the coprimality result of Ford and Konyagin to arbitrary fixed parameters $d\ge2$ and $1\le j<d$, obtaining \[ \#\Bigl\{m\le x:\gcd\Bigl(m,\binom{dm}{jm}\Bigr)=1\Bigr\} \sim\mathfrak c\frac x{\log x}. \] The zero set of the corresponding Kummer carry function is a finite union of intervals of total measure $1/2$. We combine this property with estimates for small prime factors, Selberg trigonometric approximation, and exponential sum estimates over primes to count simultaneous carry conditions. We further prove that, for every fixed integer $e\ge1$, \[ \#\Bigl\{m\le x:\gcd\Bigl(m,\binom{dm}{jm}\Bigr)=e\Bigr\} \sim\frac{\mathfrak c}{e}\frac x{\log x}. \]

title: Parity restoration in a sterile-neutrino scenario: bounds from atomic parity violation to the LHC
abstract: In a four-fermion-interaction scenario beyond the Standard Model (SM), in which right-handed (sterile) neutrinos take part in TeV-scale composite dynamics, the $Z$ boson acquires an energy-dependent right-handed coupling $\GR(q^2)$ that is expected to vanish at low energies and to restore parity symmetry at high energies. We derive the contribution of $\GR$ to neutral-current parity-violating observables. At first order in $\GR$, every low-energy parity-violating coupling is obtained from its SM value by the replacement $\sin^2θ_W\to\sin^2θ_W(1-\GR)$; in particular the nuclear weak charge is shifted by $ΔQ_W=4\sin^2θ_W\,Z\,\GR$, while the $Z$-pole effective mixing angle is shifted by $-\tfrac12(1-2\sin^2θ_W)\GR$. Using atomic parity violation in cesium, parity-violating electron scattering and $Z$-pole determinations of $\sin^2θ_{\rm eff}$, we extract $\GR$ at each momentum transfer. All data are consistent with $\GR=0$; at the $Z$ pole we find $\GR(m_Z)<1.1\times10^{-3}$ (95\% CL). We then use the CMS measurement of the Drell--Yan forward--backward asymmetry at dilepton masses above 170~GeV to constrain the coupling directly at TeV momentum transfer, finding $\GR<0.04$ (95\% CL) for $0.2<\sqrt{q^2}<2$~TeV. Combining both, the scale of parity restoration in a running $\GR=q^{2n}/(q^{2n}+Λ^{2n})$ must satisfy $Λ>3.8$, $2.1$ and $1.7$~TeV for $n=1,2,3$. Future MOLLER, P2 and HL-LHC data will improve these bounds.

title: How Reliable Are Explanations of Language Models That Detect Insider Threats?
abstract: Organizations monitor their workers' activity for insider threats, in which workers misuse their legitimate access, by copying confidential files before leaving. Detectors score how unusual each day of activity is, flagging the most unusual for an analyst to review. Prominent current approaches use opaque neural networks, so explanations of a flag point to internal features: patterns of neuron activity most active on days of misuse. We audit such explanations for language-model detectors trained on CERT's simulated workplace logs. To test an explanation, we see what happens to the detector's score when we remove its features inside the model. We compare this to a control: a change that is as similar as possible to the removal, but without actually removing the features. Because defining "similar" requires choosing a metric, our central contribution is the tipping radius: a first-order prediction of how far that metric must move before the difference between removal and control disappears, a measure of how fragile the result is to that choice. In 33 of 34 runs of seven language models, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard choices of metric. Moving that far removes at least 58% of the difference or reverses it, while random moves of the same size leave it largely intact. The result replicates in thirteen of fourteen pre-declared primary runs on openly released models, though on our trained detectors the difference is often too small to measure. We also find that a flag's score partly reflects who the worker is, not what they did, and that the features named depend on whom they are compared against. Audits should therefore fix the control's metric in advance, report its tipping radius, and disclose that comparison.

title: New Candidate Activity Periods from FRB 20240209A and Repeating Fast Radio Burst Sources in the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog
abstract: Repeating fast radio burst (FRB) sources with periodic activity provide important constraints on FRB models invoking neutron-star precession, rotation, or orbital modulation in binary systems. Although a few FRB sources exhibit evidence of periodic behavior, it remains unclear whether periodic activity is a common underlying feature of repeating FRBs. Using a new FRB periodicity search pipeline introduced by A. B. Pearlman et al. (2026), which is optimized for sparse event-arrival-time data from FRB surveys, we search for activity periods in the burst arrival times from FRB 20240209A and repeating FRBs in the Second Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME)/FRB Catalog. For FRB 20240209A, we identify a new candidate activity period of 170.4 $\pm$ 4.7 days, with a trials-corrected statistical significance of 5.3$σ$. Our larger burst sample shows no evidence of the 128.5-day activity period previously reported for this source by A. Pal (2025). We also report candidate activity periods of 28.46 $\pm$ 0.08 days, 86.7 $\pm$ 0.5 days, and 36.4 $\pm$ 0.5 days for FRB 20190208A, FRB 20200926A, and FRB 20220529A, with trials-corrected statistical significances of 3.1$σ$, 4.0$σ$, and 3.5$σ$, respectively. All statistical significances are evaluated against a homogeneous (constant-rate) Poisson null hypothesis, and we caution that they may decrease under null models that incorporate burst clustering. Collectively, our results constitute the most comprehensive search for periodic activity in the repeating FRB population to date.

title: Design and Validation of a Telescopic Chassis-Assisted Stair-Climbing Mechanism for Powered Wheelchairs
abstract: We propose a simple stair traversal mechanism that augments a four-wheel wheelchair with an auxiliary telescopic chassis actuator. The proposed mechanism provides the following key contributions during stair ascent: (A) enhanced safety by ensuring that either the front or rear wheels remain stationary at all times; (B) primary reliance of the required force and mechanical work on the telescopic chassis rather than the wheels; (C) insensitivity of the required force and mechanical work to stair inclination; and (D) reduced risk of wheel slip on steeper stairs. In addition, the telescopic chassis is expected to improve level-ground mobility by enabling tight turning with the shortest wheelbase and enhancing stability with the longest wheelbase.

title: Computational trust as intuitionistic knowledge
abstract: In this paper, we will argue that the notion of computational trust can be understood as a form of fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification. This approach naturally captures a key aspect of trust: it involves vulnerability. Specifically, it validates the principle that verification leads to trust but does not validate the opposite principle that trust leads to verification. Thus, we can trust on good grounds that some program will perform according to its specification but the program might still fail. We present a simple logic for capturing this notion of computational trust based on constructive modal propositional logic extended with a trust modality, which will be specified in an inferential fashion and by utilizing the proofs-as-programs correspondence.

title: Personalized Privacy-Aware MARL Offloading in the Edge-Cloud Continuum
abstract: Task offloading in End-Edge-Cloud computing enables resource-constrained User Devices (UDs) to execute computation-intensive applications with reduced latency and energy consumption. However, existing task offloading schemes generally overlook the heterogeneous privacy requirements of users, leading to inefficient privacy-aware offloading decisions. In this paper, we propose a personalized privacy-aware task offloading framework, where the privacy requirement of each task is quantified through a User-Centric Privacy (UCP) model that considers task sensitivity, user privacy preferences, and task urgency. The task offloading problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to jointly optimize the offloading ratio and the target computing server while minimizing the long-term system cost under latency, energy, and privacy constraints. To efficiently solve the resulting high-dimensional continuous optimization problem, we develop an Advantage-Weighted Actor-Critic (AWAC)-enhanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) algorithm under the Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves lower average system cost, lower energy consumption, and higher task success rate than representative baselines under diverse privacy requirements.

title: Fast and Accurate Body Estimation in Pixels, World Space and Scenes
abstract: We present FAB (Fast and Accurate Body estimation), a human body estimator that jointly improves inference efficiency and body-recovery fidelity. Rather than predicting only parametric mesh-model parameters, FAB directly predicts human skeleton joints and dense surface points. In images, it predicts dense 2D and 3D body points alongside a parametric Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, then fits SMPL in one learned pass followed by two Gauss-Newton steps. Its ViT-L student, FAB-L, distilled from a fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, runs in real time for one person on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, from detection to a fitted body, at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch body-only path, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks. The same network predicts heel, toe, hand, and knee contacts, which connect the body to the scene. FAB also estimates world-space motion, fuses static-scene depth around the visible person, and aligns body and scene using predicted contacts. For human-to-humanoid real-to-sim transfer, an in-model G1 head and FAB-Retarget, a motion-level retargeter that reads dense points or the fitted mesh, map motion to a Unitree G1. FAB-Retarget produces references that follow the person more closely than specialized retargeters including SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget, and substantially more closely than Fast SAM 3D Body retargeted with our sequence IK. Project page: https://www.jinkuncao.com/FAB.

title: World-delta: Continually Integrating Observations for Incremental 3D Scene Generation
abstract: Existing 3D generation methods synthesize visually compelling scenes from fixed inputs, yet struggle to continually expand and revise a 3D world as new observations arrive. Iterative approaches often fuse real observations and generated content into a single representation, treating generated content as established structure rather than revisable predictions. Consequently, early generation errors can persist and accumulate despite new evidence. We propose World-delta, an incremental 3D scene generation framework combining uncertainty-aware persistent world modeling with delta-guided diffusion for continual scene expansion and correction. Our framework comprises three components: 1) Visual Evidence Encoding integrates geometric and semantic cues from incoming images into unified world tokens. 2) Observation-Calibrated World Modeling maintains a persistent latent world state that distinguishes observation-supported content from provisional completion hypotheses. New evidence drives selective world deltas to revise conflicting hypotheses while preserving well-supported content. 3) Incremental World Diffusion Generation uses delta-derived masks to restrict diffusion to regions requiring updates, freezing unchanged regions. Only affected 3D chunks are decoded and integrated into the existing scene. Together, these components enable continual world expansion and revision while reducing redundant generation and preserving scene consistency. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of World-delta in incremental 3D scene generation, observation-driven correction, scene consistency, and update efficiency over successive scene updates.

title: The Atmospheric Circulation of Cloudy Hot and Ultra-hot Jupiters: the Need for Dissipation of Large-scale Flows to Reduce the Nightside Brightness Temperatures of Ultra-hot Jupiters
abstract: We perform general circulation modeling of hot and ultra-hot Jupiters across equilibrium temperatures of T_eq=1600 to 2800 K, incorporating cloud formation and its feedback on atmospheric dynamics. This study specifically examines whether clouds explain the systematically low nightside brightness observed in Spitzer thermal phase curves of ultra-hot Jupiters. We found that clouds generally increase phase-curve amplitudes and reduce eastward offsets, and these effects are most pronounced at relatively low T_eq and gradually weaken as T_eq increases. We discussed two mechanisms responsible for reducing the phase-curve offsets by clouds: the dynamical and geometric effects. Without explicit dissipation of large-scale winds, strong equatorial jets develop, maintaining a hot equatorial region and clearing clouds near the nightside equator at T_eq >= 2200 K, with thick clouds instead forming mainly at mid-to-high latitudes. These patchy nightside clouds do not sustain low nightside fluxes as temperatures rise, suggesting that clouds alone cannot explain the observed nightside brightness for ultra-hot Jupiters. Strong dissipation, parameterized as magnetic drags, suppresses equatorial jets and promotes nightside cloud coverage. In both clear and cloudy models, drag weakens the dependence of Spitzer nightside brightness temperature on equilibrium temperature; clouds further lower the nightside brightness temperature with the same drag prescription. Clouds also dampen amplitudes of thermal spectra on the nightside and, under small-particle conditions, can even produce emission features. Due to limited dayside cloud cover, our models yield negligible Bond albedos. Finally, interpreting simulated thermal phase curves with energy balance models in near-IR and IR bands tends to overestimate the Bond albedos of ultra-hot Jupiters by an order of magnitude or more.

title: The non-equilibrium state of the Galactic disk $-$ new insights from GALAH DR4
abstract: The non-equilibrium state of the Galactic disk has drawn extensive attention since ESA's \textit{Gaia} launch. Complex structure appears across a multi-parameter space of stellar abundances, ages, and kinematics. Using GALAH DR4, we investigate ridge and phase-spiral structures in chemical-abundance, phase ($v_i,x_i$), action--angle ($J_i,θ_i$), and frequency--action ($Ω_i,J_i$) spaces ($i=R,ϕ,z$). Our sample includes 333,412 disk stars with reliable chemodynamical data. In the $R$--$v_ϕ$ plane, ridges trace near-constant $J_ϕ$ tracks and show coherent variations in $θ_R$ and $θ_ϕ$. In $J_ϕ$--$J_R$, ridges are most prominent when encoded by $z_{\rm max}$ and preferentially associate with metal-rich, low-$α$ populations. In the solar neighbourhood ($R=7.2$--$9.2$\,kpc), we recover a clear phase spiral in $z$--$v_z$. Encoded in $v_ϕ$, $Ω_R$, or $Ω_ϕ$, one-armed spirals appear, whereas the $v_R$-encoded map shows a two-armed spiral. Projecting actions onto $z$--$v_z$ reveals residual spiral signatures in $J_R$ and $J_ϕ$, indicating that the phase spiral encodes in-plane orbital information. Both structures depend on age: ridges remain at similar locations with varying contrast, while the phase spiral is more tightly wound in younger and more loosely wound in older populations. Several ridges correspond in $J_ϕ$ to known moving groups, and excluding stars in all six moving-group regions makes the phase spiral less distinct in mean radial velocity maps. These links support interpreting ridges, phase spirals, and moving groups within a common phase-space dynamical framework. Combined with trends in orbital properties, age, and abundance, these findings suggest a common dynamical origin and distinct chemodynamical responses of a perturbed Galactic disk.

title: Sign-Controlled BIC Merging and Flatband Formation in C2-symmetric Photonic Lattices
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) on flatbands promise long-lived, weakly dispersive photons, yet their interplay remains elusive. Here, we develop a four-mode non-Hermitian Hamiltonian for $C_2$-symmetric photonic-crystal slabs. We show that the sign of the interpair coupling determines whether two Friedrich-Wintgen (FW) BICs and a symmetry-protected (SP) BIC occupy the same photonic band, a necessary condition for merging. In rectangular lattices, merging eliminates the quadratic radiative-loss term in a perfect-square form and strongly suppresses the quartic contribution, giving an effective $Q \sim k^{-6}$ scaling. Deviations from rectangular geometry induce noncollinear radiation polarizations, converting FW-BICs into quasi-BICs with $Q_{\mathrm{qBIC}} \sim (90^\circ-θ)^{-2}$ and restoring the asymptotic $Q \sim k^{-2}$ scaling. Unlike BIC band selection, quadratic band flattening is insensitive to the coupling sign and can occur without BIC merging, even in oblique lattices. Our results reveal distinct conditions governing BIC merging, higher-order radiation suppression, and band flattening.

title: Particle physics science communication with grass-roots Instagram: a success story
abstract: Communicating science to the public is an integral part of the work of a research collaboration, not an afterthought. Institutional and collaboration-level social media accounts are often run by professional communicators rather than by practising scientists, and single-scientist ``influencer'' accounts are demanding to sustain. We describe {\em CMSatDESY}, a crowd-sourced Instagram account on which the CMS group at DESY tells its own stories, each member in their own voice. In the first half of 2026, the science communication activities through this reached 140k+ unique accounts and received 250k+ views, with an engagement rate of 7\%. We discuss experiences and best practices that can be used by other groups, and describe how the account doubles as a science communication playground for outreach training for a large particle physics group.

title: Multi-scale dynamics of deep convective self-aggregation. Part I: physical-space structures and energy variance budget
abstract: Vertically resolved budget analyses of frozen moist static energy (FMSE) variance within a cloud-resolving model provide a rigorous perspective on the equilibrium state of deep convective self-aggregation. The analysis reveals that the variance budget is governed by a leading-order balance between vertical variance advection and the gradient term, which quantifies the coupling between vertical covariance FMSE fluxes and the mean vertical stratification. Because vertical FMSE covariance fluxes are strictly positive throughout the atmospheric column, the sign of the gradient term is entirely dictated by the vertical gradient of mean FMSE. The primary peak of variance production occurs at the boundary layer top, driven by the interplay between sharp FMSE gradients, intensified in dry regions where the moist boundary layer decouples from the dry free troposphere, and robust vertical covariance fluxes. The persistent positivity of these fluxes implies that moist (dry), high-energy (low-energy) anomalies are systematically tied to updrafts (downdrafts), regardless of the mean gradient sign. This breakdown of classical down-gradient mixing indicates that vertical transports are governed by non-local, long-distance interactions driven by large-scale overturning circulation. The large variance produced near the boundary layer top is subsequently transported upward and dissipated in the upper troposphere, where the gradient term turns into a sink. While radiation does not directly force local variance, it indirectly shapes the budget by establishing the mean stratification. Overall, local thermodynamic forcings are translated by the overturning circulation into the spatial redistribution of variance across multiple scales.

title: Language models represent more about emphasis than they can tell you
abstract: Prosodic prominence can largely be predicted from the words of a sentence, but part of it depends on how the speaker reads it. We study how much of prominence language models recover from text, whether they can report it when asked, and what the speech signal adds. On read English speech labelled for word-level prominence, we compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted large language models (LLMs) and speech models on the same words. All text models end within about one point of each other, at best 68.8% on the 3-way task, and largely make the same errors. With the prompts we tested, LLMs do no better than a word-majority baseline, even with 500 examples. Linear probes find more in their representations. Speech models reach 84.7%. We argue that text determines only part of prominence, and that the rest has to be heard. LLMs encode what the text determines, but prompting does not bring it out: they represent more about where the emphasis falls than they tell you.

title: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing
abstract: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.

title: Hard X-ray flux rope anchor points in the October 2024 X9 flare
abstract: In recent studies, signatures of non-thermal hard X-ray (HXR) emission at the anchor point of erupting flux ropes were reported, suggesting that accelerated electrons trapped in the erupting flux ropes can reach the chromosphere and produce Bremsstrahlung emission there. We investigated the HXR sources observed during the impulsive phase of the X9-class flare SOL2024-10-03T12:18 from AR 13842 and assessed whether any of the HXR sources are associated with the anchor points of the erupting flux rope. We analysed the evolution and location of the flare ribbon sources and coronal dimmings to diagnose the eruption process by using multi-vantage point data from the Solar Orbiter and Earth-orbiting instruments. We combined this with a pre-eruption non-linear force-free magnetic field extrapolation to reconstruct the initial magnetic connectivity and compare it to the observed flare ribbons and dimming locations. The magnetic field extrapolation shows two flux ropes before the flare onset. Tether-cutting reconnection during the impulsive phase of the flare results in a larger erupting flux rope formed by the reconnection of the two pre-existing flux ropes. The Spectrometer/Telescope for Imaging X-rays on Solar Orbiter observes at least four distinct HXR sources: two flare footpoints and two additional outer sources at the anchor points of the erupting flux rope. These observations corroborate earlier speculations that non-thermal electrons trapped in the erupting flux rope precipitate along the field lines into the denser chromosphere.

title: Inject Where It Matters: Objective-Dependent Feature Control in Rectified-Flow Image Editing
abstract: Many prompt-driven FLUX editing methods rely on injecting source features into target-conditioned generation, creating an inherent trade-off between source preservation and the desired edit. We address this problem by controlling where source features are injected and which transformer blocks are used. First, we introduce adaptive masks that spatially gate feature injection using differences between source- and target-conditioned block outputs at matched inversion states. Second, we use REINFORCE to select Top-K injection blocks under different preservation-editability objectives. The selected blocks are fixed at inference and require no online search. On PIE-Bench with FLUX.1-dev, spatial masking controls the alignment-preservation trade-off. On 60 validation examples, a learned nine-block set gives lower whole-image LPIPS than the 18-block RF-Edit set within the same masked pipeline, with slightly lower alignment. Among 50 random nine-block sets, it has the lowest LPIPS but not the highest reward. Separate objective sweeps reveal different block preferences for preservation and alignment.

title: Direct simulation Monte Carlo for dark matter production and phase-space evolution
abstract: To study the early-universe production of dark matter particles beyond thermal equilibrium often requires solving several coupled Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level. We present a new method to address this challenge using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) based on stochastic interactions of an ensemble of particles. We implement and validate efficient algorithms to describe freeze-out, decays, elastic scattering and number-changing processes within the dark sector. These algorithms do not require a discretisation of momentum space on a pre-defined grid and do not rely on approximations such as thermally averaged cross sections. As illustrative example, we consider a scenario with two-step dark matter production, leading to a bimodal phase-space distribution, and consider the subsequent evolution under elastic and number-changing processes. We show that DSMC is a flexible approach to explore out-of-equilibrium processes and solve Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level in order to predict the abundance of dark matter particles and their effect on structure formation.

title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.

title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
abstract: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.

title: What Places an Action Boundary? Structure-Aware Attribution for Temporal Action Localization
abstract: Temporal action localization (TAL) detectors must identify actions and estimate their temporal boundaries, but localization remains a major source of detection errors. While understanding what determines boundary placement requires faithful attribution of temporal evidence, existing attribution methods have not sufficiently addressed the temporal structure of TAL or the need to tailor attribution to boundary localization. We introduce a structure-aware attribution framework that averages contributions across random evidence-restoration orders following the Shapley-Shubik principle. We make it tractable by using the detector's receptive field to limit which time steps are ordered individually, and by approximating each order with a soft gradient path. For boundary predictions, we further introduce cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references that selectively remove adjacent evidence. We also adapt faithfulness evaluation to assess the joint effects of contiguous temporal evidence and the direction of boundary displacement. Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer demonstrate improved attribution faithfulness over existing methods. Attribution analysis and controlled interventions further reveal that class-score changes do not reliably track boundary displacement, providing input-level evidence that classification relies on content less informative about boundary placement. Code and evaluation artifacts will be publicly released.

title: Particle-vibration coupling model with explicit doorway states based on the Skyrme density functional
abstract: Modern $γ$-ray detectors can achieve energy resolutions of a few keV, motivating microscopic studies of strength fragmentation in nuclear excitation spectra. Particle-vibration coupling (PVC) describes the spreading of giant resonances, but conventional formulations based on an energy-dependent effective Hamiltonian in the 1 particle-1 hole (1p1h) space do not explicitly provide individual excited states and their wave functions. We develop a PVC model with explicit doorway states by directly diagonalising the PVC matrix in the space of 1p1h and 1p1h coupled to a phonon (1p1h$\otimesν$) configurations. Using the Skyrme energy density functional SkM*, we study the isovector giant dipole resonance (GDR) in $^{208}$Pb. The one-body transition densities show that the neutron and proton components of the dominant GDR states remain out of phase after including PVC, preserving their isovector character. Wave-function analysis reveals that the $2^+$ and $3^-$ phonons play a key role in GDR fragmentation. The fragmented states are dominated by 1p1h$\otimesν$ configurations, accounting for more than 80\% of the wave-function norm. Nevertheless, coherent contributions of 1p1h configurations preserve the collective character of the $E1$ transitions. Thus, PVC strongly modifies the microscopic structure and fragmentation of the GDR without changing its essential isovector collective character.

title: Wolff-type ideal theorems for slice regular functions
abstract: We study Wolff-type ideal problems in $H^\infty(\mathbb B)$, the algebra of bounded slice regular functions on the quaternionic unit ball. We construct $f,f_1,f_2\in H^\infty(\mathbb B)$ satisfying $|f|^2\le |f_1|^2+|f_2|^2$ such that $f^{\ast N}\notin\mathcal I(f_1,f_2)$ for every integer $N\ge1$, where $\mathcal I(f_1,f_2)$ denotes the right ideal generated by $f_1$ and $f_2$. We also construct intrinsic functions $a,a_1,a_2\in H^\infty(\mathbb B)$ satisfying $|a|\le |a_1|+|a_2|\le1$ and $a^{\ast2}\notin\mathcal I(a_1,a_2)$. For intrinsic data satisfying $|f|\le\sum_{\ell=1}^n|f_\ell|$, the cube $f^{\ast3}$ has a representation in the generated right ideal with intrinsic coefficients. For general data, we obtain sufficient conditions for ideal membership under a fourth-order pointwise bound with a Dini factor. If the generators preserve a common slice, a quadratic bound with a Dini factor suffices.

title: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
abstract: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.

title: SCCV-6D: Sparse Canonical Coordinate Voting for Holistic Multi-View RGB-D 6D Pose Estimation in Robotic Bin Picking
abstract: Industrial bin picking requires pose estimates that are accurate under clutter, partial occlusion, and the reflective, texture-less nature of manufactured parts. Most recent approaches to 6D pose estimation follow multi-stage pipelines. These achieve high accuracy, but incur memory and runtime footprints that do not cope with the operational constraints of many real-world industrial deployments. Holistic pipelines estimate poses in a single pass, with cost controlled through indiscriminate subsampling or lowered resolution. Continuing this line, we present SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D estimator. We reconstruct the 3D space at millimeter precision, prune background via a staged heatmap mechanism, and predict class, translation offset and rotation at highest resolution for an arbitrary number of objects simultaneously. Rotation is formulated as canonical coordinate voting. Points vote for their canonical object coordinates with an associated confidence, enabling closed-form pose recovery with a symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve. Along an in-cluster point recovery induced by offset votes, this removes time-consuming post-processing stages. We reuse the task-supervised attention priors from the heatmap formulation for a novel attention-gated distillation objective that reweights teacher-student feature alignment. On the IPD test split we report competitive 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene, significantly faster than the leading entries. On MV-YCB our approach reaches 96.1 ADD-S, and remains competitive even on the densely packed bins of ROBI.

title: Microscopic Probabilities for U-Statistics and Almost-Balanced Permutations
abstract: We estimate the probability that a vector of U-statistics lies within $C/n$ of a target in the range of typical fluctuations. For sufficiently large $C$, we prove a lower bound of the typical Gaussian order under finite variance, and a matching upper bound for bounded kernels. We show that under finite variance alone, stronger concentration may occur, and find the best possible asymptotic upper bound. Our proof is algorithmic, estimating probabilities by counting successful modifications produced by a random algorithm. We apply this result to settle a question of Beniamini, Lavee and Linial (2025), who asked if there exist permutations with $k$-order sub-pattern counts at most $O(n^{k-1})$ away from one another for $k>4$. We prove not only existence, but enumerate these permutations up to a constant factor, showing that there are $Θ(n!n^{-(k-1)^2/2})$ such permutations of size $n$.

title: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures
abstract: When an artificial intelligence agent pays with a stablecoin, the commerce protocol can specify the merchant, order, amount, and facilitator. The token contract enforces the fields the wallet signs. We call the difference the authority gap, define nine constraint classes, and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol. All 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code match the derivation. A controlled comparison shows that committing the terms in the signed nonce binds the order. When the facilitator submits a payment to a merchant account without code, binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Of 26,653 sampled USD Coin authorizations redeemed on Base, 98.7% followed a path that any holder of the signature could redeem. We prove sufficient conditions for a recipient contract to enforce the signed mandate under a trusted signer and show which recipient a wallet displays. MandateLock, a minimal implementation for immediate payments, rejects all 10,800 modified mandates on deployed token code and accepts signatures from two independent signers. It uses 25% more gas than a transfer that only the recipient can submit.

title: Limits of local curvature for constructing search subspaces in segmentation models
abstract: We examine how well subspaces constructed from local curvature represent the change in the gradient update field after a finite step in semantic segmentation models. The local response is the action of the curvature operator on the actual input displacement. In a study of 50 images and two models, we measure the ratio of the loss increase attained in a fixed subspace to that attained in the full space. This ratio decreases as the search radius increases. On ten images from the same sample, we compare the one-dimensional subspace spanned by the initial gradient with two rank-16 subspaces for both models. The two equal-rank subspaces are assessed at the same initial states, using the same actual steps and measured vectors. Adding generalised Gauss-Newton directions to the initial gradient reduces the mean relative error in representing the field change from 0.922 to 0.874 for the first model and from 0.819 to 0.763 for the second. At the same rank, including the response direction for the initial gradient nearly eliminates the error in representing the local response. The mean error in representing the field change does not decrease. A decomposition with fixed pixel weights shows that the finite-step remainder is comparable in norm to the field change and makes the largest diagonal contribution to the squared projection error of the field after the step. Evaluation of a search subspace should measure how accurately it represents the field change and the local response.

title: Square Kilometre Array Science Data Challenge 3b: EoR inference
abstract: We present and analyse the results of Science Data Challenge 3b (SDC3b; https://sdc3.skao.int/challenges/inference), an Epoch of Reionization (EoR) inference exercise organised by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) using simulated SKA data. The nine-month challenge, running from October 2024 to May 2025, represents the first community-wide comparison of EoR inference pipelines on common simulated datasets. We consider multiple datasets designed to assess performance on both foreground-free and foreground-contaminated cylindrical power spectra and imaging products, adopting different reionization scenarios and EoR simulation models. We include results from 16 teams, which employ a range of methodologies to infer the posterior distribution of the hydrogen neutral fraction across three redshift intervals spanning z=8.41 to z=6.25. The results show significant inter-team variability of the astrophysical constraints even in the simpler case where only instrumental noise is added to the cosmological signal. This underscores the need for further investigation into the relative contributions of signal modelling, the treatment of instrumental effects, and inference methods to the robustness of the resulting conclusions. Although individual methods can produce biased parameter estimates, the combined average of their estimates remains close to the input values, suggesting that independent approaches can offset method-specific biases.

title: Fusing Multimodal CNN Features with Structurally-Masked Transformers for Hierarchical Sub-Pixel Tree Species Mapping
abstract: Precise forest species mapping using spaceborne hyperspectral data is challenging due to high spectral similarity and the inherent sub-pixel heterogeneity of natural forest stands. While traditional deep learning models exploit spatial context through convolutional architectures, these approaches can introduce noise in fragmented or mixed-species forests. In this paper, we propose a hierarchy-aware, multimodal deep learning framework to resolve sub-pixel forest composition by integrating PRISMA (PRecursore IperSpettrale della Missione Applicativa) hyperspectral imagery, high-resolution panchromatic data, and digital elevation models. The architecture features a multi-branch encoder combining an EfficientNetV2-based one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) for spectral signatures and twin two-dimensional CNNs for spatial and topographic features, coupled with a novel structurally-masked Transformer. By using a binary transition tensor to condition the Transformer slot embeddings and constrain inference, the model enforces taxonomic consistency between broad forest categories and fine-grained species distributions. The framework is validated across three diverse Italian biogeographical regions (the Alps and the Central and Southern Apennines) using field-surveyed plots. The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multi-label and ranking-based paradigms, particularly in identifying subordinate species and their relative dominance. The bidirectional learning mechanism allows sub-pixel compositional features to refine macroscopic forest type predictions, while the integration of topographic priors effectively resolves spectral ambiguities in complex terrains. This knowledge-driven method supports regional-scale biodiversity monitoring and forest characterization within the evaluated PRISMA scenarios.

title: Structure-Guided Synthesis of Low-Error Syndrome Extraction Circuits
abstract: Gate orders can change fault propagation and logical error rates even when syndrome-extraction circuits implement the same ideal stabilizer measurements. Optimizing these orderings independently for every check, however, becomes computationally demanding as code size increases. We present a synthesis method for structured Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes that groups checks by recurring connectivity and shares one relative gate order per group, reducing independent ordering choices. A CP-SAT solver jointly determines the shared orders and the execution time of each physical gate, enforcing resource and measurement constraints across the circuit. Noisy circuit simulations with decoding then guide the selection of the final circuit. We compare with state-of-the-art approaches, including Auto-Stabilizer-Check (ASC), PropHunt, and AlphaSyndrome. Across 15 quantum low-density parity-check codes from ten code families, our method achieves the lowest logical error rate estimates. Relative to ASC, the strongest baseline in our evaluation, the median reduction is 11.4% and the largest is 38.6%. Our circuits improve circuit-level distance over ASC on ten instances and preserve the code distance in seven. Across five timed codes, our method reduces the mean time to the first feasible circuit by factors of 21.4-136.6 relative to ASC, at equal or lower depth.

title: A Sparse Low-Rank Biclique Decomposition for Graphs
abstract: Low-rank plus sparse decompositions, such as robust PCA, typically model the low-rank component as dense and the sparse component as corruption. This viewpoint is poorly suited to graph adjacency matrices, where sparsity is structural and dense low-rank factors destroy the combinatorial and computational properties of the graph. We propose signed biclique decomposition (SBD), a sparse low-rank decomposition for integer-weighted graphs that represents the structured component as a sum of sparse signed binary rank-one factors, together with a sparse signed residual. The resulting representation remains discrete, interpretable, sparse, and compatible with standard linear algebra. We formulate fixed-rank and greedy SBD objectives and derive a gain-based greedy algorithm with theoretical guarantees. Empirically, SBD recovers block structure in noisy graphs, while its factorized representation enables efficient sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (SpMM). On real graphs with strong shared-neighborhood structure, SBD achieves compression factors above $10$ and SpMM speedups up to $6\times$ over cuSPARSE, suggesting a practical alternative to dense low-rank decompositions for graphs. Code is available at https://github.com/IAntoineV/sbd.

title: Moiré-Enabled Recursive Phase Unwrapping for Differential Atom Interferometry
abstract: Weak equivalence principle tests comparing different elements may be more sensitive to violations than those comparing isotopes. However, differences in effective wave vector complicate common-mode rejection of vibration noise. We propose a Moiré-enabled recursive phase unwrapping (MRPU) method for differential measurements with dual-species atom interferometers. The method exploits the moiré structure of the joint phase likelihood and temporal acceleration correlations to unwrap both phases and determine the relative acceleration. We implemented an $^{85}$Rb $\mathrm{D_1/D_2}$ line dual-scale-factor interferometer with an identical normalized transfer function and a large effective wave-vector difference to emulate different atomic species. Under $40\,\mathrm{rad}$ equivalent vibrational noise, this method achieved phase unwrapping over 5000 consecutive measurements, with a relative-acceleration Allan deviation of $1.47\times10^{-8}g$ at 997 shots. Numerical simulations under random vibrations and slow drifts show a $9.76 - 26.03\,\mathrm{dB}$ increase in the tolerable narrowband vibration amplitude. This method is promising for weak equivalence principle tests based on different atomic species, dark matter and dark energy detection, and high-dynamic-range atomic gravimetry.

title: Helices at Twisted Ferroelectric Interfaces
abstract: We report that twisted interfaces, formed between two ferroelectric lithium niobate single crystals, contain arrays of coherently bonded and elastically deformed nanoscale structural helices, separated from one another by screw dislocations. The helices generate remarkable contrast in four dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D STEM) and through related differential phase contrast (DPC). Such images have been successfully rationalised by modelling the trajectory of electrons that channel along helical pathways as they traverse the interface, but the structural helices implied have also been directly imaged using electron ptychography. Importantly, as lithium niobate is a uniaxial ferroelectric, the torsional strain in these structural helices necessarily also causes dipolar helices to form, inferred through consideration of pertinent piezoelectric tensors and flexoelectric coefficients. Helices are topologically distinct from the more commonly reported vortices and, importantly, they are chiral. Helical (and hence chiral) character was confirmed by observing that DPC images were identical before and after the sample was inverted. Chirality was also established through second harmonic optical circularly-polarised dichroism measurements, in which unusually large interfacial signals were seen. It must be stressed that the arrays of helices observed are distinct from moiré patterns; they facilitate lattice rotation combining plastic and elastic deformation and are not simply a superposition of lattices, twisted with respect to one another. Thus, intimately bonded twisted oxide interfaces will have distinctly different characteristics from those of twisted stacks of two-dimensional van der Waals materials, opening up a new and distinct kind of twistronics.

title: Multi-scale dynamics of deep convective self-aggregation. Part II: scale-by-scale budget and mesoscale self-similarity
abstract: This work investigates deep convective self-aggregation in the space of scales, extending the physical-space analysis of Part I. We introduce a novel theoretical framework by examining and deriving a generalized Yaglom equation for the second-order structure function $\langle δh_f^{\prime 2} \rangle$, the scale-dependent variance of Frozen Moist Static Energy (FMSE). Self-aggregation is found to be sustained by an inverse energy cascade driven by boundary-layer production and mediated by mesoscale circulations with horizontal scales $r \sim$(100-250 km). The inverse cascade of energy is found to be realized through a series of shallow and mid-level mesoscale circulations which behave in a self-similar way. Accordingly, the scale-energy variance exhibits an extraordinary collapse across all atmospheric layers onto a robust self-similar power law, $\langle δh_f^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{6/5}$. In contrast, horizontal velocity increments show a degree of self-similarity ($\langle δu_r^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{2/5}$) that retains a residual height dependence. Interestingly, the FMSE scaling breaks down at elevations lower than 750 m and at small local scales below 100 km, allowing us to identify the boundary layer top as a scale-dependent dividing layer where the strong stratification filters the interactions between the surface and free-troposphere, so that small scale dynamics of the low and high atmospheric layers are decoupled while those at large mesoscale are coupled. The derived scaling laws are also used to quantify the moisture-convection feedback via scale-dependent correlation coefficients that show that vertical transport strengthens with scale ($ρ_{mc\perp} \sim r^{2/5}$), while horizontal convergence weakens at the exact inverse rate ($ρ_{mc\parallel} \sim r^{-2/5}$).

title: Regime-dependent reconstruction of structural connectivity: an in silico study of spatially constrained modular neuronal networks
abstract: Inferring structural connectivity from neuronal activity is a major challenge in neuroscience, yet the conditions under which inferred interactions faithfully reflect anatomical connections remain unclear. Here, we investigate in silico how spatial constraints in a neuronal network and its dynamical regime jointly shape structural recoverability. We construct modular networks with varying average axonal lengths and simulate spontaneous activity using the Izhikevich model with synaptic depression across a broad range of excitatory strengths and background noise levels. Using Generalized Transfer Entropy, we infer effective connectivity and compare it with the underlying structural ground-truth at the levels of individual connections and global topology.
